k: Secured: mortgage, equipment trust, collateral trust. Unsecured: debentures, subordinated, income bonds.
w: Leaves out collateral trust bonds, which pledge securities.
Debentures are unsecured.
Debentures are unsecured; ETCs are secured.
m: Debenture = unsecured.

q: From the issuing corporation's point of view, which is a DISADVANTAGE of raising capital by selling bonds instead of common stock?
o: Bondholders gain voting control of the company
Interest is a fixed legal obligation that increases financial leverage
e: Debt is cheaper and non-dilutive, but interest must be paid regardless of earnings, and heavy borrowing adds leverage, raising risk for bondholders and stockholders.
k: Debt: tax-deductible interest and no dilution, but fixed obligations and added leverage.
w: Interest is deductible; that's an advantage of debt.
Bondholders are creditors and don't vote.
Dilution comes from issuing stock, not bonds.

q: A $1,000 par convertible bond can be exchanged for 40 shares of the issuer's common stock. What is the conversion price?
e: Conversion price = par / conversion ratio = $1,000 / 40 = $25 per share.
k: Conversion price = par / conversion ratio (and ratio = par / price).
w: That is the conversion ratio (shares), not the price.
Decimal error; $1,000 / 40 = $25.
Decimal error the other way.

q: A $1,000 bond is convertible at $50 per share. The bond is trading at 96. What is the parity price of the common stock?
e: Conversion ratio = $1,000 / $50 = 20. Parity of the stock = bond price / ratio = $960 / 20 = $48.
k: Parity of stock = bond market price / conversion ratio.
w: That is the conversion price, fixed at issue.
Adds instead of computing bond price / ratio.
Divides the bond price by the conversion price; use the ratio (20).

q: A $1,000 bond is convertible at $20. The stock trades at $24 and the bond trades at $1,150. Which statement is TRUE?
o: The bond is below parity, so buying the bond and converting is cheaper than buying the stock
The bond is above parity, so converting would lose money
The bond is exactly at parity, so no advantage exists
The stock is below its parity price, so buy the stock instead
e: Ratio = 50 shares. Bond parity = $24 x 50 = $1,200. Buying the bond at $1,150 and converting delivers $1,200 of stock, an arbitrage opportunity.
k: Parity of bond = stock price x conversion ratio; bond below parity = arbitrage.
w: Parity is $1,200, above the $1,150 market price.
Parity is $1,200, not $1,150.
Stock parity is $23 ($1,150 / 50); stock at $24 is above it.

q:
A customer bought a convertible bond at par ($1,000) and converts it into 25 shares when the stock is at $48. Which of the following are TRUE?
I. The conversion is not a taxable event
II. The bond's $1,000 cost basis carries over to the shares
III. The customer must report a $200 gain at conversion
IV. The cost basis per share is $40
e: Converting is not a taxable event. The $1,000 basis carries over, giving $1,000 / 25 = $40 per share; the $200 unrealized gain is taxed only when the shares are sold.
k: Conversion: not taxable; basis carries over (basis per share = bond cost / shares).
w: Also true: basis per share is $1,000 / 25 = $40.
No gain is recognized at conversion.
Conversion is not taxable; III is false.
m: Tax comes at the sale, not at conversion.

q: The common stock of a company falls far below the conversion price of its convertible bonds. The bonds' market price will now be driven mainly by:
o: Their parity value, which tracks the stock
The conversion price, which floats with the stock
Their call price, which sets a minimum value
Their investment value as straight bonds, based on yield
e: When conversion is far out of reach, a convertible trades like an ordinary bond on its yield. This investment value acts as a bond floor.
k: Stock far below conversion price: convertible trades on investment value (bond floor).
w: Parity matters when the stock is near or above conversion price.
Conversion price is fixed except for anti-dilution adjustments.
Call price caps value; it doesn't set a floor.
m: Low stock = bond behaves like a bond.

q: All of the following are advantages to a corporation of issuing convertible bonds EXCEPT:
o: They carry a lower coupon than straight debt
Conversion eliminates the debt from the balance sheet
The issuer may force conversion by calling the bonds
e: Conversion creates new shares, which dilutes existing common stockholders. That is a drawback, not an advantage.
k: Convertibles: lower coupon and debt elimination for issuer; dilution for existing shareholders.
w: True advantage: investors accept less interest for upside.
True advantage: bonds become equity.
True advantage: a call can force conversion above parity.
m: Conversion adds shares = dilution.

q: In a corporate liquidation, which group is paid immediately BEFORE preferred stockholders?
e: Order: secured creditors, then general creditors (including debentures), then subordinated debentures, then preferred, then common.
k: Liquidation: secured > general creditors > subordinated > preferred > common.
w: They rank ahead of subordinated debt, two steps before preferred.
Common stock is paid after preferred, last of all.
Secured creditors are paid first from their collateral.
m: Sub debt is the last bond in line.

q: In a liquidation, first-mortgage bondholders are owed $10 million, but the pledged plant sells for only $7 million. How is the remaining $3 million claim treated?
o: It becomes an unsecured claim alongside the general creditors
It is forgiven once the collateral is sold
It moves ahead of all other creditors as a priority claim
It is converted into preferred stock of the company
e: Secured creditors are paid first up to the value of their collateral. Any shortfall joins the general (unsecured) creditors for the remainder.
k: Secured priority extends only to the collateral's value; any shortfall becomes a general claim.
w: The shortfall is still owed; it isn't canceled.
Only collateral value receives secured priority.
No automatic conversion; it is a general creditor claim.

q: A struggling corporation continues operating under court supervision while it restructures its debts, and its old bondholders receive new securities in the company. This process is:
e: Chapter 11 lets the company keep operating while debts are reorganized; bondholders often receive new securities, sometimes income bonds or stock.
k: Chapter 11 = reorganize and keep operating; Chapter 7 = liquidate.
w: Chapter 7 shuts down and sells assets to pay claims.
Refunding replaces debt with a new issue, outside bankruptcy.
Sinking funds retire bonds on schedule; not a restructuring.
m: 11 = keep going; 7 = close down.

q: A customer owns one bond described as "DEF 6 1/2s of '41." How much interest does she receive with each regular payment?
e: "6 1/2s" means a 6.5% coupon: $65 per year on $1,000 par, paid semiannually as $32.50.
k: Semiannual payment = (coupon % x $1,000) / 2.
w: That's the annual interest; corporates pay semiannually.
Uses the percentage as dollars; coupon is a percent of $1,000.
Divides by four; corporate interest is semiannual, not quarterly.
m: 's' after a number = coupon rate.

q: A 5% corporate bond pays interest F&A 15. A trade settles on October 3. Using 30/360, how much accrued interest does the buyer pay the seller per bond?
e: From August 15 up to (not including) October 3: 16 days in August + 30 in September + 2 in October = 48 days. $50 x 48/360 = $6.67.
k: Accrued interest = annual interest x days/360; count to the day before settlement.
w: Uses 49 days; accrual stops the day before settlement.
Uses 47 days; miscounts the August days.
Uses 60 days; counts two full months instead of stopping October 2.
m: Include the coupon date; exclude settlement date.

q: A customer buys 10 corporate bonds at 101 5/8. Ignoring commissions and accrued interest, the total cost is:
k: Bond price = quote% x $1,000; 1/8 point = $1.25.
w: Treats 5/8 as .58 of a point; 5/8 = .625.
Misplaces the decimal; 1 point = $10 per bond.
Treats 101 5/8 as 106.25; 5/8 is under one point.
m: Each 1/8 point = $1.25 per bond.

q: A broker-dealer sells a corporate bond to a retail customer from its own inventory and buys the bond the same day. What must the customer's confirmation generally disclose?
o: Nothing about compensation, since it was a principal trade
The firm's total profit on its bond inventory for the year
The dealer's markup on the transaction
The names of the parties who sold the bond to the dealer
e: FINRA rules adopted in 2018 require retail confirmations on most corporate and agency bond trades to disclose the markup or markdown when the dealer buys and sells the bond as principal the same day.
k: Same-day principal corporate/agency bond trades: retail confirmation must disclose the markup/markdown.
w: Since 2018, retail confirmations must disclose the markup.
Disclosure is trade-specific, not firm-wide profitability.
Counterparty names are not required on customer confirms.

q: A customer has $300,000 in a single-name certificate of deposit at one bank and no other accounts there. How much of the CD is NOT covered by FDIC insurance?
e: FDIC insurance covers $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. $300,000 - $250,000 = $50,000 uninsured.
k: FDIC limit: $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
w: FDIC coverage is capped at $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per category.
Uses the old $100,000 limit.
CDs are FDIC-insured bank deposits, up to the limit.
m: FDIC covers deposits; SIPC covers brokerage accounts.

q: All of the following statements about brokered CDs are true EXCEPT:
o: They are FDIC-insured, with insurance passing through to the customer
The broker-dealer guarantees full principal if the CD is sold before maturity
They can be sold in a secondary market, possibly below par
Some are callable by the issuing bank
e: Brokered CDs are FDIC-insured and may be callable, but if sold before maturity in the secondary market the price may be below par. No one guarantees principal on an early sale.
k: Brokered CDs: FDIC pass-through, may be callable, secondary-market price can be below par.
w: True: the broker arranges pass-through FDIC coverage.
True: early sales face market prices.
True: call features must be disclosed.
m: Selling early means market risk.

q: A customer buys a market-linked (structured) CD whose return is tied to a stock index. Which statement is MOST accurate?
o: The index return is guaranteed regardless of market performance
Principal protection generally applies only if the CD is held to maturity
It pays a fixed rate like a traditional CD
It can be redeemed at par at any time without penalty
e: Structured CDs tie returns to an index; principal is protected only if held to maturity. Their complexity raises suitability concerns.
k: Structured/market-linked CD: index-based return; principal protected only at maturity.
w: The return depends on the index and can be zero.
Its return is linked to an index, not fixed.
Early exit may mean selling below par or penalties.
m: Complex product = suitability red flag.

q: A Japanese corporation issues US-dollar-denominated bonds in the United States and registers them with the SEC. These bonds are:
e: Yankee bonds are dollar-denominated bonds sold in the US by foreign issuers and registered with the SEC; US investors face no currency risk.
k: Yankee bond: foreign issuer, in the US, in dollars, SEC-registered.
w: Eurodollar bonds are issued outside the US and not SEC-registered.
Eurodollar CDs are bank deposits held abroad.
Euroyen bonds would be yen-denominated, issued outside Japan.
m: Yankee = foreign company, US market.

q: Compared with a typical US domestic corporate bond, a Eurodollar bond generally:
o: Pays interest annually and is not registered with the SEC
Pays interest semiannually and is SEC-registered
Is denominated in euros and carries currency risk
Is issued in the US by a foreign corporation
e: Eurodollar bonds are dollar-denominated, issued outside the US, not SEC-registered, and usually pay interest annually, often in bearer form.
k: Eurodollar bond: USD, issued outside the US, unregistered, annual interest.
w: That describes domestic US corporates.
Eurodollar bonds are denominated in US dollars.
That describes a Yankee bond.
m: 'Euro' means offshore, not the euro currency.

q: A US company deposits $5 million in US dollars at a bank in Singapore. Which statement about this deposit is TRUE?
o: It is a domestic deposit insured by the FDIC up to $250,000
It cannot be a Eurodollar deposit because Singapore is not in Europe
It is subject to US bank reserve requirements
It is a Eurodollar deposit and is not FDIC-insured
e: Eurodollars are US-dollar deposits in banks outside the United States, anywhere in the world. They are not subject to US reserve requirements or FDIC insurance.
k: Eurodollars: USD deposits in banks outside the US; no FDIC, no US reserve requirements.
w: Dollar deposits in foreign banks have no FDIC coverage.
Eurodollars are dollar deposits anywhere outside the US.
Eurodollar deposits are outside US reserve rules.
m: Euro = outside the US, not necessarily Europe.

q: A customer in the 24% federal bracket is offered a corporate bond yielding 5.5%. To earn the same after-tax income, a municipal bond would need to yield approximately:
e: Tax-free equivalent yield = taxable yield × (1 − bracket) = 5.5% × 0.76 = 4.18%. Any muni yielding more than 4.18% beats the corporate after tax for this investor.
k: Tax-free equivalent yield = corporate yield × (1 − tax bracket).
w: Divides by 0.76 — that's the TEY formula run the wrong direction.
That's only the tax portion (5.5% × 0.24), not the after-tax yield.
Subtracts 0.26 points arbitrarily; no correct formula produces 5.24%.
m: Muni to corporate: divide. Corporate to muni: multiply.

q: A client in the 37% federal bracket is choosing between a 3.15% municipal bond and a 4.80% corporate bond of similar quality and maturity. Which statement is accurate?
o: The muni's TEY is 4.32%, so the corporate bond pays more after tax
The muni's TEY is 5.00%, so the muni pays more after tax
The corporate's after-tax yield is 3.02%, so the corporate pays more after tax
The muni's TEY is 8.51%, so the muni pays more after tax
e: TEY = 3.15% ÷ (1 − 0.37) = 3.15% ÷ 0.63 = 5.00%, which beats the 4.80% corporate. Equivalently, the corporate nets only 4.80% × 0.63 = 3.02% after tax, below the muni's 3.15%.
k: TEY = muni yield ÷ (1 − tax bracket).
w: Miscalculated TEY; 3.15 ÷ 0.63 is 5.00%, not 4.32%.
3.02% is correct, but it's below the muni's 3.15%, so the conclusion is backwards.
Divides by 0.37 instead of (1 − 0.37).
m: Compare like with like: TEY vs. taxable yield.

q: A customer bought a newly issued municipal bond at par ($1,000), collected tax-free interest for three years, then sold it for $1,060 after rates fell. How is the transaction taxed?
o: Neither the interest nor the $60 is taxable because the issuer is a municipality
The interest and the $60 are both taxed as ordinary income
The interest is taxable, but the $60 is tax-exempt
The interest was federally tax-exempt, but the $60 is a taxable capital gain
e: Only the interest on a muni is tax-exempt. Profit from selling the bond above its cost basis is a capital gain and is fully taxable.
k: Muni interest is tax-exempt; muni capital gains are taxable.
w: The exemption covers interest only, never gains on sale.
The interest is tax-exempt, and the gain is a capital gain, not ordinary income.
Reverses the rule: interest is exempt, the gain is taxed.
m: Tax-free means the coupon, not the trade.

q: Bond counsel delivers an unqualified legal opinion on a new municipal issue. This means counsel:
o: Has no reservations that the bonds are valid obligations and the interest is tax-exempt
Found the issuer's credit to be investment grade
Verified that the underwriter's pricing is fair and reasonable
Expressed concerns that must be disclosed in the official statement
e: The legal opinion addresses legality and tax status. 'Unqualified' means counsel has no reservations; a qualified opinion would raise concerns.
k: Unqualified legal opinion = no reservations on validity or tax exemption (good).
w: Credit quality is judged by rating agencies, not bond counsel.
Fair pricing is the dealer's duty under MSRB G-30, not counsel's opinion.
That describes a qualified opinion.
m: Unqualified = unconditionally clean.

q: A resident of Ohio buys a general obligation bond issued by the State of Michigan. The interest is generally:
o: Exempt from federal income tax but subject to Ohio income tax
Taxable federally but exempt from Ohio income tax
Exempt from federal, Ohio and local income tax
Subject to federal and Ohio income tax
e: Muni interest is federally exempt for everyone, but the state exemption usually applies only to residents of the issuing state. An Ohio resident owning a Michigan bond generally pays Ohio tax on the interest.
k: Federal exemption for all; state exemption usually only for in-state residents.
w: That's the Treasury pattern, the reverse of munis.
Triple exemption needs an in-state or territory bond.
The interest is still exempt from federal tax.
m: Out-of-state muni: federal-free, home-state taxable.

q: A customer insists on interest that is exempt from federal income tax. Which of the following would NOT meet that objective?
o: A Build America Bond issued by a city
A G.O. bond issued by a county
A revenue bond issued by a water authority
e: Build America Bonds are taxable municipal bonds; the issuer receives a federal subsidy instead of the investor getting a tax exemption. The other choices pay federally tax-exempt interest.
k: Taxable munis (e.g., Build America Bonds) pay federally taxable interest.
w: Standard G.O. interest is federally tax-exempt.
Ordinary revenue bond interest is federally tax-exempt.
Territory bonds are triple tax-exempt for all US investors.
m: Not every muni is tax-free — watch for 'taxable muni.'

q: An investor wants to read the official statement and recent trade prices for a school district bond she owns. Which free resource provides both?
e: The MSRB's Electronic Municipal Market Access (EMMA) site publishes official statements, continuing disclosures and municipal trade data.
k: EMMA = MSRB site for muni official statements, continuing disclosure and trade data.
w: EDGAR holds SEC filings; munis are exempt from SEC registration.
TRACE reports corporate and agency bond trades, not munis.
BrokerCheck shows firm and rep backgrounds, not bond data.
m: Munis: EMMA. Corporates: TRACE. SEC filings: EDGAR.

q:
Which of the following are TRUE of municipal securities?
I. They are exempt from registration under the Securities Act of 1933
II. They are exempt from the Trust Indenture Act
III. They are exempt from the anti-fraud provisions of federal securities law
IV. The issuer prepares an official statement instead of a prospectus
e: Munis are exempt from 1933 Act registration and the Trust Indenture Act, and use an official statement for disclosure. Anti-fraud rules apply to every security, including munis.
k: Munis: exempt from registration, never from anti-fraud rules.
w: Omits IV; the official statement is the muni disclosure document.
Includes III; anti-fraud provisions apply fully to munis.
Includes III and omits II.
m: No security is exempt from anti-fraud rules.

q: A homeowner's property is assessed at $250,000, and the town levies 12 mills to service its G.O. debt. What is the annual tax for debt service?
e: One mill is $1 per $1,000 of assessed value (0.1%). 12 mills × 250 = $3,000.
k: Property tax = assessed value × mills ÷ 1,000.
w: Divides by 10,000; a mill is 0.001, not 0.0001.
Treats a mill as 1%; it is 0.1%.
Multiplies 12 by $1,000 instead of using the assessed value.
m: 1 mill = $1 per $1,000 of assessed value.

q: An analyst reviewing a city's G.O. bonds adds in the county and school district debt that is also paid by the city's taxpayers. This added amount is called:
e: Overlapping debt is debt of other jurisdictions that share the same tax base. It matters because the same taxpayers must support all of it.
k: Overlapping debt = debt of other jurisdictions levied on the same taxpayers.
w: Net direct debt is the city's own tax-supported debt only.
Coverage ratios analyze revenue bonds, not G.O. tax burden.
A debt limit caps borrowing; it doesn't measure others' debt.
m: Same taxpayers, different issuers = overlapping.

q: All of the following are useful in evaluating a general obligation bond EXCEPT:
o: Trends in property values and population
The size of unfunded pension liabilities
An engineering feasibility study for the financed project
e: G.O. bonds are repaid from taxes, so analysis focuses on the tax base, debt burden and budget health. A feasibility study projects a single project's revenue — a revenue bond tool.
k: Feasibility study = revenue bond analysis; tax base and debt load = G.O. analysis.
w: Property values drive the ad valorem tax base for G.O.s.
Debt per capita is a core G.O. burden measure.
Unfunded pensions compete with bondholders for tax dollars.
m: G.O. = taxpayers; revenue = project.

q: A city issues bonds for its water system that are paid from water fees, with the city's taxing power pledged if fees fall short. These bonds are:
o: Moral obligation bonds, backed by a non-binding legislative pledge
Double-barreled bonds, generally rated like G.O. bonds
Special assessment bonds, backed by levies on benefited property
Industrial development bonds, backed by a corporate lease
e: Double-barreled bonds have two sources of repayment: project revenue and the issuer's full faith and credit. Because taxing power stands behind them, they are rated as G.O.s.
k: Double-barreled = revenue plus taxing power backup; rated as G.O.
w: A moral obligation pledge is non-binding; here taxing power is pledged.
Special assessments fall only on benefited properties, not general taxes.
IDBs rely on a private corporation, not city taxes.
m: Two barrels: revenue first, taxes second.

q: A bridge authority has gross revenues of $15 million and operating and maintenance expenses of $6 million. Annual debt service is $4 million ($1.5 million principal and $2.5 million interest). What is the debt service coverage ratio?
e: Coverage = net revenue ÷ annual debt service. Net revenue is $15M − $6M = $9M, and $9M ÷ $4M = 2.25 times.
k: Debt service coverage = (gross revenue − O&M) ÷ (principal + interest).
w: Uses gross revenue; expenses must be paid first.
Divides by interest only; debt service includes principal.
Divides expenses by debt service, which measures nothing useful.
m: Net revenue on top; principal plus interest on the bottom.

q: Under a typical net revenue pledge, the first use of a revenue bond project's gross revenues is to pay:
e: In the flow of funds, operations and maintenance are paid first, then debt service, then reserves, then surplus. A project that isn't kept running can't generate revenue for bondholders.
k: Flow of funds: O&M → debt service → reserves → surplus.
w: Debt service comes second, after the project is kept running.
Reserve funds are filled after debt service.
Surplus gets whatever is left at the end.
m: Keep the lights on first, then pay bondholders.

q: A toll road authority promises bondholders that it will set tolls high enough to cover operating costs and debt service. This promise is a:
e: A rate covenant obligates the issuer to charge user fees sufficient to cover expenses and debt service.
k: Rate covenant = issuer will charge fees high enough to cover costs and debt service.
w: That test limits new debt with an equal claim on revenue.
A maintenance covenant promises to keep the facility in good repair.
An insurance covenant promises to insure the facility.
m: Rate covenant = pricing promise.

q: A revenue bond indenture states that the issuer may sell new bonds with an equal claim on the project's revenues only if earnings meet a specified coverage level. This protects existing bondholders and is known as:
e: The additional-bonds test keeps the issuer from diluting existing bondholders' claim on revenue unless coverage is adequate.
k: Additional-bonds test limits new parity debt to protect existing holders.
w: That covenant bars free service to favored users, not new debt.
A rate covenant sets fee levels, not limits on new bonds.
Flow of funds sets the order revenues are applied.
m: New debt with equal claim? Check the additional-bonds test.

q: Which statement about a moral obligation bond is accurate?
o: If project revenues fall short, the state legislature may, but is not legally required to, appropriate funds
The state's full faith and credit is legally pledged as backup to project revenues
It is repaid solely from a dedicated tax such as a gasoline or hotel tax
It is backed by the US government and considered the safest municipal bond
e: A moral obligation bond is a revenue bond with a non-binding promise that the legislature may step in. The backup is moral, not legal.
k: Moral obligation = non-binding legislative backup; requires a vote to appropriate.
w: A legally binding tax pledge describes a double-barreled bond.
That describes a special tax bond.
That describes public housing authority (PHA/NHA) bonds.
m: 'Moral' means no legal obligation.

q: A county issues industrial development revenue bonds to build a plant leased to a manufacturer. The bonds' credit quality depends primarily on the:
o: State legislature's willingness to appropriate funds
Manufacturer's ability to make its lease payments
Federal guarantee on the plant's mortgage
e: IDRs are repaid from the private corporation's lease payments, so their credit is essentially the corporation's credit. They are private activity bonds, often subject to AMT.
k: IDR credit = the private corporate lessee's credit; usually AMT bonds.
w: The county does not pledge taxes on an IDR.
That's the moral obligation feature, not an IDR.
IDRs have no federal guarantee.
m: IDR: municipal name, corporate risk.

q: Which type of municipal bond is considered the safest because it is ultimately backed by the US government?
e: PHA/NHA bonds are backed by the US government, making them the safest municipal bonds.
k: PHA/NHA bonds: US government backed, the safest munis.
w: Moral obligation backup is non-binding, so they're riskier.
Special tax bonds depend on one tax source's collections.
COPs rely on lease appropriations and avoid voter approval.
m: PHA = federal backing.

q: A town must meet payroll this month but won't collect its semiannual property taxes for four more months. To bridge the gap, it would most likely issue:
e: TANs are short-term notes repaid from upcoming tax collections, bridging the gap between spending and tax receipts.
k: TAN = repaid from future tax collections.
w: BANs are repaid from a future long-term bond sale.
GANs are repaid from expected federal or state grants.
CLNs fund housing construction until permanent financing.
m: Name the money coming in: tax, revenue, bond or grant.

q: A state transportation department will receive federal highway funds next year and borrows short-term now against that money. The notes are:
e: GANs are repaid from expected federal or state grant money.
k: GAN = repaid from expected federal/state grants.
w: TANs rely on the issuer's own tax collections.
BANs rely on a future long-term bond issue.
CLNs fund housing construction, repaid from permanent financing.

q: Which feature of a variable-rate demand obligation (VRDO) allows it to be treated as a money-market instrument even though its stated maturity is long-term?
o: A put allowing holders to tender at par on reset dates
A call allowing the issuer to redeem after 10 years
A sinking fund that retires bonds annually
A fixed coupon guaranteed by bond insurance
e: VRDO rates reset daily or weekly, and the demand (put) feature lets investors sell back at par on reset dates, giving short-term liquidity.
k: VRDO = periodic rate reset plus put at par on reset dates.
w: A call benefits the issuer and adds no short-term liquidity.
Sinking funds retire debt but don't give holders a par exit.
VRDOs float; they don't pay a fixed coupon.
m: VRDO: 'demand' means the holder can demand par.

q: Moody's uses which rating scale specifically for short-term municipal notes?
e: Moody's rates municipal notes MIG 1–3 (VMIG for variable-rate demand notes). S&P's municipal note scale is SP-1 to SP-3.
k: Moody's muni notes: MIG 1–3 (VMIG for VRDOs); S&P: SP-1 to SP-3.
w: That's Moody's long-term bond scale.
Prime ratings are Moody's commercial paper scale.
That's S&P's note scale, not Moody's.
m: MIG = Moody's Investment Grade (notes).

q: A municipal syndicate has more orders than bonds. Under the usual priority, which type of order is filled LAST?
e: Standard priority is pre-sale, then group net, then designated, then member orders. Member orders benefit only the placing member, so they come last.
k: Muni order priority: pre-sale → group net → designated → member.
w: Pre-sale orders, taken before the award, are filled first.
Group net orders come second, benefiting the whole syndicate.
Designated orders come third, ahead of member orders.
m: Memory aid: 'Please Go Down Memory lane.'

q: A hospital revenue authority picks one underwriting firm and works out the bond's interest rates and price directly with it. This is a:
o: Negotiated underwriting, typical for revenue bonds
Competitive sale awarded on lowest net interest cost
Competitive sale announced through a notice of sale
Private placement exempt from MSRB rules
e: In a negotiated sale the issuer selects an underwriter and negotiates terms, the usual method for revenue bonds. Competitive sales use a notice of sale and award to the best bid.
k: Negotiated sale = issuer picks underwriter; typical for revenue bonds.
w: Competitive sales award to the lowest-cost bidder, not a chosen firm.
A notice of sale invites competing bids, the opposite of choosing a firm.
Dealers in a private placement still follow MSRB rules.
m: G.O. → competitive; revenue → negotiated.

q: A dealer sells a municipal bond to a customer. Within what time frame must the trade generally be reported to the MSRB's RTRS?
e: Municipal trades are reported to the MSRB's Real-Time Transaction Reporting System within 15 minutes and then displayed on EMMA.
k: Muni trades: report to RTRS within 15 minutes.
w: Ten seconds is the equity tape standard, not muni reporting.
End-of-day reporting would not be real-time.
Settlement timing is separate from trade reporting.
m: RTRS = 15 minutes; then shown on EMMA.

q: A municipal bond with a 6% coupon pays interest January 1 and July 1. A customer buys $1,000 par in a regular-way trade on Tuesday, March 9. How much accrued interest does the buyer pay the seller?
e: Regular-way settlement is T+1, Wednesday, March 10. Using 30/360, interest accrues from January 1 up to but not including March 10: 30 + 30 + 9 = 69 days, so $60 × 69/360 = $11.50.
k: Muni accrued interest = annual interest × 30/360 days to (not including) settlement.
w: Uses actual/365 (68 days), the Treasury convention.
Counts only to trade date (68 days) instead of settlement.
Counts 70 days by including the settlement date.
m: Accrue to settlement, not trade date; munis use 30/360.

q: Under MSRB Rule G-20, the most a municipal securities representative may give in gifts to a person, in connection with that person's employer's business, per year is:
e: MSRB G-20 now caps gifts at $300 per person per year, matching FINRA Rule 3220. Ordinary business entertainment is excluded from the limit.
k: MSRB G-20 and FINRA 3220 gift limit: $300 per person per year.
w: $100 was the old limit before the 2026 increase.
$250 is the G-37 political contribution limit, not gifts.
No gift rule sets a $500 limit.
m: Gifts $300; G-37 contributions $250.

q: A municipal finance professional who lives in Connecticut contributes $150 to the campaign of a New York City mayoral candidate. If the candidate wins, under MSRB Rule G-37 the MFP's firm:
o: Is barred from negotiated underwriting with the city for two years
Must report the gift but may continue all business with the city
Is unaffected because the contribution is under $250
Is permanently barred from all municipal business with the city
e: The $250 de minimis applies only to candidates the MFP is entitled to vote for. A Connecticut resident can't vote in a New York City election, so any contribution triggers the two-year ban on negotiated business.
k: G-37: $250 per election only if MFP can vote for candidate; else two-year ban.
w: Reporting doesn't cure a ban-triggering contribution.
The $250 exception requires that the MFP be eligible to vote for the candidate.
The ban lasts two years and covers negotiated business, not permanently.
m: Can't vote for them? Any amount triggers the ban.

q: A customer buys a municipal bond in the secondary market at 92. It was originally issued at par, and she holds it to maturity. How is the 8-point discount taxed?
o: As tax-exempt interest, like original issue discount
It is not taxed because the issuer is a municipality
e: A market discount on a muni bought in the secondary market is taxed as ordinary income when realized. Only original issue discount accretes tax-free.
k: Muni market discount = ordinary income; muni OID = tax-exempt accretion.
w: Only original issue discount is treated as tax-exempt interest.
Market discount is taxed as ordinary income, not capital gain.
The exemption covers coupon interest and OID, not market discount.
m: Discount at issue = tax-free; discount bought later = taxable.

q: A customer buys a municipal bond at 108 and holds it until it matures at par. What is the tax result?
o: An 8-point capital loss deductible at maturity
An 8-point ordinary loss spread over the bond's life
No gain or loss, because the amortized premium lowered her cost basis to par
A capital gain because the bond paid tax-exempt interest
e: Muni premiums must be amortized, reducing cost basis to par by maturity. Because the interest is tax-free, the amortization isn't deductible, so there's no loss at maturity.
k: Muni premium: must amortize; basis falls to par; no deductible loss.
w: Amortization eliminates the loss; nothing is left to deduct.
Muni premium amortization isn't deductible at all.
Redeeming at an amortized basis of par produces no gain.
m: Muni premium held to maturity = no loss to claim.

q: For which customer would individual municipal bonds be MOST suitable?
o: A 30-year-old seeking long-term growth in a Roth IRA
A retiree in the 12% bracket who wants the highest after-tax income
A couple in the 35% bracket seeking income in a taxable brokerage account
A 401(k) participant choosing a conservative fund option
e: Munis fit high-bracket investors seeking tax-free income in taxable accounts, where the exemption has real value.
k: Best muni buyer: high tax bracket, wants income, taxable account.
w: Growth seeker in a tax-free account wastes the exemption.
Low brackets usually net more from taxable bonds.
401(k) earnings are already tax-deferred, so the exemption is wasted.
m: High bracket + taxable account + income = munis.

q: Congress debates a proposal to cap the federal tax exemption on municipal bond interest, and muni prices fall. This illustrates:
e: Legislative risk is the danger that a change in law, such as the tax code, reduces a security's value. Munis are vulnerable because their appeal rests on the exemption.
k: Legislative risk: a law change (e.g., tax code) reduces a security's value.
w: Nothing about the issuer's ability to pay has changed.
Call risk is early redemption when rates fall.
Reinvestment risk is reinvesting cash flows at lower rates.
m: Tax-law change → legislative risk.

q: A customer owns $15,000 of a small, rarely traded water district bond and may need to sell on short notice. Which risk is her greatest concern?
e: The muni secondary market is thin, and many small issues rarely trade. Selling a small block quickly may require a price concession.
k: Munis carry liquidity risk because of a thin secondary market.
w: Inflation risk exists but isn't tied to needing a quick sale.
No tax law change is involved in this scenario.
Prepayment risk applies mainly to mortgage-backed securities.
m: Thin market + quick sale = liquidity risk.

q: A customer in a high federal bracket has $20,000 to invest and wants tax-free income with diversification. The most suitable recommendation is:
o: A single long-term municipal revenue bond
e: A muni bond fund or ETF provides tax-free income and diversification to an investor who can't buy enough individual bonds to diversify.
k: Muni funds/ETFs: tax-free income plus diversification for smaller investors.
w: One bond gives no diversification.
STRIPS interest is federally taxable and pays no current income.
Corporate bond interest is fully taxable.

q: An individual submits a non-competitive bid at a 26-week T-bill auction. Which statement is TRUE?
o: She names the lowest yield she will accept, and the bid may go unfilled
Her bid is filled only after all competitive bids are satisfied
She accepts the yield set at the auction, and her bid is filled first
She must submit the bid through a primary dealer
e: Non-competitive bidders agree to accept the auction's yield and are always filled before competitive bidders.
k: Non-competitive bid: accepts auction yield; filled first.
w: Naming a yield is what competitive bidders do.
Non-competitive bids are filled first, not last.
Individuals can bid through TreasuryDirect or any broker.
m: Non-competitive = guaranteed fill, take the auction rate.

q: A Treasury bill is quoted 4.10 bid, 4.05 ask. Which statement is correct?
o: The ask price is lower than the bid price because 4.05 is less than 4.10
The quote is in 32nds, so the ask price is $1,000.50
The bill pays a coupon of 4.05% at maturity
The bid yield is higher, so the bid price is lower than the ask price
e: T-bills are quoted on a discount yield basis. A higher discount means a lower price, so the 4.10 bid corresponds to a lower dollar price than the 4.05 ask, as dealers expect.
k: T-bills are quoted by discount yield: higher number = lower price.
w: Backwards: for bills a lower yield means a higher price.
Only Treasury notes and bonds are quoted in 32nds.
Bills pay no coupon; they're bought at a discount and mature at par.
m: Bills: yields quoted, so bid number > ask number.

q: A Treasury note is quoted at 101-20. What is the dollar price per $1,000 par?
e: Treasury notes are quoted in 32nds. 101-20 = 101 20/32 = 101.625% of par = $1,016.25.
k: Treasury price = (points + 32nds ÷ 32)% × $1,000.
w: Reads 20/32 as 0.20 of a point.
Reads the 20 as 2.0 points.
Uses 100 points instead of 101 before adding 20/32.
m: Each 32nd = $0.3125 per $1,000 bond.

q: An investor holding a 30-year Treasury bond faces all of the following risks EXCEPT:
e: Treasuries are backed by the full faith and credit of the US and are considered free of default risk. They still carry interest-rate, inflation and reinvestment risk.
k: Treasuries: no credit risk, but interest-rate, inflation and reinvestment risk.
w: Long Treasuries are highly sensitive to rate changes.
Fixed coupons lose purchasing power as prices rise.
Coupons may be reinvested at lower rates.
m: Risk-free means credit-risk-free, not risk-free.

q: New US Treasury securities are issued:
o: In book-entry form only, in denominations as small as $100
As registered certificates in minimum denominations of $1,000
In bearer form, in minimum denominations of $5,000
In book-entry form, in minimum denominations of $10,000
e: Treasuries are issued only in book-entry form with a $100 minimum denomination.
k: Treasuries: book-entry only, $100 minimum.
w: No physical certificates are issued, and the minimum is $100.
Bearer bonds are no longer issued in the US.
The minimum denomination is $100, not $10,000.

q: A customer buys $1,000 of TIPS with a 1.5% coupon. Over the next year the CPI rises 4%. What is the annual interest based on the adjusted principal?
e: TIPS principal adjusts with CPI: $1,000 × 1.04 = $1,040. The fixed 1.5% coupon rate applies to the adjusted principal: $1,040 × 1.5% = $15.60.
k: TIPS interest = fixed coupon rate × CPI-adjusted principal.
w: Uses the original principal, ignoring the inflation adjustment.
That's the principal increase, not interest.
Adds the CPI change to the coupon rate; TIPS adjust principal.
m: TIPS: rate fixed, principal floats with CPI.

q: Because of deflation over its life, a $1,000 TIPS has an inflation-adjusted principal of $980 at maturity. The investor receives:
o: $980 plus a deflation credit set by the Treasury
e: At maturity a TIPS holder receives the greater of the adjusted principal or the original principal, so deflation can't push the redemption below $1,000.
k: TIPS at maturity: greater of adjusted or original principal.
w: The original principal is protected at maturity.
Deflation doesn't create a bonus above par.
No separate deflation credit exists; the floor is original par.
m: TIPS principal floor = original par, at maturity only.

q: Which tax consequence is a disadvantage of holding TIPS in a taxable account?
o: The annual inflation increase to principal is taxed in the year it occurs, though not received until maturity
Interest is taxed at the state level but exempt federally
The entire return is taxed as a capital gain at maturity
Interest is subject to the alternative minimum tax
e: The yearly inflation adjustment is taxable as income even though the investor doesn't receive it until maturity, creating 'phantom income.' That's why TIPS are often held in tax-deferred accounts.
k: TIPS principal increases are taxed annually as phantom income.
w: Reversed: Treasury interest is federally taxable, state-exempt.
Interest and inflation adjustments are taxed annually as income.
AMT applies to some private activity munis, not Treasuries.
m: Phantom income: TIPS and zeros.

q: Which zero-coupon security is a direct obligation of the US Treasury?
e: STRIPS are backed directly by the Treasury. Treasury receipts such as CATS and TIGRs are created by broker-dealers and collateralized by Treasuries held in trust, but aren't direct Treasury obligations.
k: STRIPS = direct Treasury zeros; Treasury receipts = dealer-created, not direct obligations.
w: TIGRs are a broker-dealer-created Treasury receipt.
CATS are a broker-dealer-created Treasury receipt.
Receipts are only collateralized by Treasuries held in trust.
m: Only STRIPS carry the Treasury's direct backing.

q: If interest rates rise sharply, which Treasury security will likely fall the most in price?
e: Price sensitivity is greatest with long maturity and low (zero) coupon. A 30-year STRIPS has both, so it moves the most.
k: Most rate-sensitive Treasury: long-term STRIPS (long maturity, zero coupon).
w: FRNs reset weekly and have minimal rate risk.
Shorter maturity means less price sensitivity.
Same maturity, but its coupons reduce duration versus a zero.
m: Longest and lowest coupon = most volatile.

q: A client wants to sell her Series EE savings bonds through her brokerage account. The rep should explain that:
o: They can be sold in the OTC market at prevailing prices
They must be sold through a primary dealer
They can be sold only after 30 years
They are non-negotiable and can only be redeemed with the Treasury
e: Savings bonds are non-negotiable: they cannot be sold or transferred in the market, only redeemed through the Treasury.
k: Savings bonds (EE, I) are non-negotiable; redeem, don't sell.
w: Savings bonds have no secondary market.
Primary dealers trade marketable Treasuries, not savings bonds.
They can be redeemed before 30 years; they just can't be sold.
m: Savings bonds: no secondary market.

q: A Treasury security with a 2-year maturity whose interest rate resets weekly based on the 13-week T-bill auction rate is a:
e: Treasury FRNs have 2-year maturities and rates that reset weekly to the 13-week bill rate, giving them minimal interest-rate risk.
k: Treasury FRN: 2-year, resets weekly to 13-week T-bill rate.
w: TIPS adjust principal for CPI, not the coupon for bill rates.
I bonds add an inflation component and are non-marketable.
STRIPS pay no periodic interest at all.

q: Which statement about mortgage-backed securities issued by Fannie Mae is accurate?
o: They carry the explicit full faith and credit of the US government
Their interest is exempt from state and local income tax
They are issued by an agency within HUD
Fannie Mae is a GSE, and its MBS have only implied government backing
e: Fannie Mae is a publicly traded GSE (in conservatorship since 2008). Its MBS are not legally backed by the government, and their interest is taxable at all levels.
k: Fannie and Freddie MBS: implied backing only; taxable at all levels.
w: Only Ginnie Mae carries full faith and credit backing.
Fannie/Freddie MBS interest is taxed at federal, state and local levels.
That describes Ginnie Mae, not Fannie Mae.
m: Ginnie = government; Fannie and Freddie = GSEs.

q: A customer in a high-tax state wants agency debt whose interest is exempt from state income tax. Which security fits?
e: Federal Home Loan Bank and Farm Credit debt pays interest that's federally taxable but state-exempt. Mortgage-backed agency securities are taxable at every level.
k: FHLB and Farm Credit interest: state-exempt; agency MBS: taxable at all levels.
w: GNMA interest is taxable at all levels.
FNMA MBS interest is taxable at all levels.
CMOs are taxable at all levels.
m: Mortgage-backed = taxed everywhere.

q: A customer bought a mortgage pass-through expecting an 8-year average life. Interest rates then rise sharply. What is the most likely result?
o: Prepayments slow and the average life lengthens
Prepayments accelerate and the average life shortens
The issuer must call the certificates at par
Monthly payments switch from principal-and-interest to interest only
e: When rates rise, homeowners don't refinance, so prepayments slow and the security stays outstanding longer — extension risk.
k: Rising rates → slower prepayments → extension risk.
w: That happens when rates fall (prepayment risk).
Pass-throughs aren't called by the issuer when rates rise.
Principal still passes through with every monthly payment.
m: Rates up: extension. Rates down: prepayment.

q: In a CMO, which tranche absorbs most of the prepayment variability so that the planned amortization class (PAC) tranche can have a predictable cash flow?
e: PAC tranches get the most predictable cash flows because companion (support) tranches absorb excess or deficient prepayments.
k: PAC = most predictable; companion/support tranche absorbs prepayment risk.
w: Z-tranches accrue interest like zeros; they don't serve as PAC buffers.
IO strips are a different structure, not the PAC's support.
Sequential tranches receive principal in order; they don't protect PACs.
m: Companions protect PACs and take the volatility.

q: A Ginnie Mae holder receives a monthly payment of $640, of which $500 is interest and $140 is return of principal. How much is taxable, and at what levels?
o: $140, at the federal, state and local levels
$500, at the federal, state and local levels
e: Only the interest portion of a pass-through payment is income; return of principal isn't taxed. GNMA interest is taxable at federal, state and local levels.
k: GNMA: interest taxable at all levels; principal portion is a nontaxable return of capital.
w: Principal returned is not income, and the state also taxes GNMA interest.
Treats GNMA like Treasuries; GNMA interest is also state-taxable.
The $140 is return of principal, not income.
m: Full government backing doesn't mean a state exemption.

q: Large banks and broker-dealers approved to bid at every Treasury auction and to trade directly with the Fed in open-market operations are called:
e: Primary dealers are approved by the Fed to bid in every Treasury auction and to serve as counterparties in open-market operations.
k: Primary dealers: bid at every Treasury auction; Fed's open-market counterparties.
w: Market makers quote securities generally; Fed approval isn't required.
Broker's brokers serve dealers, mainly in munis.
DMMs manage NYSE-listed stocks.

q: A 10-year corporate bond yields 6.10% while the 10-year Treasury yields 4.30%. The 180-basis-point difference mainly compensates investors for:
e: With the same maturity, the yield spread over Treasuries reflects the corporate's credit (default) risk, since Treasuries have none.
k: Spread over same-maturity Treasury = compensation for credit risk.
w: Both bonds pay coupons and share reinvestment risk.
Inflation hits both bonds; it's priced into the Treasury too.
Equal maturities share similar interest-rate risk.
m: Same maturity, different issuer: the spread is credit risk.

q: Which yield is the primary benchmark for 30-year fixed mortgage rates?
e: The 10-year Treasury yield is the benchmark for mortgage rates and corporate bonds. The 3-month bill serves as the 'risk-free rate' in financial models.
k: 10-year Treasury = benchmark for mortgage and corporate rates.
w: The 3-month bill is the model risk-free rate, not the mortgage benchmark.
Fed funds affects the short end, not long mortgage pricing.
Prime drives many consumer loans, not 30-year mortgages.

q: Besides the seven Fed governors, which official holds a permanent voting seat on the FOMC?
o: The president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York
The chair of the House Financial Services Committee
e: The FOMC's 12 voting members are the 7 governors, the NY Fed president (always) and 4 regional Fed presidents on a rotating basis.
k: FOMC = 7 governors + NY Fed president + 4 rotating regional presidents.
w: The Fed is independent of the Treasury in setting policy.
The OCC regulates national banks; it has no FOMC seat.
Congress sets fiscal policy and doesn't vote on the FOMC.
m: The NY Fed runs open-market operations, hence the permanent seat.

q: The Federal Reserve's dual mandate is to pursue:
o: A strong dollar and a trade surplus
Low interest rates and rising stock prices
e: Congress gave the Fed a dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices (controlling inflation).
k: Fed dual mandate: maximum employment + stable prices.
w: Budgets and taxes are fiscal policy (Congress and the President).
Currency and trade balance aren't part of the mandate.
The Fed doesn't target permanently low rates or stock prices.

q: A customer's $50,000 balance in a retail money market fund is counted in which money supply measure?
e: M1 is currency plus checking (and, since 2020, savings) deposits. M2 adds small time deposits and retail money market funds, so a retail MMF counts in M2 but not M1.
k: M2 = M1 + small time deposits + retail money market funds.
w: Money market funds aren't part of M1.
Retail MMFs are added at the M2 level, not in M1.
Retail MMFs are specifically included in M2.
m: M1 = spendable cash; M2 adds near-money.

q:
Which of the following are likely effects of an easy (expansionary) monetary policy?
I. Lower short-term interest rates
II. A stronger US dollar
III. Increased borrowing and spending
IV. Rising bond prices
e: Easy money lowers rates, which raises bond prices and encourages borrowing. Lower rates tend to weaken the dollar, not strengthen it.
k: Easy money: rates down, bond prices up, borrowing up, dollar tends to weaken.
w: Omits IV; falling rates raise bond prices.
Includes II; lower rates tend to weaken the dollar.
Includes II; a stronger dollar follows higher rates.
m: Rates and bond prices move opposite.

q: Which of the following rates is set directly by the Federal Reserve?
e: The Fed directly sets the discount rate it charges member banks at the discount window. The fed funds rate is market-determined within the FOMC's target range.
k: Discount rate = set directly by the Fed; fed funds = market rate the FOMC targets.
w: The FOMC sets only a target range; banks set the actual rate.
Commercial banks set prime for their best corporate customers.
Banks set the rate they charge broker-dealers.
m: Fed sets discount; targets fed funds.

q: The interest a broker-dealer charges customers on margin debit balances is typically based on the:
e: The broker call (call money) rate is what banks charge broker-dealers for loans financing customer margin accounts; firms add a markup when charging customers.
k: Broker call rate = bank loans to BDs financing margin accounts.
w: The discount rate applies to Fed loans to member banks.
Prime is for banks' best corporate customers.
Fed funds is for overnight loans between banks.
m: Margin interest = broker call rate + markup.

q: Which benchmark, published by the New York Fed from repo transactions, replaced LIBOR for most floating-rate products?
e: The Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), based on Treasury repo transactions, replaced LIBOR as the main floating-rate benchmark.
k: SOFR (NY Fed, repo-based) replaced LIBOR.
w: Prime is set by commercial banks for their best borrowers.
The FOMC sets a target range, not a repo-based benchmark.
That rate sets Treasury FRN coupons, not a LIBOR replacement.

q: If US interest rates rise significantly, which outcome is most likely?
o: The US dollar weakens as foreign capital leaves
Utility stocks outperform the broad market
The US dollar strengthens as foreign capital flows in
e: Higher US rates attract foreign investment, increasing demand for dollars. Rising rates also push bond prices down and hurt rate-sensitive sectors like utilities.
k: Higher US rates → foreign capital inflow → stronger dollar.
w: Higher rates draw capital in, not out.
Utilities are rate-sensitive and tend to lag when rates rise.
Bond prices fall when rates rise.

q: Which Federal Reserve tool is considered the most powerful but is the least frequently used?
e: Changing reserve requirements has a sweeping effect on bank lending, so it's rarely used; the ratio has been 0% since 2020.
k: Reserve requirements: most powerful, least used (0% since 2020).
w: Open-market operations are the most frequently used tool.
The discount rate mostly signals intent and is adjusted more often.
Interest on reserves is a modern primary tool used routinely.
m: Most used: OMO. Least used: reserve requirements.

q: To fight rising inflation, the Federal Reserve could take all of the following actions EXCEPT:
o: Selling Treasuries in the open market
e: Fighting inflation calls for tightening. Lowering reserve requirements frees banks to lend more, which is an easing move.
k: Tighten: sell securities, raise discount rate, raise reserves and interest on reserves.
w: Selling securities drains reserves — a tightening move.
A higher discount rate makes borrowing costlier — tightening.
Higher interest on reserves pushes fed funds up — tightening.
m: Sell = soak up money.

q: With short-term rates already near zero, the Fed buys large amounts of long-term Treasuries and MBS to push long-term rates lower. This is called:
e: Quantitative easing is large-scale buying of long-term securities to lower long rates when short rates can't go much lower.
k: QE = large-scale long-term bond purchases; QT = letting holdings run off.
w: QT shrinks the Fed's holdings — the opposite.
A reverse repo temporarily drains reserves.
Raising reserve requirements tightens credit.

q: To drain reserves from the banking system temporarily, the Fed's open-market desk would use:
e: In a reverse repo the Fed sells securities with an agreement to buy them back, temporarily taking cash out of the system. A repo is a temporary purchase that adds reserves.
k: Fed repo = temporary buy (adds reserves); reverse repo = temporary sale (drains).
w: A repo is a temporary purchase, which adds reserves.
Outright purchases add reserves permanently.
Discount loans add reserves to the borrowing bank.
m: From the Fed's view: repo buys, reverse repo sells.

q: Cars built at a Japanese-owned assembly plant in Kentucky are counted in:
o: Neither US GDP nor US GNP
e: GDP counts all output produced within US borders regardless of ownership. GNP counts output of US-owned entities anywhere.
k: GDP = output within the US; GNP = output of US-owned entities anywhere.
w: GNP counts US-owned producers; this plant is Japanese-owned.
Japan's GDP counts only production inside Japan.
Production on US soil is always in US GDP.
m: GDP: where it's made. GNP: who owns it.

q: A recession is commonly defined as:
o: Two consecutive months of rising unemployment
Two consecutive quarters of declining real GDP
Six consecutive quarters of declining GDP
e: The common definition of a recession is two consecutive quarters of declining GDP; the NBER officially declares recessions.
k: Recession = 2 straight quarters of declining GDP (NBER declares).
w: Unemployment is a lagging indicator, not the definition.
Six-plus quarters describes a depression.
A 20% stock drop defines a bear market, not a recession.
m: Recession = 2 quarters; depression = longer and deeper.

q: All of the following are lagging economic indicators EXCEPT:
o: Average weekly hours worked in manufacturing
e: Average weekly manufacturing hours is a leading indicator; employers adjust hours before hiring or firing. The others change after the economy turns.
k: Lagging: unemployment duration, CPI, prime rate, corporate profits, consumer debt.
w: Unemployment duration lags the cycle.
CPI/inflation is a lagging indicator.
Banks change prime after conditions shift — lagging.
m: Hours change before headcount — leading.

q: Which economic indicator generally moves at the same time as the overall economy?
e: Coincident indicators — GDP, industrial production, personal income, nonfarm payrolls — move with the economy.
k: Coincident: GDP, industrial production, personal income, nonfarm payrolls.
w: Jobless claims are a leading indicator.
Corporate profits are a lagging indicator.
The stock market is a leading indicator.

q: An economy with little or no growth, high unemployment and rising prices is experiencing:
e: Stagflation combines stagnant growth with high inflation.
k: Stagflation = stagnant growth + high inflation.
w: Deflation is falling prices, not rising ones.
An expansion has growth, not stagnation.
A trough is the low point of the cycle, not a price condition.
m: Stag (no growth) + flation (rising prices).

q: During a recession, Congress passes and the President signs a broad tax cut along with new infrastructure spending. This is an example of:
e: Fiscal policy is taxation and spending set by Congress and the President. Cutting taxes and raising spending is expansionary and typically widens the deficit.
k: Expansionary fiscal = cut taxes, raise spending (Congress and President).
w: Contractionary fiscal raises taxes and cuts spending.
Monetary policy belongs to the Fed, not Congress.
QE is Fed bond-buying, a monetary tool.
m: Taxes and spending = fiscal. Money and rates = monetary.

q: Persistent federal budget deficits require heavy Treasury borrowing, which can push interest rates up and reduce private borrowing. This effect is called:
e: Crowding out occurs when government borrowing competes for funds, raising rates and squeezing out private borrowers.
k: Crowding out: heavy government borrowing raises rates, displacing private borrowing.
w: QT is the Fed shrinking its holdings, not deficit financing.
Disintermediation is money leaving banks for higher market yields.
Stagflation is weak growth plus high inflation.

q: Compared with monetary policy, fiscal policy is generally:
o: Faster to implement and set by the FOMC
Slower to implement but able to target specific groups
Faster to implement because it needs no legislation
e: Fiscal policy requires legislation, so it's slower than Fed action, but taxes and spending can be aimed at particular sectors or groups. It's rooted in Keynesian theory.
k: Fiscal: Congress/President, slow, targetable, Keynesian. Monetary: Fed, fast, monetarist.
w: The FOMC sets monetary, not fiscal, policy.
Fiscal changes require legislation, which takes time.
Fiscal policy is Keynesian; monetarism focuses on money supply.
m: Fiscal = slow but targeted.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three classifications of investment companies defined by the Investment Company Act of 1940?
e: The 1940 Act recognizes face-amount certificate companies, UITs and management companies. REITs are real estate companies registered under the 1933 Act, not 1940 Act investment companies.
k: 1940 Act classes: face-amount certificate companies, UITs, management companies (open-end and closed-end).
w: A real 1940 Act class, though nearly extinct today.
A real 1940 Act class: fixed, unmanaged portfolio.
A real 1940 Act class, split into open-end and closed-end.
m: REITs look like funds but are not 1940 Act companies.

q: Before an investment company may make a public offering of its shares, it must have a minimum net worth of:
e: The 1940 Act requires an investment company to have at least $100,000 of net worth before it offers shares to the public.
k: Investment company needs $100,000 net worth (seed capital) before a public offering.
w: Too low; the seed-capital requirement is double this.
Not the 1940 Act figure; confuses with other thresholds.
That's the accredited-investor net worth test, not fund seed capital.

q: At least what percentage of a mutual fund's board of directors must be independent (non-interested) directors?
e: Under the 1940 Act, at least 40% of a fund's directors must be independent of the adviser and underwriter.
k: Fund board: at least 40% independent (non-interested) directors.
w: Too low; confuses with the unrestricted 25% in the diversification test.
A majority is not the stated minimum for this rule.
Confuses with the 75% part of the 75-5-10 diversification test.

q: Which of the following actions by a mutual fund requires approval by a majority vote of the fund's shareholders?
o: Declaring an annual capital gains distribution
Changing the investment objective from growth to income
e: A fund cannot change its investment objective without a majority shareholder vote. Hiring service providers and declaring distributions are board decisions.
k: Changing a fund's investment objective requires a majority shareholder vote.
w: The board hires and replaces the custodian.
Distributions are declared by the board, not voted by shareholders.
The board hires service providers like the transfer agent.
m: Shareholders vote on: board, adviser contract, objective, fees.

q: A mutual fund shareholder never received her quarterly dividend check and her account statement shows the wrong address. Which party is responsible for these records and payments?
e: The transfer agent issues and redeems shares, maintains shareholder records, and sends statements and distributions.
k: Transfer agent: shareholder records, issues/redeems shares, sends distributions and statements.
w: The custodian safeguards the fund's cash and securities, not shareholder records.
The adviser manages the portfolio, not shareholder accounts.
The underwriter markets shares and collects sales charges.
m: Custodian holds assets; transfer agent handles shareholders.

q: For most mutual funds, the largest single annual operating expense is the:
o: Management fee paid to the investment adviser
e: The investment adviser's management fee is typically the fund's largest expense; its contract is approved by the board and shareholders.
k: Management (advisory) fee is usually a fund's largest expense.
w: Capped at 1.00% and usually smaller than the advisory fee.
Custody costs are a minor expense.
Record-keeping costs are a minor expense.

q: Which statement about money market mutual funds is TRUE?
o: They seek a stable $1.00 NAV, but it is not guaranteed
They are FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor
They typically carry a front-end sales charge of up to 5.75%
They invest mainly in long-term corporate bonds
e: Money market funds hold short-term debt and aim for a stable $1.00 NAV, but the price is not guaranteed or insured.
k: Money market fund: short-term debt, stable $1.00 NAV goal, not guaranteed, no sales charge.
w: Money market funds are securities, not bank deposits; no FDIC coverage.
Money market funds are generally sold with no sales charge.
They hold short-term debt like T-bills, CP and repos.

q: A 30-year-old customer wants a single fund for her 401(k) that will automatically shift toward bonds and cash as she nears her planned retirement in 2061. Which fund BEST fits?
e: A target-date (lifecycle) fund follows a glide path, becoming more conservative as the target date approaches.
k: Target-date fund: allocation grows more conservative as the target year approaches (glide path).
w: Keeps roughly fixed proportions, such as 60/40; no glide path.
Manager shifts mix based on markets, not a retirement date.
Equity fund mixing growth and income; no automatic de-risking.

q: Which type of fund is generally LEAST appropriate for a customer's traditional IRA?
e: Muni fund income is already federally tax-free; inside a tax-deferred IRA that benefit is wasted and withdrawals become taxable.
k: Never put tax-exempt municipal investments in an IRA; the tax advantage is wasted.
w: Low-cost and suitable for long-term retirement savings.
Long-term appreciation fits a retirement horizon.
Taxable income is sheltered inside an IRA.

q: Which list ranks fund types from LOWEST to HIGHEST risk?
o: Government bond, money market, balanced, aggressive growth
Money market, government bond, balanced, aggressive growth
Money market, balanced, government bond, aggressive growth
Balanced, money market, government bond, aggressive growth
e: From least to most risky: money market, government bond, investment-grade bond, balanced, growth and income, growth, aggressive growth.
k: Risk ladder: money market < government bond < balanced < growth < aggressive growth/sector.
w: Money market funds carry less risk than government bond funds.
Balanced funds hold stocks, so they're riskier than government bond funds.
Balanced funds are riskier than both money market and government bond funds.

q: A customer redeems mutual fund shares on Monday. The fund must send the redemption proceeds within:
e: The Investment Company Act requires a fund to pay redemption proceeds within 7 calendar days of receiving a proper request.
k: Mutual fund redemption proceeds must be paid within 7 calendar days.
w: T+1 is regular-way settlement for trades, not the redemption deadline.
An old settlement cycle; not the 1940 Act redemption rule.
Far too long; no such deadline exists.

q: A customer's order to buy a mutual fund arrives at 2:30 p.m. ET. Yesterday's closing NAV was $15.20. The order will be filled at:
o: The NAV computed at today's 4:00 p.m. ET close, plus any sales charge
Yesterday's NAV of $15.20, plus any sales charge
The NAV in effect at 2:30 p.m. when the order arrived
e: Forward pricing fills orders at the next NAV calculated after the order is received, normally at the 4:00 p.m. ET close.
k: Forward pricing: orders fill at the next NAV computed after receipt (4:00 p.m. ET).
w: Using the prior price is backward pricing, which is not allowed.
Mutual funds price once a day, not continuously.
Funds have no opening market price; they price at NAV after the close.

q: A broker-dealer has a selling agreement with a mutual fund's underwriter. The broker-dealer is prohibited from:
o: Forwarding customer purchase orders to the fund
Receiving part of the sales charge as a dealer concession
Keeping an inventory of fund shares to resell to customers
e: A broker-dealer may not maintain an inventory of fund shares or hold itself out as buying shares at a discount; it places orders with the fund at the next price.
k: Broker-dealers may not inventory mutual fund shares; orders go to the fund at the next price.
w: Placing orders through the underwriter is exactly what a selling agreement allows.
Prospectus delivery is required, not prohibited.
Selling dealers are normally paid from the sales charge.

q: Mutual fund shareholders must receive financial reports at least:
o: Semiannually, with the annual report audited
e: Funds send shareholders semiannual reports with financial statements and holdings; the annual report must be audited.
k: Shareholder reports: semiannual; the annual report is audited.
w: Quarterly reports are not the required standard, and only the annual is audited.
Two reports a year are required, and the annual must be audited.
Confuses account statements with the fund's shareholder reports.

q: A customer wants more detailed information than the prospectus provides about a fund's operations and the backgrounds of its directors. The rep should tell the customer to request the:
e: The SAI supplements the prospectus with more detail on fund operations, policies and management, and is available on request.
k: The SAI expands on the prospectus and is provided free on request.
w: Shorter than the full prospectus, not more detailed.
The disclosure document for private placements, not registered funds.
Form U4 registers individual representatives, not fund disclosure.

q: Which of the following is NOT required to appear in a mutual fund's prospectus?
o: A fee table showing sales charges and annual expenses
A projection of next year's expected return
e: A prospectus shows the objective, risks, fee table and historical 1-, 5- and 10-year performance. Projecting future returns is not allowed.
k: Prospectus: objective, risks, fee table, 1/5/10-year past performance; never projected returns.
w: The objective is a core prospectus item.
The fee table is required in every prospectus.
Standardized performance is shown for these periods.
m: Past performance yes; projections never.

q: A mutual fund quotes an NAV of $23.00 and a public offering price of $25.00. What is the sales charge percentage?
e: The sales charge is always stated as a percentage of the POP: ($25 - $23) / $25 = 8.0%.
k: Sales charge % = (POP - NAV) / POP.
w: Not derived from these prices.
Divides the load by NAV instead of POP.
Not derived from these prices.
m: Always divide by POP, never by NAV.

q: A mutual fund has total assets of $520 million, total liabilities of $20 million, and 25 million shares outstanding. What is the NAV per share?
e: NAV per share = (assets - liabilities) / shares = ($520M - $20M) / 25M = $20.00.
k: NAV per share = (Total assets - Total liabilities) / Shares outstanding.
w: Adds liabilities to assets instead of subtracting.
Ignores liabilities entirely.
Subtracts liabilities twice.

q: Which event would NOT change a mutual fund's NAV per share?
o: An investor buys 100,000 new shares of the fund
The fund's portfolio securities fall in value
The fund pays a capital gains distribution
The fund receives interest on its bonds
e: When investors buy or redeem, cash and shares change proportionally, so NAV per share is unchanged.
k: Purchases and redemptions do not change NAV per share; portfolio values and distributions do.
w: Portfolio value changes move NAV directly.
NAV drops by the distribution amount on the ex-date.
Income received raises net assets and NAV.

q: A customer signed a letter of intent for $50,000 in a fund family. Over 13 months she invested $42,000 of new money, which has grown to $51,000. What happens?
o: She has met the LOI because her account value exceeds $50,000
She has not met the LOI, so the higher sales charge is collected from escrowed shares
The LOI is automatically extended another 13 months
She keeps the reduced charge because the LOI is non-binding
e: Only new deposits count toward an LOI. Falling short means the fund retroactively collects the higher charge, using shares held in escrow.
k: LOI: 13 months, new money only; shortfall means higher charge taken from escrowed shares.
w: Appreciation does not count toward an LOI; only new money does.
There is no automatic extension; the 13-month window is fixed.
Non-binding on the investor, but the fund recovers the discount via escrow.
m: Appreciation counts for ROA, not for an LOI.

q: A customer originally invested $38,000 in a fund family; the holdings are now worth $47,000. The family's next breakpoint is $50,000. If she invests another $5,000, which is TRUE?
o: No reduced charge applies because her cost basis is under $50,000
She receives a refund of excess sales charges on her earlier purchases
She must sign a letter of intent to receive any reduction
The $5,000 purchase gets the $50,000 breakpoint rate under rights of accumulation
e: Rights of accumulation use the current value of existing holdings plus the new purchase: $47,000 + $5,000 = $52,000 reaches the breakpoint.
k: ROA: current value + new purchase crosses breakpoint; reduced charge on new purchase, not retroactive.
w: ROA uses current value, including appreciation, not cost.
ROA is not retroactive; it applies to the new purchase only.
ROA works without any LOI.

q: Which of the following purchasers is NOT eligible to receive breakpoint discounts on a combined purchase?
o: A husband and wife buying in a joint account
A parent buying for a minor child's custodial account
An investment club pooling its members' money
A trust buying for its beneficiaries
e: Breakpoints are available to individuals, spouses, parents with minor children, and most trusts and corporations, but not groups formed to pool purchases.
k: No breakpoints for investment clubs or groups formed to pool purchases.
w: Married couples may combine to reach breakpoints.
Parents and minor children may be combined.
Most trusts qualify for breakpoints.

q:
Under FINRA rules, a mutual fund may charge the maximum 8.5% sales charge only if it offers which of the following?
I. Breakpoints
II. Rights of accumulation
III. Reinvestment of dividends at NAV
IV. An exchange privilege
e: The 8.5% maximum is allowed only when the fund offers breakpoints, rights of accumulation, and automatic reinvestment of dividends at NAV.
k: 8.5% max load requires breakpoints, ROA and dividend reinvestment at NAV.
w: Missing dividend reinvestment at NAV.
Missing breakpoints.
An exchange privilege is not one of the three conditions.

q: A fund sells its shares at NAV with no front-end or back-end sales charge, but charges an annual 12b-1 fee of 0.35%. May it describe itself as a no-load fund?
o: Yes, because it charges no front-end sales charge
Yes, because its 12b-1 fee is below the 1.00% maximum
No, because no-load funds may not charge any 12b-1 fee
e: A fund may call itself no-load only if it has no sales charges and a 12b-1 fee of no more than 0.25%.
k: No-load: no sales charge and 12b-1 fee of 0.25% or less.
w: No front load alone isn't enough; the 12b-1 must be 0.25% or less.
The 1.00% is the overall 12b-1 cap, not the no-load limit.
No-load funds may charge up to 0.25%.

q: A customer invests $600 a month in a mutual fund for three months, buying at $20, $30 and $15 per share. What is the customer's average cost per share?
e: The customer bought 30 + 20 + 40 = 90 shares for $1,800, so the average cost is $20.00, below the $21.67 average price, as dollar cost averaging produces.
k: Average cost = total invested / total shares bought; DCA cost is below average price.
w: Not derived from these figures.
Not derived from these figures.
That's the average price, not the average cost.
m: Average cost < average price with dollar cost averaging.

q: A fund's NAV rose from $40.00 to $42.00 over the year, and it paid $1.20 per share in distributions. What was the total return?
e: Total return = (ending NAV - beginning NAV + distributions) / beginning NAV = ($2.00 + $1.20) / $40 = 8.0%.
k: Total return = (Ending NAV - Beginning NAV + Distributions) / Beginning NAV.
w: Counts only the distributions.
Counts only the NAV change.
Not derived from these figures.

q: A customer bought a mutual fund three months ago. The fund now pays a distribution of long-term capital gains it realized on portfolio sales. How is it taxed to the customer?
o: As a short-term capital gain because she held the shares under a year
As ordinary income because it is paid by a fund
e: Long-term capital gains distributions are taxed as long-term gains regardless of how long the shareholder has owned the fund.
k: LT capital gains distributions are LT to the shareholder regardless of holding period.
w: The fund's holding period controls, not the shareholder's.
Long-term gains keep their character when distributed.
Distributions are taxable whether taken in cash or reinvested.

q: In early December, a rep urges a customer to buy a fund right away, before it pays a large capital gains distribution, saying the customer will "get the payout." This is improper because:
o: Mutual funds may not pay distributions in December
The customer will have to pay a contingent deferred sales charge
Distributions are paid only to shareholders of record for over one year
NAV drops by the distribution, so the customer just gets a tax bill with no economic gain
e: Buying right before a distribution ("buying the dividend") gives no gain since NAV falls by the payout, but creates an immediate tax liability.
k: Buying the dividend: NAV drops by the payout; investor gets only a tax bill.
w: Funds commonly pay capital gains distributions late in the year.
A CDSC applies on redemption, not on receiving a distribution.
Any holder of record on the record date receives the distribution.

q: Which statement about 12b-1 fees is TRUE?
o: They are a one-time charge deducted from each purchase
They are paid by the shareholder only when shares are redeemed
They are deducted annually from fund assets to pay for distribution and marketing
They may be adopted by the investment adviser without board approval
e: 12b-1 fees are annual charges against fund assets for distribution and service, capped at 1.00% in total and reviewed annually by the board.
k: 12b-1: annual fee from fund assets for distribution; max 0.75% + 0.25% service = 1.00%.
w: That describes a front-end sales charge.
That describes a CDSC (back-end load).
Board approval, including independent directors, and shareholder approval are required.

q: A fund has average net assets of $800 million and total annual operating expenses of $6 million. What is its expense ratio?
e: Expense ratio = annual operating expenses / average net assets = $6M / $800M = 0.75%.
k: Expense ratio = Annual operating expenses / Average net assets.
w: Misplaces the decimal.
Not derived from these figures.
Divides assets by expenses and misplaces the decimal.

q: A customer is investing $20,000 that she expects to withdraw for a home down payment in about two years. Which mutual fund share class is generally MOST appropriate?
o: Class A with a letter of intent
e: Class C shares have little or no front load and a CDSC only in the first year, making them generally best for short holding periods.
k: Class C: level load, 1% CDSC first year, best for short-term (1-3 years).
w: A front-end load on a small, short-term investment is costly.
Its CDSC would still be high if sold after two years.
An LOI doesn't help; she isn't adding money toward a breakpoint.
m: Short horizon points to C.

q: What typically happens to Class B shares once the contingent deferred sales charge schedule runs out?
o: They convert to Class A shares with a lower 12b-1 fee
They convert to Class C shares with a level load
They must be redeemed at NAV
Their 12b-1 fee rises to the 1.00% maximum
e: After the CDSC declines to zero, usually in 6 to 8 years, Class B shares convert to Class A, which carries a lower 12b-1 fee.
k: Class B: declining CDSC, then converts to Class A (lower 12b-1).
w: Class C shares never convert, and B shares don't convert into C.
There is no forced redemption; the shares continue.
Backwards; the 12b-1 fee falls after conversion.
