q: A customer bought Class B shares for $10,000. Two years later she redeems them when they are worth $8,000. The CDSC for that year is 4%. What is the CDSC?
e: The CDSC is assessed on the lesser of the original purchase price or the current value: 4% x $8,000 = $320.
k: CDSC = rate x lesser of original cost or current value.
w: A CDSC applies even if the shares lost value.
Not derived from these figures.
Uses the original price; CDSC uses the lesser value.

q: A rep recommends Class C shares to a customer who plans to hold the fund for 20 years. The main concern with this recommendation is that Class C shares:
o: Cannot be held for more than 10 years
Carry a higher 12b-1 fee that never ends, making them costly long-term
Lose their dividend reinvestment privilege after 5 years
e: Class C shares carry an ongoing 1.00% 12b-1 fee and never convert to A, so over long periods they are usually the most expensive class.
k: Class C never converts; ongoing 1% 12b-1 makes it costly for long holding periods.
w: There is no maximum holding period.
C shares have little or no front-end load.
No such restriction exists.
m: Long horizon with C shares is a red flag.

q: A fund distributes only 85% of its net investment income to shareholders this year. Under Subchapter M, the fund will:
o: Be taxed only on the 15% it kept
Pay no tax, because it still distributed most of its income
Be taxed on all of its income like a regular corporation
Be taxed on the 85% it distributed
e: A fund must distribute at least 90% of net investment income to be a regulated investment company. Failing the test makes all its income taxable to the fund.
k: Subchapter M: distribute at least 90% of NII or the fund is taxed on all income.
w: That is the result only if the 90% test is met.
Falling below 90% removes conduit treatment.
Distributed income is taxed to shareholders, not to the fund.

q: A regulated investment company distributes 95% of its net investment income. On what portion does the fund itself pay income tax?
e: A RIC acts as a conduit: it is untaxed on distributed income and pays tax only on what it retains.
k: A qualifying RIC is taxed only on undistributed income; shareholders pay on distributions.
w: A qualifying fund still pays tax on any income it keeps.
That applies only if the fund fails the 90% test.
Distributed income is taxed to the shareholders.

q: A closed-end fund has an NAV of $15.00 per share, and its shares trade on the NYSE at $13.80. The fund is trading at:
e: Market price is below NAV, so it trades at a discount: ($15.00 - $13.80) / $15.00 = 8.0%.
k: Premium/discount = (Market price - NAV) / NAV; price below NAV is a discount.
w: Price below NAV is a discount, not a premium.
Divides by market price instead of NAV.
Treats the dollar difference as a percentage.

q: A customer buys shares of a closed-end fund on the NYSE a year after the fund's IPO. Which is TRUE?
o: She pays the next computed NAV plus a sales charge
She pays a brokerage commission and buys from another investor
She may later redeem the shares with the fund at NAV
e: After the IPO, closed-end shares trade in the secondary market between investors at supply-and-demand prices, with commissions instead of sales charges.
k: Closed-end fund: one IPO, then exchange trading with commissions; not redeemable.
w: That describes buying an open-end mutual fund.
Closed-end shares trade in whole shares only.
Closed-end funds don't redeem; she must sell in the market.

q: What mechanism keeps the market price of an ETF close to its NAV?
o: The fund redeeming any investor's shares at NAV each day
The exchange halting trading whenever price strays from NAV
Forward pricing of all orders at the 4:00 p.m. close
Authorized participants creating and redeeming large blocks of shares in kind
e: Authorized participants exchange baskets of underlying securities for creation units, and vice versa, arbitraging away premiums and discounts.
k: ETF creation/redemption by authorized participants keeps price near NAV.
w: Retail ETF investors sell on the exchange; only APs deal with the fund.
No such rule exists for ETFs.
ETFs trade continuously at market prices, not forward pricing.

q: Which of the following can an investor do with an ETF but NOT with a traditional mutual fund?
o: Place a stop order during the trading day
e: ETFs trade intraday on exchanges, so investors can use limit and stop orders, margin and short sales; mutual funds trade only with the fund at NAV.
k: ETFs: intraday trading, limit/stop orders, margin and short sales; mutual funds: none of these.
w: Both mutual funds and ETF holders can reinvest distributions.
Both provide diversification.
Both pay dividends to shareholders.

q: A customer expects the S&P 500 to fall over the next few days and wants to profit without opening a margin account or selling short. Which product fits this goal?
e: Inverse ETFs seek the opposite of an index's daily return, letting investors bet against the market without shorting. They reset daily, so they suit short holding periods.
k: Inverse ETF: opposite of index's daily return; daily reset, short-term tool.
w: Leveraged ETFs magnify gains when the index rises.
Profits only when the index rises.
Still a long equity position; loses when the market falls.

q: Which statement about exchange-traded notes (ETNs) is TRUE?
o: They generally pay no periodic interest; return comes at sale or maturity
They hold the index's securities in a trust for investors
They are registered investment companies under the 1940 Act
They are FDIC-insured up to $250,000 because a bank issues them
e: An ETN is unsecured bank debt that pays an index's return, minus fees, at maturity; it makes no interest payments, and gains are usually capital gains.
k: ETN: unsecured bank note, no portfolio, no periodic interest; return at sale or maturity.
w: ETN holders own no portfolio, just the issuer's promise.
ETNs are debt securities of a bank, not funds.
Bank-issued notes are not insured deposits.

q: A unit investment trust holds a fixed portfolio of municipal bonds. When the last of the bonds matures, the UIT will:
o: Have its adviser reinvest the proceeds in new bonds
Hold a board vote on whether to extend the trust
Convert into an open-end mutual fund
Terminate and distribute the proceeds to unitholders
e: A UIT is a fixed, unmanaged portfolio created under a trust indenture; it terminates on a set date, such as when its bonds mature, and pays out.
k: UIT: fixed, unmanaged portfolio; no board or adviser; terminates and distributes proceeds.
w: UITs have no investment adviser and no active management.
UITs have no board of directors.
UITs don't convert; they end on schedule.

q: The risk-free rate is 2%, the market return is 10%, and a fund with a beta of 0.8 returned 9.5%. Using CAPM, what is the fund's alpha?
k: CAPM: Expected = Rf + Beta x (Rm - Rf); Alpha = Actual - Expected.
w: Compares to the market return, ignoring beta.
Not derived from CAPM.
Subtracts only the risk-free rate.

q: The risk-free rate is 2%. Fund A returned 10% with a standard deviation of 8%; Fund B returned 12% with a standard deviation of 15%. Which statement is TRUE?
o: Fund B has the higher Sharpe ratio because its return was higher
Both funds have the same Sharpe ratio
Fund A has the higher Sharpe ratio, so it delivered more return per unit of risk
Sharpe ratios can't be compared without each fund's beta
e: Sharpe = (return - risk-free) / standard deviation. Fund A: 8/8 = 1.0; Fund B: 10/15 = 0.67. Fund A delivered better risk-adjusted return.
k: Sharpe ratio = (Return - Risk-free rate) / Standard deviation; higher is better.
w: B's Sharpe is (12 - 2) / 15 = 0.67, below A's 1.0.
A = 1.0, B = 0.67; they differ.
Sharpe uses standard deviation, not beta.

q: A REIT whose income comes mainly from interest on the real estate loans it makes and the mortgage securities it buys is a(n):
e: Mortgage REITs lend to property owners or buy mortgages and MBS, earning interest; they are especially sensitive to interest rates.
k: Equity REIT = rents; mortgage REIT = interest; hybrid = both.
w: Equity REITs own properties and earn rents.
Hybrids combine property ownership and lending.
Private describes registration status, not income source.

q: To avoid corporate income tax, a REIT must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income and hold at least what percentage of its assets in real estate?
e: A REIT must have at least 75% of its assets in real estate and earn at least 75% of gross income from real estate, plus distribute 90% of taxable income.
k: REIT: distribute 90% of taxable income; 75% of assets and income from real estate.
w: Too low; not the REIT asset test.
Confuses the asset test with the 90% distribution rule.
Confuses with the unrestricted 25% in the fund diversification test.

q: A customer in a high tax bracket expects her REIT dividends to be taxed at the 15% qualified dividend rate. The rep should explain that REIT dividends are generally taxed as:
e: Because the REIT itself pays no corporate tax, its dividends are generally taxed as ordinary income, though investors may get the 20% QBI deduction.
k: REIT dividends are generally taxed as ordinary income, not qualified dividends.
w: REIT dividends generally don't meet the qualified dividend rules.
Only capital gain distributions get that treatment.
Only municipal interest is federally tax-exempt.

q: A REIT reports a large net loss after writing down several office properties. How does this affect its shareholders' tax returns?
o: They deduct their share as a passive loss
They deduct their share as an ordinary loss
They cannot deduct the loss; REITs don't pass losses through
They deduct their share as a capital loss
e: REITs pass through income but not losses. This is a key difference from DPPs and limited partnerships.
k: REITs pass through income, never losses; DPPs pass through both.
w: Passive loss pass-through applies to DPPs, not REITs.
REITs pass through no losses of any kind.
Only a sale of REIT shares at a loss creates a capital loss.
m: REIT vs DPP: losses flow through only in DPPs.

q: Which statement about how REITs are regulated is TRUE?
o: They are not investment companies under the 1940 Act
They are registered as closed-end funds under the 1940 Act
They are exempt from registration under the Securities Act of 1933
They may be sold only to accredited investors
e: REITs are not 1940 Act investment companies; public REITs register under the 1933 Act and their shares trade under the 1934 Act.
k: REITs: registered under '33 Act, trade under '34 Act; not 1940 Act investment companies.
w: They resemble closed-end funds but aren't 1940 Act companies.
Public REITs register their offerings under the 1933 Act.
Listed REITs can be bought by anyone; only private REITs are limited.

q: A REIT that is not registered with the SEC and is sold only to accredited investors is a:
e: Private REITs are unregistered and limited to accredited investors; non-traded REITs are registered but don't trade; listed REITs trade on exchanges.
k: REIT forms: listed (registered, trades), non-traded (registered, illiquid), private (unregistered, accredited only).
w: Non-traded public REITs are SEC-registered, just not listed.
Listed REITs are registered and open to anyone.
Hybrid describes holdings (property and mortgages), not registration.

q: A customer wants real estate exposure, regular income, and the ability to sell on any trading day. Which investment is MOST suitable?
e: Listed REITs trade on exchanges like stocks, offering liquidity along with rental income from the properties.
k: Listed REITs offer real estate income plus daily liquidity; non-traded REITs and DPPs are illiquid.
w: Illiquid with limited redemption programs and high fees.
DPPs are illiquid with long holding periods.
Illiquid and produces no income, only potential appreciation.

q: Which development would MOST likely cause REIT share prices, especially mortgage REITs, to fall?
e: REITs carry interest-rate risk: rising rates make their dividends less attractive and raise borrowing costs; mortgage REITs are hit hardest.
k: Rising interest rates hurt REIT prices, mortgage REITs most.
w: Higher rents raise REIT income and dividends.
Falling rates generally help REIT prices.
Higher property values support equity REIT prices.

q:
Which of the following are TRUE of an equity REIT?
I. It owns and operates income-producing properties
II. Its income comes mainly from rents and property appreciation
III. It passes operating losses through to shareholders
IV. It must distribute at least 90% of taxable income to avoid corporate tax
e: Equity REITs own properties and earn rents and appreciation, and must distribute 90% of taxable income. No REIT passes losses through.
k: Equity REIT: owns property, earns rents, 90% distribution, no loss pass-through.
w: Leaves out the 90% distribution requirement.
Statement III is false; REITs don't pass through losses.
Statement III is false and II is omitted.

q: A hedge fund charges "2 and 20." An investor puts in $1,000,000 and the fund gains 15% for the year. If the 2% fee is based on the $1,000,000 starting value, what are the investor's total fees?
e: Management fee = 2% x $1,000,000 = $20,000; performance fee = 20% x $150,000 profit = $30,000; total $50,000.
k: 2 and 20: 2% of assets plus 20% of profits.
w: Counts only the management fee.
Counts only the performance fee.
Bases the 2% on the ending value instead of the stated starting value.

q: Which customer qualifies as an accredited investor eligible to buy a hedge fund?
o: A married couple with joint income of $260,000 in each of the last two years
A single person who earned $230,000 in each of the last two years and expects the same this year
A single person with $900,000 net worth excluding her home
A person with $1.4 million net worth, $600,000 of it in her primary residence
e: Accredited investors have net worth over $1 million excluding the primary residence, or income over $200,000 individually ($300,000 jointly) in each of the last two years.
k: Accredited: $1M net worth (ex-home) or $200k individual / $300k joint income for two years.
w: Joint income must exceed $300,000.
Net worth must exceed $1 million excluding the primary residence.
Excluding the home leaves only $800,000, below $1 million.

q: Six months after investing in a hedge fund with a one-year lock-up, a customer needs her money. Generally, she:
o: Cannot redeem until the lock-up ends, then only at set windows with notice
Can sell her interest on an exchange at market price
Can redeem at NAV on any business day, paying a 2% fee
Can redeem at NAV within 7 days, like a mutual fund
e: Hedge funds are illiquid: lock-up periods are common, and redemptions after that are allowed only at quarterly or annual windows with advance notice.
k: Hedge funds: lock-ups (often 1 year+), then periodic redemption windows with notice.
w: Hedge fund interests are private and not exchange-traded.
Hedge funds don't offer daily redemptions.
The 7-day redemption rule applies to registered mutual funds.

q: Compared with investing directly in a hedge fund, a key drawback of a registered fund of hedge funds is:
o: It is available only to qualified purchasers
It cannot hold more than one hedge fund
It removes all exposure to leverage
A second layer of fees on top of the underlying funds' fees
e: Funds of hedge funds can be registered and sold to retail investors with lower minimums, but they add a second layer of fees and keep the underlying illiquidity.
k: Fund of hedge funds: retail access, lower minimums, but double fees.
w: Registered funds of funds can be sold to retail with lower minimums.
By definition it holds several hedge funds.
The underlying funds still use leverage and carry their risks.

q: Instead of a prospectus, investors in a privately offered hedge fund typically receive a(n):
e: Hedge funds are Reg D private placements, not SEC-registered, so they provide an offering memorandum rather than a prospectus.
k: Private placements like hedge funds use an offering memorandum, not a prospectus.
w: The SAI supplements a registered fund's prospectus.
Official statements are municipal bond disclosure documents.
A summary prospectus is used by registered mutual funds.

q: A hedge fund relying on Section 3(c)(1) to avoid registering under the Investment Company Act of 1940 is limited to:
e: Section 3(c)(1) funds may have no more than 100 investors; 3(c)(7) funds may have unlimited investors, but all must be qualified purchasers.
k: 3(c)(1): 100 investors or fewer; 3(c)(7): qualified purchasers only.
w: That is the Reg D 506(b) limit, not the 1940 Act exemption.
That is the Section 3(c)(7) exemption.
Not the 3(c)(1) limit.

q: A customer invests $500,000 as a limited partner in a heavily leveraged hedge fund that collapses and owes its lenders far more than its assets. The customer's maximum loss is:
o: Unlimited, because the fund used leverage
$500,000 plus her pro rata share of the fund's debts
e: A hedge fund itself can be wiped out by leverage, but as a limited partner the investor cannot lose more than she invested.
k: Hedge fund limited partners can lose their whole investment, but no more.
w: Limited partners have limited liability.
LPs aren't liable for fund debts beyond their investment.
No doubling rule exists.

q: Which of the following is NOT a typical characteristic of hedge funds?
o: Use of leverage and short selling
Returns often uncorrelated with the broad market
e: Hedge funds are illiquid, with lock-ups and periodic redemption windows; daily redemption at NAV is a mutual fund feature.
k: Hedge funds: leverage, shorting, 2-and-20 fees, low liquidity, little transparency.
w: Leverage and shorting are core hedge fund strategies.
The 20% performance fee is standard.
Low correlation is the main diversification argument.

q: A limited partner in a real estate program begins negotiating leases and making daily decisions about tenants. The main risk to the limited partner is:
o: Forfeiting her share of depreciation deductions
Losing limited liability and being treated like a general partner
Having her interest converted to a REIT share
e: Limited partners must stay passive; participating in management risks losing limited status and facing unlimited liability.
k: LPs who participate in management risk losing limited liability.
w: Management activity affects liability, not deductions.
Her actions don't automatically dissolve the partnership.
No such conversion exists.

q: An investor officially becomes a limited partner in a DPP when:
o: The general partner accepts the investor's subscription agreement
The certificate of limited partnership is filed with the SEC
The investor's broker-dealer approves the purchase
e: The investor signs a subscription agreement, but admission occurs only when the general partner accepts it.
k: Subscription agreement: investor signs, GP accepts to admit the limited partner.
w: Payment alone doesn't admit the investor; the GP must accept.
The certificate is filed with the state, and it doesn't admit investors.
The GP, not the broker-dealer, decides whom to admit.

q: Which of the following is a restriction on the general partner of a limited partnership?
o: It must own at least 10% of the partnership
It may not compete with the partnership
It may not receive any compensation
It may not make decisions without an LP vote
e: The GP manages the business, owes a fiduciary duty, must keep at least a 1% interest, and cannot compete with the partnership.
k: GP: manages, unlimited liability, fiduciary duty, at least 1% interest, cannot compete.
w: The minimum GP interest is 1%, not 10%.
GPs are paid for managing the partnership.
The GP makes management decisions; LPs vote only on major matters.

q: Which real estate DPP provides NO depreciation deductions?
e: Land is not depreciable, so raw land programs offer only potential appreciation; they are the most speculative real estate DPPs.
k: Raw land: no depreciation, no income, appreciation only (most speculative).
w: Existing buildings generate income and depreciation.
Buildings under construction are depreciated once placed in service.
Offers depreciation plus tax credits.

q: An investor wants oil and gas exposure with immediate cash flow and the lowest risk. Which program is MOST suitable?
e: Income programs buy already-producing wells, providing immediate income with the lowest risk among oil and gas programs.
k: Oil & gas risk: exploratory (highest) > developmental > income (lowest, immediate cash flow).
w: Drilling near proven reserves still carries drilling risk.
Wildcat drilling is the riskiest program.
Includes drilling and so carries more risk than income programs.

q: Which tax benefit is specific to oil and gas drilling programs?
o: Immediate deduction of intangible drilling costs
e: Intangible drilling costs (labor, fuel, site prep) can be deducted in the year incurred; oil and gas programs also get depletion.
k: Oil & gas: IDCs deducted immediately plus depletion.
w: Equipment leasing and real estate programs also depreciate assets.
These credits come from government-assisted housing programs.
Every DPP passes losses through.

q: A program buys railcars and leases them to railroads. Besides lease income, its main tax benefit for investors is:
e: Equipment leasing programs provide lease income plus depreciation deductions on the equipment.
k: Equipment leasing DPP: lease income plus depreciation.
w: Depletion is for natural resources like oil, gas and minerals.
IDCs apply to oil and gas drilling.
Housing credits come from government-assisted housing.

q: An investor puts $50,000 cash into an equipment leasing limited partnership and is responsible for $30,000 of the partnership's recourse debt. What is the investor's cost basis?
e: DPP basis = cash invested + share of recourse debt = $50,000 + $30,000 = $80,000. Deductible losses can't exceed basis.
k: DPP cost basis = cash invested + share of recourse debt (plus nonrecourse for real estate).
w: Subtracts the debt instead of adding it.
Counts only the debt.
Ignores her share of recourse debt.

q: A real estate limited partnership sells a building on which partners have taken years of depreciation deductions. Some of the gain may be:
o: Tax-free because the property was held long-term
Recaptured and taxed as ordinary income
e: Depreciation previously deducted can be recaptured on sale and taxed as ordinary income.
k: Depreciation recapture: prior depreciation taxed as ordinary income when the asset is sold.
w: Holding period doesn't erase prior depreciation.
Partnership gains are not dividends.
Gain is recognized when the asset is sold.

q: When a limited partnership dissolves, limited partners are paid:
o: After general creditors but before the general partner
At the same time as general creditors
e: Dissolution order: secured creditors, general creditors, limited partners, then the general partner.
k: LP dissolution order: secured creditors, general creditors, limited partners, general partner.
w: Secured creditors are paid first.
The GP is paid last.
General creditors come before any partners.

q: When evaluating a direct participation program, the MOST important factor is:
o: The size of the projected tax deductions
Whether the units are listed on an exchange
The economic viability of the business
e: A DPP should make sense as a business apart from tax benefits; economic viability comes first, followed by the GP's track record and costs.
k: Evaluate a DPP on economic viability first, tax benefits second.
w: Tax benefits shouldn't be the main reason to invest.
Partner count says nothing about the venture's merits.
DPP units are generally not listed.

q: A rep recommends a real estate limited partnership for a customer's IRA. The main problem with this recommendation is that:
o: The program's pass-through tax benefits are wasted in a tax-deferred account
IRAs may not hold any securities other than mutual funds
The customer would have unlimited liability
e: DPPs are bought largely for their pass-through losses and deductions, which provide no benefit inside an IRA; DPPs are also illiquid.
k: DPP tax benefits are wasted in retirement accounts.
w: IRAs can hold stocks, bonds and many other securities.
Many DPPs produce rental or lease income.
LPs have limited liability regardless of account type.

q:
Which of the following pass operating losses through to their investors?
I. A REIT
II. A real estate limited partnership
III. A hedge fund organized as a limited partnership
e: Partnerships, including DPPs and hedge funds organized as LPs, pass through income and losses. REITs pass through only income.
k: Losses flow through partnerships (DPPs, hedge fund LPs), never REITs.
w: REITs don't pass losses through.
REITs don't pass losses through.
Includes the REIT, which passes through only income.

q: Which party to a listed option contract is obligated to perform if the option is exercised?
o: The exchange where the option trades
e: The writer (seller) receives the premium and in exchange takes on the obligation to buy or sell the stock if assigned. Buyers of calls and puts have rights, not obligations.
k: Buyer (long) has the right; writer (short) has the obligation.
w: A call holder has the right to buy, not an obligation.
A put holder has the right to sell, not an obligation.
Exchanges provide the marketplace; they are not a party to the contract.
m: Rights = buyer. Obligations = seller.

q: A customer enters an order to "Sell 2 MNO Oct 35 puts @ 1.50." If the order is filled, the customer:
o: Pays $300 and has the right to sell 200 shares at $35
Receives $300 and may be obligated to buy 200 shares at $35
Receives $150 and may be obligated to buy 100 shares at $35
Receives $300 and may be obligated to sell 200 shares at $35
e: Selling (writing) puts brings in premium: 1.50 x 100 x 2 contracts = $300. A put writer is obligated to buy the stock at the strike if assigned, here 200 shares at $35.
k: Put writer receives premium; obligated to BUY at strike. Premium x 100 x contracts.
w: That describes buying puts; a seller receives the premium.
Counts only one contract; the order is for two contracts.
Call writers must sell; put writers must buy.

q:
Which of the following option positions are bullish?
I. Long call
II. Short call
III. Long put
IV. Short put
e: A call buyer profits when the stock rises, and a put writer profits when the stock stays at or above the strike. Short calls and long puts are bearish.
k: Bullish: long call, short put. Bearish: short call, long put.
w: A short call loses money as the stock rises; it is bearish.
Both of these positions are bearish.
A long put is bearish; only the short put is bullish.
m: Buy call / sell put = bullish.

q: Which statement about standard listed equity options is TRUE?
o: They may be exercised at any time up to expiration
They may be exercised only on the expiration date
Standard monthly contracts expire on the third Monday
e: All listed equity options are American style, so the holder can exercise at any time before expiration. Standard contracts cover 100 shares and monthly options expire on the third Friday.
k: Equity options: American style, 100 shares, expire third Friday of the month.
w: A standard equity contract covers 100 shares.
That is European style, used by most index options.
Standard monthly options expire on the third Friday.
m: American = anytime; European = expiration only.

q: A customer is opening an account to trade listed options. At or before account approval, the firm must deliver:
o: A prospectus registered under the Securities Act of 1933
The OCC's audited annual financial statements
A copy of the Cboe's exchange rulebook
e: Options are not sold with a traditional prospectus. Customers must receive the ODD, Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options, at or before account approval.
k: Deliver the ODD (Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options) at or before options approval.
w: Listed options are not offered with a traditional 1933 Act prospectus.
OCC financials are not a required customer delivery.
Exchange rules are not delivered to customers at approval.
m: ODD comes first, before or at approval.

q: A customer buys 5 XYZ calls in a regular-way trade on Monday. Absent a holiday, the trade settles on:
e: Option trades settle regular way T+1, one business day after the trade date, so a Monday trade settles Tuesday.
k: Option trades settle T+1; stock delivered on exercise also settles T+1.
w: Same-day settlement is cash settlement, not regular way.
T+2 was the old stock settlement cycle; options settle T+1.
T+3 is an outdated settlement cycle.
m: Options and stock both settle T+1 now.

q: All of the following statements about listed options are true EXCEPT:
o: The OCC guarantees performance on every listed contract
The OCC standardizes strike prices and expiration dates
The Cboe is the largest options exchange
Each option series is offered with its own registered prospectus
e: Listed options do not have an issuer in the corporate sense and are not sold with a separate prospectus; customers instead receive the ODD. The OCC issues, guarantees and standardizes contracts.
k: OCC issues and guarantees listed options; customers get the ODD, not a prospectus.
w: True: the OCC stands between every buyer and seller.
True: the OCC sets standardized terms.
True: the Cboe is the chief options exchange.

q: ABC stock is trading at $47. Which of the following options is in the money?
e: A put is in the money when the stock is below the strike. With ABC at 47, the 50 put has 3 points of intrinsic value.
k: Call Up, Put Down: call ITM if stock > strike; put ITM if stock < strike.
w: Stock above a put's strike makes it out of the money.
Stock below a call's strike makes it out of the money.
Stock equal to the strike is at the money, not in the money.
m: Call Up, Put Down.

q: XYZ is trading at $38. An XYZ 35 call is quoted at 4.50. The time value of the call is:
e: Intrinsic value is 38 - 35 = 3. Time value is the premium minus intrinsic value: 4.50 - 3 = 1.50.
k: Time value = premium - intrinsic value. Call intrinsic = stock - strike.
w: The call has premium above its intrinsic value, so time value exists.
3.00 is the intrinsic value, not the time value.
4.50 is the full premium, which includes intrinsic value.
m: Premium = intrinsic + time.

q: All of the following would generally increase an option's premium EXCEPT:
o: Higher volatility in the underlying stock
The option moving deeper into the money
A longer time remaining until expiration
Expiration drawing closer with no change in the stock price
e: As expiration approaches, time value decays, so the premium falls if nothing else changes. Volatility, intrinsic value and more time all add to the premium.
k: Premium rises with time remaining, volatility and depth in the money.
w: Greater volatility raises the chance of a large move, increasing premium.
More intrinsic value means a higher premium.
More time means more time value.
m: Time decay works against the option buyer.

q: On expiration day, GHI is trading at $55. Ignoring transaction costs, a GHI 60 put should be worth approximately:
e: At expiration an option is worth only its intrinsic value. The put is 60 - 55 = 5 points in the money, or $500 per contract.
k: At expiration, premium = intrinsic value only. Put intrinsic = strike - stock.
w: Time value is gone, but the put still has intrinsic value.
$5,500 is the stock's value per 100 shares, not the option.
$6,000 is the aggregate strike price, not the option's value.

q: A customer who wrote an XYZ call two months ago wants to eliminate her obligation before expiration. She should enter:
e: A writer opened the position with a sale, so she closes it by buying the same option back, a closing purchase.
k: Writer exits with a closing purchase; buyer exits with a closing sale.
w: Selling another call adds a new short position.
A closing sale is how a holder exits a long option.
An opening purchase creates a new long position, not a close.
m: Close by doing the opposite of how you opened.

q: When a broker-dealer receives an exercise notice from the OCC, it may allocate the assignment to customers by any of the following methods EXCEPT:
o: To the customer holding the largest short position
e: Firms must allocate assignments fairly: randomly, first-in-first-out, or another fair method. Assigning by largest position is not permitted.
k: Assignment: random, FIFO or other fair method; never largest position first.
w: Random selection is an accepted method.
FIFO is an accepted method.
Any fair and reasonable method is accepted.
m: Never largest position first.

q: A customer holds 1 JKL 25 call. On expiration day JKL closes at $25.03, and the customer gives no instructions. The call will most likely:
o: Be automatically exercised by the OCC
Expire worthless because it is less than $0.25 in the money
Remain open for three business days for the customer to decide
e: The OCC automatically exercises equity options that are in the money by $0.01 or more at expiration unless the holder instructs otherwise. This call is $0.03 in the money.
k: OCC auto-exercises equity options $0.01 or more in the money at expiration.
w: The auto-exercise threshold is $0.01, not $0.25.
Options cannot be exercised after the expiration cut-off.
Equity options settle in stock, not cash.
m: Auto-exercise = one cent ITM.

q: An investor bought 1 RST 50 put at 2. She later exercises it, delivering 100 shares she already owned. For tax purposes, her sale proceeds are:
e: When a put is exercised, the buyer's sale proceeds equal the strike minus the premium paid: (50 - 2) x 100 = $4,800.
k: Put exercised: buyer's sale proceeds = strike - premium.
w: Ignores the premium, which reduces the put buyer's proceeds.
Adds the premium; that is the call rule for basis.
$200 is only the premium paid.
m: Calls add premium; puts subtract it.

q: An investor holds 1 XYZ 90 call. XYZ effects a 3-for-2 stock split. After the OCC adjustment, the investor holds:
e: For uneven splits, the number of contracts stays the same, shares per contract rise to 150 and the strike falls to 90 x 2/3 = 60. Aggregate value stays $9,000.
k: Uneven split: same contracts, more shares per contract, proportionally lower strike.
w: Fractional contracts are not created.
That is the 2-for-1 even-split adjustment.
The strike must drop; otherwise value rises to $13,500.
m: Check: contracts x shares x strike stays constant.

q: ABC declares its regular quarterly cash dividend of $0.40 per share. Holders of ABC listed options will see:
o: Additional contracts at a lower strike
e: The OCC does not adjust contracts for ordinary cash dividends; only unusually large or special dividends trigger an adjustment.
k: No OCC adjustment for ordinary cash dividends.
w: Strikes are not reduced for regular cash dividends.
That is how uneven splits and stock dividends are handled.
That is how even splits are handled.
m: Ex-date price drop hurts call holders, helps put holders.

q: An investor owns 1 DEF 66 call. DEF pays a 10% stock dividend. After the adjustment, the investor holds:
e: Stock dividends are treated like uneven splits: one contract, now for 110 shares, with the strike reduced to 6,600 / 110 = 60.
k: Stock dividend: shares per contract increase, strike reduced; total value unchanged.
w: The strike must drop; otherwise aggregate value rises.
Fractional contracts are not created.
Shares per contract must increase to 110.

q: An investor buys 1 DEF Sep 70 call at 3.50. At expiration DEF is $72 and the investor closes the position at intrinsic value. The result is:
e: The call is worth its intrinsic value of 72 - 70 = 2 at expiration. The investor paid 3.50, so the result is a 1.50 loss, or $150.
k: Long call: profit only above breakeven = strike + premium.
w: Ignores the 3.50 premium paid.
$350 is the loss only if the call expired worthless.
Stock is below the 73.50 breakeven, so there is no profit.
m: Breakeven here is 73.50.

q: A customer expects to receive a large bonus in three months and wants to lock in today's purchase price on a stock she believes will rise. The MOST suitable option strategy is to:
o: Write a call on the stock
Buy a put on the stock
Write a covered call on the stock
Buy a call on the stock
e: A long call gives the right to buy at the strike, locking in a purchase price for a limited cost (the premium) while she waits for the cash.
k: Long call = bullish; locks in a purchase price; max loss = premium.
w: A short call is bearish and creates an obligation to sell.
A long put is bearish; it locks in a sale price.
She doesn't own the stock yet, so she can't write a covered call.

q: An investor writes 1 uncovered GHI 80 call at 5. At expiration GHI is $92 and the call is assigned. The investor's result is:
e: The writer must deliver stock worth 92 for 80, a 12-point loss, offset by the 5-point premium received, for a net 7-point loss, or $700.
k: Short call loss = (stock price - strike) - premium, x 100.
w: Ignores the $500 premium received.
The writer keeps the premium only if the call expires worthless.
Adds the premium instead of subtracting it.
m: Short call breakeven = strike + premium = 85.

q: A customer writes 1 uncovered KLM 45 call at 2.25. At what stock price at expiration does the customer break even?
e: The breakeven for a short call is the same as for a long call: strike + premium = 45 + 2.25 = 47.25. The writer profits below that price.
k: Call breakeven (long or short) = strike + premium.
w: Subtracts the premium; that is the put rule.
At $45 the writer keeps the full premium, a profit.
Adds the premium twice.
m: Calls add, puts subtract.

q: An investor buys 1 TUV 60 put at 4. TUV falls to $51 at expiration and the investor closes the put at intrinsic value. The profit is:
e: The put is worth 60 - 51 = 9 at expiration. Subtracting the 4 premium paid leaves a 5-point profit, or $500.
k: Long put profit = (strike - stock price) - premium, x 100.
w: $900 ignores the $400 premium paid.
$400 is the premium, the maximum loss.
Confuses breakeven ($56) with a dollar profit.

q: An investor buys 1 WXY 35 put at 1.25. The maximum potential gain is:
e: A long put's best case is the stock falling to zero: the investor sells at 35 a stock worth nothing, minus the 1.25 premium, or 33.75 x 100 = $3,375.
k: Long put max gain = (strike - premium) x 100.
w: Ignores the premium paid.
Adds the premium instead of subtracting it.
A stock can only fall to zero, so put gains are capped.

q: LMN trades at $52. A customer would gladly own it at $50 and writes 1 LMN 50 put at 2. If the put is assigned, her effective cost per share is:
e: If assigned, she buys at the $50 strike but keeps the $2 premium, so her net cost is 50 - 2 = $48 per share, which is also her breakeven.
k: Short put breakeven / effective cost = strike - premium.
w: $52 is today's market price, not her cost if assigned.
Ignores the premium she keeps.
Adds the premium; put calculations subtract.
m: Writing puts = getting paid to wait to buy.

q: A short put is considered covered (cash-secured) when the writer:
o: Owns 100 shares of the underlying stock
Has also written a call on the same stock
Owns a call on the same stock and strike
Has cash on deposit equal to the strike price x 100
e: The put writer's obligation is to buy the stock, so it is covered by cash equal to the aggregate strike price (or by a short position in the stock).
k: Short put is covered by cash equal to the strike x 100, or by short stock.
w: Owning stock covers a short call, not a short put.
Writing a call adds a second obligation; it covers nothing.
A long call does not supply cash to buy shares if assigned.

q: An investor sells short 100 shares of XYZ at $40 and buys 1 XYZ 45 call at 2. The investor's maximum potential loss is:
e: The call caps the repurchase price at 45, a 5-point loss on the short sale, plus the 2-point premium, for a maximum loss of 7 points, or $700.
k: Protective call max loss = (strike - short sale price) + premium.
w: $200 is only the premium.
$500 ignores the premium paid.
Buying the call removes the unlimited risk of the short sale.
m: Short stock is hedged with a long call.

q: An investor buys 100 shares of RST at $60 and at the same time buys 1 RST 55 put at 3. The breakeven point is:
e: With a protective put, the stock must rise enough to recover the premium paid: 60 + 3 = $63.
k: Protective put breakeven = stock cost + premium.
w: Strike minus premium is the breakeven for a put alone.
Subtracts the premium from the stock cost.
Adds the premium to the strike instead of the stock cost.
m: Hedged stock: breakeven = cost + premium paid.
steps: Protective put breakeven = stock cost + premium

q:
Which of the following positions provide protection (a hedge) against an adverse move in a stock position?
I. Long stock and long put
II. Long stock and long call
III. Short stock and long call
IV. Short stock and long put
e: A long stock position loses when the price falls, so it is hedged with a put. A short stock position loses when the price rises, so it is hedged with a call.
k: Hedge long stock with a long put; hedge short stock with a long call.
w: A long call adds to, rather than hedges, long stock's exposure.
Both pair the stock with an option that profits the same way.
Short stock plus long put doubles bearish exposure.
m: Hedge with the option that profits when the stock hurts you.

q: An investor owns 100 shares of NOP bought at $30 and writes 1 NOP 35 call at 1.50. The breakeven point is:
e: In a covered call, the premium received lowers the effective cost of the stock: 30 - 1.50 = $28.50.
k: Covered call breakeven = stock cost - premium.
w: Adds the premium to the stock cost.
Subtracts the premium from the strike, not the stock cost.
Adds the premium to the strike; that is the naked call breakeven.
steps: Covered call breakeven = stock cost - premium

q: A retiree has held DEF stock in her IRA for years. She expects the price to stay flat for several months and would like to generate extra income from the shares. The MOST suitable strategy is to:
e: Writing covered calls on stock already owned produces premium income and suits a neutral to mildly bullish outlook. It is the most conservative option strategy and is commonly permitted in retirement accounts.
k: Covered call = income on owned stock; neutral to mildly bullish; most conservative.
w: Buying puts costs premium; it hedges rather than earns income.
Buying calls costs money and is a bullish speculation.
Index puts hedge a diversified portfolio and cost premium.
m: Income on stock you own = write covered calls.

q: The main drawback of writing covered calls on stock already owned is that the investor:
o: Faces unlimited loss if the stock rises
Must buy more shares if the call is assigned
Gives up any appreciation above the strike price
Can no longer receive dividends on the stock
e: If the stock rises above the strike, the shares are called away at the strike, so gains above that level are given up in exchange for the premium.
k: Covered call caps upside at the strike; max gain = (strike - cost) + premium.
w: Owning the shares covers the call; rising prices don't create unlimited loss.
Assignment requires delivering shares already owned, not buying more.
The owner keeps receiving dividends until the shares are delivered.

q: An investor exercises 1 SPX 5,800 put when the index settles at 5,740. The investor will receive:
o: 100 shares of each stock in the index
e: Index options are cash settled. The put is 5,800 - 5,740 = 60 points in the money, and 60 x the $100 multiplier = $6,000, paid the next business day.
k: Index option exercise: ITM points x $100 multiplier, paid in cash T+1.
w: Uses a $10 multiplier instead of $100.
Index options are cash settled; no stock is delivered.
That is the index value x 100, not the in-the-money amount.
m: Index options never deliver stock.

q: A client with a large, diversified stock portfolio is worried about a broad market decline over the next few months but does not want to sell her holdings. Which strategy BEST addresses her concern?
o: Buy puts on her single largest holding
e: Long index puts gain value as the overall market falls, offsetting losses in a diversified portfolio without selling the stocks.
k: Hedge a diversified portfolio by buying broad-based index puts.
w: Index calls profit from a rising market, not a decline.
Protects one stock only, not the whole portfolio.
Writing puts adds losses if the market falls.
m: Portfolio hedge = long index puts.

q: Long-term equity anticipation securities (LEAPS) may have expirations of up to approximately:
e: LEAPS are long-dated options with expirations up to 39 months, far longer than standard monthly options.
k: LEAPS = long-term options, up to 39 months.
w: Nine months is typical of standard option cycles, not LEAPS.
LEAPS extend well beyond one year.
Exceeds the LEAPS maximum.

q: A customer elects to reinvest all dividends from her stock mutual fund into additional fund shares. The reinvested dividends are:
o: Taxable in the year they are paid
Not taxed until the fund shares are sold
Taxable only if they exceed the annual exclusion
e: Dividends are taxable in the year paid whether taken in cash or reinvested. The reinvested amounts are added to her cost basis.
k: Dividends are taxable when paid, cash or reinvested; reinvestments add to basis.
w: Reinvesting does not defer tax in a taxable account.
Tax deferral applies to retirement accounts and annuities, not this.
There is no annual exclusion for dividend income.
m: Reinvested = still taxed now.

q: Which of the following distributions would MOST likely be taxed at ordinary income rates rather than qualified dividend rates?
o: A dividend from a US manufacturer held for two years
A dividend from a real estate investment trust
A long-term capital gains distribution from a mutual fund
A dividend from a US bank stock held for five years
e: REIT dividends generally are non-qualified and taxed as ordinary income. Dividends from US corporations held long enough qualify for long-term capital gains rates.
k: REIT, money market and short-term gain distributions = ordinary income.
w: A US corporation's dividend held this long is qualified.
LT capital gains distributions get long-term rates.
A US bank's dividend held five years is qualified.
m: REITs pass through income; dividends mostly non-qualified.

q: An investor owns 200 shares of XYZ with a total cost basis of $6,000. XYZ pays a 25% stock dividend. Which statement is TRUE?
o: She now owns 250 shares with a $24 basis per share and owes no tax now
She owes tax on the value of the 50 new shares this year
Her basis remains $30 per share on all 250 shares
Her total cost basis increases to $7,500
e: Stock dividends are not taxable when received. The total $6,000 basis is spread over 250 shares, lowering the per-share basis to $24.
k: Stock dividends/splits: not taxable; same total basis spread over more shares.
w: Stock dividends aren't taxed until the shares are sold.
Per-share basis must fall; total basis is unchanged.
Total basis stays $6,000; no new money was invested.

q: ABC Corp. owns 5% of the common stock of an unaffiliated US corporation and receives $100,000 of dividends from it. Under the dividends-received deduction, ABC can generally exclude from taxable income:
e: A corporation owning less than 20% of a domestic payer can generally exclude 50% of dividends received, or $50,000. The 65% exclusion requires 20% or more ownership.
k: DRD: corporations exclude 50% of domestic dividends (65% if they own 20%+).
w: The DRD does apply to corporate recipients.
65% requires owning 20% or more of the payer.
Dividends are not fully excluded at this ownership level.
m: DRD explains why corporations like preferred stock.

q: An investor bought shares of a mutual fund four months ago. The fund now pays a long-term capital gains distribution. For the investor, the distribution is taxed as:
o: Short-term, because she owned the fund less than a year
Tax-free until the fund shares are sold
Ordinary income, like a money market dividend
Long-term, regardless of how long she owned the fund
e: Long-term capital gains distributions are long-term to the shareholder no matter how long the fund shares have been held. The fund's holding period, not the investor's, determines the character.
k: Fund LT capital gains distributions are long-term regardless of the shareholder's holding period.
w: The investor's holding period doesn't change a fund's LT distribution.
Distributions are taxable in the year paid.
Only short-term gain distributions are taxed as ordinary income.
m: Reported on Form 1099-DIV.

q: A US investor receives dividends from a foreign company, and taxes are withheld by the company's home country. The investor can usually:
o: Claim a foreign tax credit on her US return
Recover the withheld tax by filing Form W-8BEN
Deduct the withheld tax as a capital loss
Exclude the foreign dividends from US income
e: Foreign taxes withheld on dividends can usually be claimed as a foreign tax credit, reducing US tax owed on the same income.
k: Foreign tax withheld on dividends: usually claimed as a US foreign tax credit.
w: W-8BEN is filed by foreign investors in US securities.
Withheld taxes aren't treated as capital losses.
Foreign dividends are still taxable US income.

q: A resident of a high-tax state wants interest income that is exempt from state income tax but is willing to pay federal tax. Which of the following fits?
o: Interest on Ginnie Mae pass-through certificates
Interest on bank certificates of deposit
e: Interest on US Treasury securities is subject to federal income tax but exempt from state and local income tax.
k: Treasuries: federally taxable, state and local tax exempt.
w: Ginnie Mae interest is taxable at federal, state and local levels.
Corporate bond interest is taxable at all levels.
CD interest is taxable at all levels.
m: Mortgage-backed agencies get no state break.

q:
Interest from which of the following is exempt from state income tax?
I. Treasury bills
II. Ginnie Mae certificates
III. Federal Home Loan Bank bonds
IV. Corporate commercial paper
e: Treasuries and most federal agency debt, such as FHLB bonds, are state tax exempt. Mortgage-backed agency securities like Ginnie Mae, and corporate debt, are taxed at all levels.
k: Treasuries and most agencies (FHLB, Farm Credit) are state-exempt; GNMA/FNMA/FHLMC are not.
w: Ginnie Mae interest is taxable at the state level.
Both GNMA and commercial paper interest are state-taxable.
Commercial paper interest is taxable at all levels.
m: GNMA has full-faith backing but no state exemption.

q: An investor buys a municipal bond in the secondary market at 92 and holds it to maturity at 100. The 8-point market discount is generally:
o: Not taxable because the bond is a municipal security
e: Market discount on a bond bought below par in the secondary market is taxed as ordinary interest income when the bond is sold or matures. This applies even to munis.
k: Market discount (secondary purchase below par) = ordinary income at sale/maturity, even on munis.
w: Only the coupon and OID accretion on munis are tax-exempt.
Market discount is taxed as ordinary income, not capital gain.
Muni status doesn't shelter market discount.
m: OID on munis = tax-free; market discount on munis = taxable.

q: An investor buys a municipal bond at 108 and holds it until it matures at par. For tax purposes:
o: She must amortize the premium and has no deductible loss
She reports an $80 capital loss per bond at maturity
She deducts the $80 premium against ordinary income
She may choose whether to amortize the premium
e: Premium on tax-exempt munis must be amortized, reducing basis to par by maturity. The amortized premium is not deductible, so there is no loss.
k: Muni premium: amortization required, not deductible; no loss at maturity.
w: Amortization brings basis to par, so no loss occurs.
Amortized muni premium is not deductible.
Amortization is optional for taxable bonds, required for munis.

q: An investor holds a municipal zero-coupon bond originally issued at a deep discount. The annual accretion is:
o: Taxable each year as phantom income
A capital gain taxed only at maturity
Tax-exempt interest that increases cost basis
Taxable as ordinary income only at maturity
e: For municipal OID, the accretion is treated as tax-exempt interest. The investor's basis still rises each year, so there's no gain if held to maturity.
k: Muni OID accretion = tax-exempt interest; basis still accretes.
w: Phantom income applies to corporate and Treasury zeros.
Accretion is interest, not capital gain.
Muni OID accretion is tax-exempt, not deferred ordinary income.

q: A buyer of a corporate bond pays the seller $40 of accrued interest at settlement. A few weeks later the buyer receives a $250 semiannual coupon. For tax purposes, the buyer reports interest income of:
e: Accrued interest paid to the seller is deducted from the buyer's first interest payment. The seller reports the $40 as interest income, and the buyer reports $250 - $40 = $210.
k: Accrued interest paid by the buyer reduces the buyer's first interest payment for tax.
w: $40 is the seller's interest income, not the buyer's.
Ignores the accrued interest the buyer paid the seller.
Adds the accrued interest instead of subtracting it.

q: Which statement about interest on Series EE savings bonds is TRUE?
o: It is taxed annually at the federal level as it accrues
It is subject to state and local income tax
It is exempt from federal tax in all cases
It is tax-deferred until redemption and may be federally tax-free if used for qualified education expenses
e: Savings bond interest is federally taxable but deferred until redemption, and it can be federally tax-free when used for qualified higher-education expenses, subject to income limits. Like other Treasuries, it is state tax exempt.
k: EE/I bonds: tax-deferred until redemption; possibly tax-free for education; state exempt.
w: Federal tax is deferred until redemption.
Savings bonds are Treasury obligations, exempt from state tax.
Only education use (with income limits) can make it federally tax-free.

q: An investor buys stock with a trade date of March 3, 2025. What is the earliest trade date on which she can sell and receive long-term capital gain treatment?
e: Long-term requires holding more than one year. The holding period begins the day after the purchase trade date, so a sale on March 3, 2026 is exactly one year (short-term); March 4, 2026 qualifies.
k: Long-term = held more than one year; holding period starts the day after trade date.
w: That sale date is less than one year after purchase.
Exactly one year is still short-term.
Six months is far short of the one-year requirement.
m: One year or less = short-term.

q: An investor buys 100 shares at $40 and pays a $25 commission. She later sells them at $52 and pays a $30 commission. Her capital gain is:
k: Gain = net proceeds (less commission) - cost basis (plus commission).
w: Ignores both commissions.
Deducts only the purchase commission.
Adds the commissions instead of subtracting them.
m: Commissions raise basis and reduce proceeds.

q: A married investor filing separately has a net capital loss of $5,000 for the year and no other capital gains. She may:
o: Deduct $3,000 against ordinary income and carry forward $2,000
Deduct $1,500 against ordinary income and carry forward $3,500
Deduct the full $5,000 against ordinary income
Carry forward the loss for up to five years only
e: The annual limit on net capital losses deducted against ordinary income is $3,000, or $1,500 for married filing separately. The remaining $3,500 carries forward indefinitely.
k: Net capital loss deduction: $3,000/yr ($1,500 married filing separately); rest carries forward indefinitely.
w: $3,000 is the limit for other filers, not married filing separately.
Deductions against ordinary income are capped each year.
Unused capital losses carry forward indefinitely.
m: MFS = half the $3,000 limit.

q: An investor bought 100 shares of ABC at $50. On November 1 she sells them at $42 for an $800 loss, and on November 20 she buys 100 ABC at $44. Her cost basis in the new shares is:
e: The repurchase within 30 days triggers the wash sale rule, disallowing the $800 loss. The disallowed loss is added to the new shares' basis: $4,400 + $800 = $5,200.
k: Wash sale: disallowed loss is added to the cost basis of replacement shares.
w: Ignores the disallowed loss added to basis.
Uses the sale price, not the repurchase price plus loss.
Original basis; the new basis is cost plus disallowed loss.
m: Wash sale defers the loss; it isn't lost forever.

q: An investor sells shares of Alpha Motors at a loss. Which of the following purchases within 30 days would NOT cause the loss to be disallowed under the wash sale rule?
o: Bonds convertible into Alpha Motors common stock
Shares of Beta Motors, a competitor in the same industry
Alpha Motors common stock bought 25 days before the sale
e: Buying a different company, even in the same industry, is not substantially identical and does not trigger the wash sale rule.
k: Wash sale covers the same stock, its options/warrants and convertibles, 30 days before or after.
w: Options on the same stock are substantially identical.
Securities convertible into the stock are substantially identical.
The window covers 30 days before the sale too.
m: 61-day window centered on the sale date.

q: An investor bought three lots of 100 XYZ shares at $20, $35 and $50. XYZ is now $45 and he wants to sell 100 shares while minimizing his tax bill. He should:
o: Let the IRS default apply, selling the $20 lot
Use specific identification and sell the $50 lot
Use specific identification and sell the $20 lot
Use average cost, giving a $35 basis
e: Specific identification lets the investor choose the highest-cost lot. Selling the $50 lot at $45 produces a loss instead of a gain.
k: Specific identification is most flexible; sell the highest-cost lot to minimize gain.
w: FIFO sells the $20 lot, creating the largest gain.
Selling the lowest-cost lot maximizes the taxable gain.
Average cost is permitted for mutual fund shares, not individual stocks.
m: FIFO = IRS default; usually biggest gain in rising market.

q: A donor gives 100 shares she bought at $40 to her nephew when the stock is worth $25. The nephew later sells at $20. His deductible loss is:
e: When the value at the gift date is below the donor's basis, the recipient's basis for a loss is the fair market value at the gift. Loss = ($25 - $20) x 100 = $500.
k: Gift at a loss: recipient's loss basis = FMV at gift date.
w: Uses the donor's $40 basis; not allowed for losses here.
That is the donor's pre-gift loss, which doesn't transfer.
A loss below the gift-date value is deductible.
m: Donor's built-in loss doesn't pass to the recipient.

q: In 2026, a married couple wants to give cash to their son without filing a gift tax return. The most they can give him together is:
e: The 2026 annual gift tax exclusion is $19,000 per donor per recipient, so a married couple can give $38,000 to one person without filing a gift tax return.
k: 2026 annual gift exclusion: $19,000 per recipient; $38,000 for a married couple.
w: Outdated exclusion amount.
That is the limit for one donor, not a couple.
Outdated doubled amount.
m: Spousal gifts are unlimited.

q: An investor inherits stock and sells it two months after the owner's death. The gain or loss is treated as:
o: Short-term, because the heir held it less than a year
Long-term, regardless of the holding period
Long-term only if the deceased held it more than a year
Not taxable, because inherited property is exempt
e: Inherited securities automatically receive long-term treatment, with basis stepped up (or down) to the fair market value on the date of death.
k: Inherited securities: stepped-up basis to date-of-death value; automatically long-term.
w: Inherited holdings are automatically long-term.
The deceased's holding period doesn't matter for inherited assets.
Gains above the stepped-up basis are taxable.
m: Inheritance = step-up + automatic long-term.

q:
Which of the following are NOT taxable events for the investor when they occur?
I. Exchanging shares of one fund for another in the same fund family
II. Converting a convertible bond into common stock
III. Receiving a return-of-capital distribution
IV. Selling stock at a gain
e: Converting a bond into the issuer's stock is not taxable, and return of capital is not taxed when received but reduces cost basis. Fund exchanges and sales at a gain are taxable.
k: Not taxable now: bond conversion, return of capital (reduces basis). Fund exchanges are taxable sales.
w: A fund exchange within a family is a taxable sale.
Both are taxable sales.
A sale at a gain is a taxable event.
m: Exchange = sale for tax purposes.

q: An investor writes 1 XYZ call at 3, and the option expires unexercised seven months later. The tax result is:
o: No tax, because the option was never exercised
e: A writer whose option expires has a capital gain equal to the premium, and it is short-term.
k: Expired written option = short-term capital gain equal to the premium.
w: A writer's gain on expiration is short-term.
Option premiums are capital in nature, not interest.
Expiration closes the position and realizes the gain.

q: This year an investor has a $50,000 salary, $3,000 of dividends, $5,000 of income from a limited partnership and an $8,000 loss from a different limited partnership. How much of the loss can she use this year?
o: $5,000, against her passive income, carrying forward $3,000
e: Passive losses can offset only passive income. The $8,000 LP loss offsets the $5,000 of LP income, and the remaining $3,000 carries forward.
k: Passive losses offset only passive income; unused passive losses carry forward.
w: Salary is earned income; passive losses can't offset it.
Dividends are portfolio income; passive losses can't offset them.
Neither earned nor portfolio income can absorb passive losses.
m: Keep income buckets separate.

q:
Which of the following is classified as portfolio income?
I. Dividends
II. Rental income from a limited partnership
III. Capital gains
IV. Wages
e: Portfolio income includes interest, dividends, capital gains and royalties. LP rental income is passive, and wages are earned income.
k: Portfolio = interest, dividends, capital gains, royalties. Passive = LPs. Earned = wages.
w: LP rental income is passive income.
These are passive and earned income.
Wages are earned income.

q: A high-income client who is subject to the alternative minimum tax asks about municipal bonds. The rep should point out that interest on which bonds may be a tax preference item?
o: Revenue bonds for a public water system
e: Interest on private activity municipal bonds is an AMT preference item, so investors subject to AMT should be cautious about them.
k: Private activity muni interest is an AMT preference item.
w: GO bond interest is not an AMT preference item.
Public-purpose revenue bonds aren't private activity bonds.
Territory bonds are tax-exempt everywhere, not AMT items.
m: AMT client? Avoid private activity bonds.

q: A taxpayer owes $15,000 of federal income tax on $100,000 of taxable income, and his top bracket is 22%. His effective tax rate is:
e: The effective rate is total tax divided by total income: $15,000 / $100,000 = 15%. The 22% is his marginal rate on the next dollar.
k: Effective rate = total tax / total income; marginal rate = rate on next dollar.
w: That is the gap between the marginal and effective rates.
That is the marginal rate.
That is the top federal bracket, not his rate.

q: A customer sells stock at a gain with a trade date of December 31, 2026; the trade settles in January 2027. The gain is reported for tax year:
o: Either year, at the investor's election
2027, but only if proceeds are withdrawn in January
e: For securities sales, the trade date determines the tax year. A December 31 trade counts for that year even though it settles in January.
k: Trade date, not settlement date, determines the tax year of a sale.
w: Settlement date does not control the tax year.
The investor cannot choose the year.
Withdrawal of proceeds is irrelevant to timing.
m: Last-day sales count for the current year.

q: Under an asset-location strategy, which holding would be LEAST appropriate to place in a traditional IRA?
e: Muni interest is already tax-exempt, so holding it in a tax-deferred account wastes the benefit and turns tax-free income into taxable withdrawals. Munis belong in taxable accounts.
k: Asset location: tax-inefficient assets in tax-deferred accounts; munis in taxable accounts.
w: REIT dividends are tax-inefficient; a good fit for an IRA.
Taxable bond interest is a good fit for an IRA.
STRIPS create phantom income; ideal for tax-deferred accounts.
m: Never put munis in an IRA.

q: An issuer sells 5 million shares at a public offering price of $20. The issuer receives $18.60 per share. The manager's fee is $0.20 and the underwriting fee is $0.40. What is the selling concession per share?
e: The total spread is $20.00 - $18.60 = $1.40. Subtracting the manager's fee ($0.20) and the underwriting fee ($0.40) leaves an $0.80 selling concession.
k: Selling concession = total spread - manager's fee - underwriting fee.
w: Adds the two fees together instead of subtracting them from the spread.
Spread minus only the manager's fee; the underwriting fee was ignored.
This is the entire spread, not just the concession.
m: The concession is always the largest slice of the spread.

q: A broker-dealer joins an offering as a selling group member rather than as a syndicate member. Which statement about the firm is accurate?
o: It shares liability for any unsold shares in the offering
It earns the underwriting fee on every share in the deal
It runs the books and manages the stabilizing bid
It acts as agent and earns only the selling concession
e: Selling group members help distribute the issue but take no underwriting risk. They act as agents and are paid only the selling concession on the shares they sell.
k: Selling group: no underwriting risk, earns only the selling concession.
w: Unsold-share risk belongs to syndicate members, not the selling group.
The underwriting fee goes to syndicate members for taking risk.
Running the books and stabilizing are the manager's jobs.
m: Selling group = sells only, no risk, concession only.

q: Which document binds the members of an underwriting syndicate to one another and sets out each member's share of the risk?
o: The underwriting agreement with the issuer
The registration statement on Form S-1
The letter of intent filed with FINRA
e: The agreement among underwriters (the syndicate agreement) governs the relationship among the syndicate members. The underwriting agreement is the contract between the issuer and the syndicate.
k: Syndicate agreement = among underwriters; underwriting agreement = issuer and underwriters.
w: This contract is between the issuer and the syndicate, not among members.
The S-1 is the issuer's disclosure filing with the SEC.
Not a real syndicate document; a distractor using familiar terms.
m: Two contracts: issuer-to-syndicate and member-to-member.

q: In reviewing a registration statement for a new stock issue, the SEC's role is to:
o: Judge whether the stock is a suitable investment for the public
Guarantee the accuracy of the issuer's financial statements
Set the public offering price with the managing underwriter
Check that the required disclosures are complete
e: The SEC reviews registration statements for completeness of disclosure. It never rules on the merits of a security, guarantees accuracy, or sets prices.
k: SEC reviews for completeness only; never approves merits or accuracy.
w: Merit review is not part of the SEC's federal role.
Auditors and the issuer stand behind the financials; the SEC guarantees nothing.
Pricing is negotiated between the issuer and the underwriter.
m: SEC = complete, not approved.

q: A small company hires an underwriter on an all-or-none basis to raise $8 million. By the end of the offering period only $6.5 million has been sold. What happens?
o: The underwriter buys the remaining $1.5 million for its own account
The offering is cancelled and investors' escrowed funds are returned
The issuer keeps the $6.5 million and the deal closes early
The underwriter extends the offering by 90 days automatically
e: In an all-or-none best efforts deal, the entire amount must be sold or the offering is cancelled. Investor funds held in escrow are returned.
k: All-or-none: whole issue sells or deal is cancelled; funds held in escrow.
w: Buying the unsold portion describes a firm commitment, not best efforts.
Keeping partial proceeds would fit a mini-max deal, not all-or-none.
No automatic extension exists; this is made up.
m: AON = escrow until everything sells.

q: A company offers new shares to its existing shareholders through a rights offering and arranges for an investment bank to buy any shares the shareholders do not subscribe for. This arrangement is called a:
e: A standby underwriting is a form of firm commitment used with rights offerings: the underwriter stands by to purchase any shares left unsubscribed.
k: Standby underwriting = firm commitment to buy unsubscribed shares in a rights offering.
w: Mini-max sets a minimum and maximum; the underwriter buys nothing.
In best efforts the underwriter never commits to buy shares.
A shelf takedown is a sale off a Rule 415 shelf registration.
m: Rights offering + leftover shares bought = standby.

q: During the distribution of a new issue priced at $25, the managing underwriter may place a stabilizing bid at:
o: $25.50, as long as it is disclosed
Any price set by the syndicate
e: A stabilizing bid may be entered at or below the public offering price, never above it. It must be disclosed in the prospectus.
k: Stabilizing bid: at or below the POP, never above; disclosed in prospectus.
w: A bid above the POP would push the price up, which is manipulation.
Disclosure does not permit a bid above the offering price.
The price is capped at the POP; it is not open-ended.
m: Stabilize to support, never to raise.

q:
Which of the following statements about a firm commitment underwriting are TRUE?
I. The underwriter acts as principal
II. The issuer bears the risk of unsold shares
III. The underwriter is compensated through the spread
IV. It is commonly used for DPP offerings by small issuers
e: In a firm commitment, the underwriter buys the whole issue as principal and earns the spread; the underwriter (not the issuer) bears the unsold-share risk. Small, risky issuers and DPPs typically use best efforts.
k: Firm commitment: underwriter is principal, bears risk, earns the spread.
w: DPPs and small issuers typically use best efforts, not firm commitment.
The underwriter, not the issuer, holds unsold shares in a firm commitment.
Both describe best efforts features, not firm commitment.
m: Who owns the leftovers? Firm commitment: the underwriter.

q: A city plans to issue general obligation bonds and invites underwriting syndicates to submit sealed bids, awarding the deal to the lowest interest cost. This is an example of a:
e: In a competitive bid, syndicates submit sealed bids and the issuer chooses the one with the lowest cost. This method is typical for municipal G.O. bonds.
k: Competitive bid = sealed bids, lowest cost wins; common for muni G.O. bonds.
w: In a negotiated deal the issuer picks one underwriter and negotiates terms.
Mini-max describes the commitment type, not how the underwriter is chosen.
A public bond sale with syndicates is not a private placement.
m: G.O. bonds: usually competitive. Revenue bonds: usually negotiated.

q: A public company sells 3 million newly issued shares while two of its founders sell 1 million of their existing shares in the same registered offering. This is a:
e: An offering that is partly primary (new shares from the issuer) and partly secondary (existing holders selling) is a split, or combined, offering.
k: Split offering = part primary (issuer's new shares) + part secondary (existing holders).
w: This is still a registered offering, not ordinary exchange trading.
A direct listing involves no underwritten offering of new shares.
Shelf registration is about timing sales over 3 years, not who sells.
m: Mix of new and existing shares = split.

q: A seasoned issuer files a shelf registration under Rule 415. For how long may it sell securities off the shelf under that registration?
e: Rule 415 shelf registration lets a seasoned issuer register once and sell over up to 3 years, filing a prospectus supplement with each takedown.
k: Shelf registration (Rule 415): sell off the shelf for up to 3 years.
w: Too short; 12 months is a common Reg A/Reg D lookback, not shelf life.
Too short for a shelf registration.
Too long; the shelf period is 3 years.
m: Shelf = 3 years.

q: A private technology company lists its existing shares on a stock exchange without hiring an underwriter or issuing new shares. Which statement is correct?
o: It is a direct listing and raises no new capital
The company raises new capital at the opening trade
It is a SPAC merger requiring a blank check vehicle
It is a follow-on offering by a seasoned issuer
e: In a direct listing, existing shares begin trading on an exchange without an underwritten offering. No new shares are sold, so the company raises no new capital.
k: Direct listing: existing shares list on exchange; no underwriter, no new capital.
w: No new shares are sold, so no proceeds go to the company.
A SPAC is a shell that IPOs and later merges with a private company.
A follow-on is a new share sale by an already public company.
m: No new shares = no new money.

q: All of the following are primary offerings EXCEPT:
o: A company's initial public offering of new shares
A follow-on offering of newly created shares by a public company
A rights offering of new shares to existing shareholders
A registered sale of shares owned by a venture capital fund
e: In a primary offering the issuer sells new shares and receives the proceeds. When an existing holder such as a VC fund sells its own shares, it is a secondary offering and the holder gets the money.
k: Primary = issuer sells new shares, gets proceeds; secondary = existing holders sell.
w: An IPO of new shares is a primary offering.
A follow-on of new shares still raises money for the issuer.
New shares sold via rights are primary; the issuer gets proceeds.
m: Ask: who gets the money? Issuer = primary.

q: Before a company files its registration statement, a registered rep calls clients to ask whether they would like to reserve shares in the upcoming IPO. This is:
o: Permitted if the rep uses a tombstone script
Permitted because no money changes hands
Prohibited gun-jumping in the pre-filing period
e: No offers or solicitations of interest are allowed before the registration statement is filed. Soliciting reservations in the pre-filing period is gun-jumping.
k: Pre-filing period: no offers, no sales, no solicitation of interest (gun-jumping).
w: Tombstone ads are allowed only after filing, during cooling-off.
Even without payment, soliciting interest pre-filing is illegal.
Accredited status creates no pre-filing exception for a public IPO.
m: Pre-filing = nothing. Cooling-off = interest only.

q: During the cooling-off period, a customer asks his rep to put him down for 500 shares of the upcoming IPO and offers to send a check now. The rep should:
o: Record a non-binding indication of interest and accept no money
Accept the check and hold it until the effective date
Enter a binding order at the expected price range
Refuse to discuss the offering until it becomes effective
e: During cooling-off, a rep may take non-binding indications of interest but may not accept orders or money. Sales can occur only once the registration is effective.
k: Cooling-off: indications of interest allowed; no orders, no sales, no money.
w: Accepting money before effectiveness is prohibited.
No binding orders may be taken until the registration is effective.
Discussing the deal and providing a red herring are allowed during cooling-off.
m: No money until effective.

q: The SEC sends an issuer a deficiency letter on day 12 of the cooling-off period. Which statement is correct?
o: The 20-day cooling-off clock is paused until the issues are fixed
The registration becomes effective automatically on day 20
Sales may begin while the issuer answers the letter
The issuer must withdraw and refile under Regulation A
e: A deficiency letter stops the 20-day cooling-off clock until the issuer corrects the problems. The registration does not become effective in the meantime.
k: Cooling-off lasts at least 20 days; a deficiency letter pauses the clock.
w: A deficiency letter prevents effectiveness until the problems are resolved.
No sales are permitted until the registration is effective.
Deficiencies are corrected by amendment, not by switching exemptions.
m: Deficiency = clock stops.

q: Which item will NOT appear in a preliminary prospectus (red herring)?
e: The red herring contains everything in the final prospectus except the final offering price and the effective date. It may show an estimated price range.
k: Red herring lacks the final offering price and effective date.
w: Risk factors are included in the red herring.
Audited financials are part of the red herring.
Use of proceeds is disclosed in the red herring.
m: Red herring: no final price, no effective date.

q: An issuer is completing an IPO that is registered with the SEC and will be sold in 12 states. The issuer files with the states at the same time it files with the SEC. This state registration method is:
e: Registration by coordination means filing with the state at the same time as with the SEC. It is the typical blue-sky method for IPOs.
k: Blue-sky: coordination (with SEC filing), qualification (no SEC filing), notice filing (covered securities).
w: Qualification is full state review when there is no SEC registration.
Notice filing is for federal covered securities like listed stocks.
An IPO sold to the public generally must register, not claim exemption.
m: Coordination = coordinated with the SEC filing.

q: During the cooling-off period, a rep sends a client the red herring with key passages highlighted and a one-page sales flyer attached. This is:
o: Acceptable if a principal approves the flyer
Acceptable as long as no order is taken
Prohibited only if the flyer mentions a price
Prohibited; the red herring may not be marked up or sent with sales literature
e: The preliminary prospectus may not be marked up, highlighted, or accompanied by sales literature during the cooling-off period.
k: Red herring: no highlighting, no markings, no accompanying sales literature.
w: Principal approval does not cure the ban on marked or supplemented red herrings.
Taking no order does not make the altered red herring acceptable.
The ban applies whether or not a price is mentioned.
m: Send the red herring clean.

q: When is the final public offering price of an IPO typically set?
o: When the registration statement is first filed
At the start of the cooling-off period
On the evening before the effective date
e: The underwriter builds the book from indications of interest and sets the final price on the evening before the registration becomes effective.
k: IPO price is set the evening before the effective date, based on the book.
w: At filing only a price range, if any, is shown.
The book is still being built during cooling-off.
The price must be set before any sales are made.
