o: Tax- and penalty-free, as a return of contributions
Taxable on $3,000 of earnings plus a penalty
Penalty-free but taxed as ordinary income
e: Roth withdrawals come from contributions first. Contributions were made with after-tax money and can be withdrawn anytime without tax or penalty.
k: Roth: contributions come out first and are always tax- and penalty-free.
w: Roth contributions were already taxed.
Earnings aren't reached until all $15,000 of contributions are out.
Return of after-tax contributions isn't taxed.
m: Roth basis out first, tax-free.

q: A high-income employee is covered by her employer's 401(k) plan and wants to contribute to a traditional IRA. Which is TRUE?
o: She is barred from contributing to any IRA
She may contribute, and the contribution is fully deductible
She may contribute only to a SEP IRA
She may contribute, but it may be non-deductible
e: Being covered by an employer plan with income above the phase-out doesn't prevent a traditional IRA contribution; it only limits deductibility, creating after-tax basis.
k: Plan coverage + high income limits the traditional IRA deduction, not the right to contribute.
w: Traditional IRAs have no income limit to contribute.
Coverage and high income phase out the deduction.
A SEP is employer-sponsored, not an individual alternative.
m: High earner + plan = non-deductible IRA.

q: A variable life policyholder decides she wants a guaranteed cash value. During the first 24 months after issue, she may:
o: Exchange it for a fixed whole life policy from the same insurer without evidence of insurability
Cancel and receive a refund of all premiums paid plus interest
Convert it to a variable annuity with a guaranteed rate
Exchange it for term insurance from any insurer without underwriting
e: Variable life owners have at least 24 months to exchange into a fixed (whole) life policy from the same insurer without proving insurability.
k: Variable life: at least 24 months to exchange into fixed life with the same insurer, no evidence of insurability.
w: The full-refund cancellation is the short free-look period.
VAs don't offer a guaranteed rate; the exchange is to fixed life.
The exchange is to the same insurer's permanent fixed policy.
m: VL exchange right: 24 months, same insurer.

q: Over the life of a variable life insurance policy, sales charges are capped at:
e: Sales charges on variable life are limited to 9% of total premiums over the policy's life (measured over a maximum of 20 years).
k: Variable life sales charges: max 9% of total premiums over the policy life (up to 20 years).
w: The cap is higher than 5%.
8.5% is the mutual fund maximum sales charge.
Twenty is the maximum years in the computation, not a percentage.
m: VL 9%; mutual funds 8.5%.

q: All of the following are tax-free Section 1035 exchanges EXCEPT:
o: A life insurance policy for another life policy
A life insurance policy for an annuity
An annuity for a life insurance policy
e: Section 1035 allows life-to-life, life-to-annuity and annuity-to-annuity exchanges. An annuity can't be exchanged tax-free for life insurance.
k: 1035: life to life, life to annuity, annuity to annuity; never annuity to life.
w: Life-to-life is a permitted 1035 exchange.
Life-to-annuity is permitted.
Annuity-to-annuity is permitted.
m: Annuity to life: not allowed.

q: Which risk is borne primarily by the owner of a fixed annuity?
o: Investment risk on the general account
Mortality risk on the insurer's pool
e: In a fixed annuity the insurer guarantees the rate and bears investment risk; the owner's fixed payments can lose value to inflation.
k: Fixed annuity: insurer bears investment risk; owner bears inflation risk; not a security.
w: The insurer bears general-account investment risk.
Separate accounts back variable, not fixed, annuities.
Mortality risk is the insurer's, covered by the M&E charge.
m: Fixed annuity owner fears inflation.

q: When a variable annuity owner annuitizes, the accumulation units are converted into:
o: A fixed number of annuity units whose value varies
A variable number of annuity units of fixed value
Shares of the insurer's general account
e: At annuitization, accumulation units convert to a fixed number of annuity units; each unit's value, and so each payment, changes with performance relative to the AIR.
k: Annuitization: fixed number of annuity units; unit value varies with performance vs. AIR.
w: The count is fixed; the unit value changes.
Variable annuities stay in the separate account.
Variable payouts aren't fixed dollar amounts.
m: Number fixed, value varies.

q: An investor put $100,000 into a variable annuity and made no withdrawals. During the accumulation phase the contract value falls to $82,000, and she dies. Her beneficiary receives at least:
e: The guaranteed minimum death benefit is typically the greater of contract value or total premiums paid (less withdrawals), so the beneficiary gets at least $100,000.
k: VA death benefit during accumulation: greater of contract value or premiums paid, less withdrawals.
w: That's the loss, not the benefit.
Ignores the guaranteed minimum death benefit.
Not a recognized death benefit calculation.
m: Death benefit protects the premiums paid.

q: A retiree annuitizes a non-qualified variable annuity purchased with after-tax money. How is each payment taxed?
o: Entirely tax-free as a return of premium
Partly tax-free return of basis, partly ordinary income
e: An exclusion ratio splits each annuitized payment into a tax-free return of cost basis and a taxable portion taxed as ordinary income.
k: Annuitized non-qualified payments: exclusion ratio splits basis (tax-free) and earnings (ordinary income).
w: Earnings in each payment are taxable.
Fully taxable treatment applies to qualified annuities.
Annuity earnings are never capital gains.
m: Annuitized = exclusion ratio; random withdrawals = LIFO.

q: A grandmother wants to make a large one-time 529 plan contribution for her grandson in 2026 without using any lifetime gift tax exemption. Using the 5-year election, the most she can contribute is:
e: The 5-year front-loading election treats one contribution as made over 5 years: 5 x $19,000 = $95,000 per donor ($190,000 for a couple).
k: 529 front-loading = 5 x annual exclusion ($95,000 per donor in 2026).
w: That's one year's annual exclusion.
That's a couple's one-year exclusion.
That's the limit for a married couple, not one donor.
m: 529 superfunding: 5 years of exclusions at once.

q: A child's parents and grandparents each want to contribute $2,000 this year to a Coverdell ESA for the same child. In total, how much may be contributed for the child this year?
e: The Coverdell limit is $2,000 per beneficiary per year from all contributors combined, not per contributor.
k: Coverdell ESA: $2,000 per beneficiary per year, all contributors combined.
w: Treats the limit as per family branch.
Treats the limit as per contributor.
There's no per-contributor limit; it's per child.
m: Coverdell limit is per child.

q:
Which of the following are TRUE of a Coverdell Education Savings Account?
I. Contributions are limited to $2,000 per beneficiary per year
II. There are no income limits on contributors
III. Funds generally must be used by the beneficiary's age 30
IV. Qualified K-12 expenses may be paid tax-free
e: Coverdells cap contributions at $2,000 per beneficiary, impose income limits on contributors, require use by age 30, and cover qualified K-12 and college expenses.
k: Coverdell: $2,000/yr, income limits, contribute until 18, use by 30, K-12 allowed.
w: Coverdells do have income limits.
Item II is false; income limits apply.
Item II is false; that describes 529 plans.
m: No income limits = 529, not Coverdell.

q: Which account offers deductible contributions, tax-free growth, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified medical expenses?
e: An HSA is the only account with a triple tax advantage: deductible contributions, tax-free growth, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified medical expenses. It requires a high-deductible health plan.
k: HSA: deductible in, tax-free growth, tax-free out for medical; requires a high-deductible health plan.
w: Roth contributions aren't deductible.
529 contributions aren't federally deductible.
ABLE contributions aren't federally deductible.
m: Triple tax advantage = HSA.

q: How is the Securities and Exchange Commission led?
o: By five commissioners appointed by the President to staggered five-year terms
By seven governors appointed by the President to fourteen-year terms
By a board elected by the FINRA member firms it supervises
By nine commissioners chosen by Congress with no party limits
e: The SEC is headed by five presidentially appointed commissioners serving staggered five-year terms, with no more than three from one political party.
k: SEC: 5 commissioners, appointed by the President, 5-year staggered terms, max 3 from one party.
w: Seven governors with 14-year terms describes the Federal Reserve Board.
The SEC is a federal agency; FINRA members don't elect its leadership.
Congress doesn't appoint commissioners, and party balance is required.
m: SEC = government agency; FINRA = private non-profit SRO.

q: A bank dealer's municipal securities department violates an MSRB fair-dealing rule. Which body would enforce the rule against the bank dealer?
o: The bank dealer's federal banking regulator
The municipal issuer whose bonds were sold
e: The MSRB writes rules but cannot enforce them. FINRA and the SEC enforce MSRB rules for securities firms, while bank regulators enforce them for bank dealers.
k: MSRB writes muni rules but has no enforcement power; bank regulators enforce them for bank dealers.
w: The MSRB has no enforcement power at all.
FINRA enforces MSRB rules for securities firms, not banks.
The MSRB and its rules have no authority over municipal issuers.
m: MSRB makes the rules; others enforce them.

q: A registered representative loses a FINRA disciplinary hearing and wants to appeal. Under FINRA's Code of Procedure, the first level of appeal is to:
e: Hearing panel decisions are appealed first to FINRA's National Adjudicatory Council (NAC). After that the SEC can review the case, followed by federal court.
k: FINRA appeals path: hearing panel, then NAC, then SEC, then federal court.
w: The SEC reviews the case only after the NAC has ruled.
State Administrators play no part in FINRA disciplinary appeals.
Federal court is the last step, after the NAC and the SEC.
m: Appeal order: NAC, SEC, courts.

q: An investment adviser that manages $60 million of client assets and does not qualify for any special exemption generally registers with:
e: Advisers with at least $100 million in assets under management register with the SEC. Smaller advisers generally register with the states.
k: Investment advisers: $100 million+ AUM register with SEC; below that, with the state.
w: SEC registration generally starts at $100 million of AUM.
Investment advisers have no SRO; FINRA oversees broker-dealers.
The MSRB writes municipal securities rules, not adviser registration rules.
m: Under $100 million AUM, think state.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts broker-dealers and investment advisers?
o: Advisers owe a fiduciary duty at all times; broker-dealers follow Reg BI for retail recommendations
Broker-dealers are fiduciaries at all times; advisers follow Regulation Best Interest
Both are supervised by FINRA as their self-regulatory organization
Advisers register on Form BD; broker-dealers register on Form ADV
e: Investment advisers are fiduciaries at all times. Broker-dealers follow Reg BI when recommending to retail customers and suitability for institutional ones.
k: IA = fiduciary always (Form ADV, no SRO); BD = Reg BI for retail recommendations (Form BD, FINRA).
w: This reverses the two standards.
Investment advisers have no SRO; they answer to the SEC or the states.
The forms are reversed: BDs file Form BD, advisers file Form ADV.
m: Adviser = fiduciary; broker = best interest.

q: The SEC has all of the following powers EXCEPT:
o: Approving rule changes proposed by FINRA
Seeking injunctions and disgorgement in civil court
Prosecuting criminal securities fraud cases itself
e: The SEC brings civil enforcement actions only. It refers criminal cases to the Department of Justice, which prosecutes them.
k: SEC = civil enforcement; criminal cases are referred to the Department of Justice.
w: The SEC must approve SRO rules.
Civil injunctions, fines and disgorgement are SEC remedies.
The SEC registers exchanges, SROs, transfer agents and clearing agencies.
m: Criminal prosecution = DOJ, not the SEC.

q: A trader enters several large buy orders just below the best bid with no intention of letting them execute. Once other buyers push the price up, he sells shares he already owns and cancels the buy orders. This is:
e: Spoofing or layering means entering orders you never intend to execute to move the price, then cancelling them. It is market manipulation.
k: Spoofing/layering: orders entered without intent to execute, to move the price, then cancelled.
w: Front-running means trading ahead of a known customer order or a research report.
Marking the close means trading near the close to set the closing price.
Backing away is a market maker refusing to honor its firm quote.
m: Fake orders that get cancelled = spoofing.

q: A rep learns that her firm's analysts will publish a strong buy rating on a stock tomorrow morning. She buys the stock for her own account this afternoon. This is:
o: Permitted, because research reports become public
e: Trading ahead of a firm's upcoming research report, to profit from the expected price move, is front-running.
k: Front-running: trading ahead of a large customer order or an upcoming research report.
w: Interpositioning puts an unneeded third party between the firm and the best market.
Painting the tape is a series of trades meant to show false activity.
The report isn't public yet, so trading ahead of it is prohibited.
m: Trading ahead of your own firm's report = front-running.

q: A stock's IPO is priced at $20.00 per share. Which bid by the managing underwriter is permitted?
o: A bid at $20.25 to show strong demand
A bid at $21.00 to push trading above the offering price
e: Stabilization is the only permitted price-supporting activity. The bid must be disclosed and placed at or below the public offering price.
k: Stabilizing bid: allowed only if disclosed and at or below the public offering price.
w: A stabilizing bid may not be above the offering price.
Stabilization must be disclosed to be legal.
Pushing the price above the offering price is manipulation, not stabilization.
m: Stabilize at or below the POP, never above.

q: A customer buys $8,000 of stock in a cash account and sells it two days later without ever paying, planning to cover the purchase with the sale proceeds. What happens to the account?
o: It is converted to a margin account
It is closed and reported to FINRA
e: Buying and selling without paying is freeriding. The account is frozen for 90 days, and during that time the customer must pay in full before any purchase.
k: Freeriding in a cash account results in a 90-day freeze.
w: Freeriding doesn't convert the account to margin.
The freeze lasts 90 days, not 30.
The penalty is a freeze, not automatic closure.
m: Freeriding = 90-day freeze.

q: A market maker quotes a stock at 25.10-25.20 for 500 shares. Another dealer tries to sell 500 shares at 25.10, and the market maker refuses the trade. This is:
e: A market maker must honor its firm quotes. Refusing to trade at a firm quote for the size shown is backing away.
k: Backing away: a market maker refusing to honor its own firm quote.
w: Capping means trading to hold a stock's price down.
Interpositioning puts an unnecessary third party into a customer trade.
Trading ahead means the firm trades before a customer's limit order.
m: Firm quote means firm; refusing it = backing away.

q:
Which of the following are forms of market manipulation?
I. Marking the close
II. Interpositioning
III. A disclosed stabilizing bid at the offering price
IV. Pegging
e: Marking the close, interpositioning and pegging are all prohibited. A disclosed stabilizing bid at or below the offering price is the only permitted price support.
k: Only a disclosed stabilizing bid at or below the POP is permitted; the rest is manipulation.
w: Stabilization is permitted, and II and IV are manipulative.
Marking the close (I) is also manipulation.
A disclosed stabilizing bid (III) is permitted.

q: When a regulator decides whether a customer's account was churned, the central question is whether:
o: The customer lost money on most of the trades
The account had written discretionary authority
Each trade, viewed alone, was suitable
Trading was excessive for the customer's objectives and resources
e: Churning is trading that is excessive given the customer's objectives and resources, done to generate commissions. A loss in the account is not required.
k: Churning = excessive trading relative to the customer's profile; the rep's commissions matter, not the customer's losses.
w: Churning can happen in a profitable account.
Discretion draws more scrutiny but isn't required for churning.
Trades that are suitable one by one can still be excessive in total.
m: Churning is judged by frequency and cost, not by profit.

q: A rep puts 10% of the money into a joint account with her husband, who is her customer. With the firm's and husband's prior written approval, she may share in the account's profits:
o: Only up to 10%, matching her contribution
In any proportion, because her husband is immediate family
Not at all, since reps may never share in customer accounts
Only after FINRA approves the arrangement
e: Sharing requires prior written approval from the firm and the customer. Proportional sharing is not required when the customer is an immediate family member, such as a spouse.
k: Account sharing: written approval needed; proportional to contribution unless the customer is immediate family.
w: Proportionality doesn't apply to immediate family members.
Sharing is allowed with prior written approval.
The firm and the customer approve; FINRA does not.
m: Family is the exception to proportional sharing.

q: A nervous customer will buy a recommended stock only if the rep promises to cover any loss. The rep agrees to repay losses from his own funds. This arrangement is:
o: Permitted if the customer signs a written agreement
Permitted if a principal approves it in advance
Permitted only for immediate family accounts
e: Reps and firms may never guarantee a customer against loss. No written agreement, approval or family relationship changes this.
k: Guaranteeing a customer against loss is always prohibited.
w: A written agreement doesn't make a guarantee legal.
Principal approval cannot authorize a guarantee.
The family exception applies to sharing, not guarantees.
m: Never guarantee against loss, no exceptions.

q: A rep recommends that a customer sell one fund family's Class A shares and buy another family's Class A fund with the same objective. The only result is a new front-end sales charge. This practice is:
e: Moving a customer between fund families or variable annuities to create new sales charges, without a legitimate reason, is switching.
k: Switching: moving a customer between funds or VAs to generate new sales charges without reason.
w: Breakpoint selling keeps a purchase just below a discount level.
Commingling mixes customer assets with firm or rep assets.
Blanket recommendations give every customer the same security.
m: New load, same objective = switching.

q: Without asking, a rep buys 200 shares of a stock for a customer whose account is non-discretionary, expecting the customer to approve. The stock rises 15% and the customer is pleased. Which statement is true?
o: There is no violation because the customer approved afterward
There is a violation only if the customer files a complaint
The trade is acceptable if it is confirmed within 24 hours
The trade was unauthorized and a violation despite the profit
e: A trade entered without the customer's permission or written discretionary authority is unauthorized. That is true even when the trade makes money.
k: Unauthorized trading is a violation even if it's profitable or later accepted.
w: Approval after the fact doesn't fix an unauthorized trade.
The violation exists whether or not anyone complains.
Sending a confirmation is not the same as authorization.
m: Profit doesn't excuse an unauthorized trade.

q: Which of the following is NOT a prohibited practice?
o: Keeping customer checks in the rep's personal bank account until month-end
Accurately telling a customer a bond pays its stated 5% coupon
Holding a customer's position in a relative's account to avoid limits
Telling a customer the SEC has approved a fund's prospectus
e: Accurately describing an issuer's own obligation, such as a bond's stated coupon, is not a guarantee. Commingling, parking and claiming SEC approval are all violations.
k: Describing an issuer's own obligation is fine; reps may not personally guarantee returns.
w: This is commingling customer funds with the rep's own money.
Hiding positions in other accounts is parking or a fictitious account.
The SEC never approves securities; saying so is misrepresentation.

q: Before a failed drug trial is announced, a company executive sells 10,000 shares at $40. After the announcement the stock trades at $28. What is the maximum civil penalty under ITSFEA?
e: The executive avoided a $120,000 loss. ITSFEA allows a civil penalty of up to three times the profit gained or loss avoided, which is $360,000.
k: ITSFEA civil penalty = up to 3 x (profit gained or loss avoided).
w: That is only the loss avoided, before tripling.
That doubles the loss avoided; the penalty is treble.
That is the full $400,000 sale proceeds, not three times the loss avoided.
m: Insider civil penalty = treble damages.

q:
Which of the following would NOT be insider trading?
I. Buying a stock after overhearing an unconfirmed rumor at a restaurant
II. A lawyer buying shares of a target her client plans to acquire
III. An officer selling under a 10b5-1 plan set up a year earlier
IV. An officer telling a friend about a pending merger, without trading himself
e: Trading on rumors and trading under a pre-arranged 10b5-1 plan are not insider trading. The lawyer is liable under misappropriation, and the officer is liable as a tipper even without trading.
k: Rumors, public info, mosaic research and 10b5-1 plans aren't insider trading; tipping and misappropriation are.
w: Both II and IV are violations: misappropriation and tipping.
IV is a violation; the tipper is liable without trading.
II is misappropriation, so it is a violation.
m: Tippers are liable even if they never trade.

q: An employee of a financial printer typesets a confidential tender offer document and buys the target company's stock. He has no relationship with the target. He is liable under:
o: No theory, since he is not a corporate insider
e: Under the misappropriation theory, anyone who trades on confidential information taken from a source that trusted them is liable, even with no duty to the issuer.
k: Misappropriation theory: trading on confidential information taken from any source is insider trading.
w: Reg FD governs issuer disclosures to analysts and investors.
Section 16 applies to officers, directors and 10% holders of the issuer.
Printers, lawyers and other outsiders can still be liable.
m: Stealing the information = misappropriation.

q: A company director buys her company's stock in March and sells it at a profit in July. She had no material non-public information. Which statement is true?
o: No rule applies because she had no inside information
She must return the profit to the company under the short-swing rule
She owes treble damages under ITSFEA
Her broker-dealer must file a SAR on the trade
e: Section 16 requires insiders to give back profits from purchases and sales within six months, whether or not they had MNPI.
k: Section 16 short-swing rule: insiders return profits on buys and sells within 6 months.
w: The short-swing rule applies even without MNPI.
ITSFEA penalties require trading on MNPI.
A short-swing profit is not, by itself, suspicious activity.
m: Insider round trip in under 6 months = give back profit.

q: During a private call, a CFO accidentally reveals next quarter's sales outlook to a few institutional analysts. Under Regulation FD, the company must:
o: Disclose the information to the public promptly
Do nothing, because the disclosure was unintentional
Bar the analysts from trading the stock for 6 months
e: Reg FD requires simultaneous public disclosure for intentional selective disclosures and prompt public disclosure for accidental ones.
k: Reg FD: intentional selective disclosure means simultaneous public release; accidental means prompt public release.
w: Accidental disclosure still requires prompt public release.
Reg FD is an SEC rule about public disclosure, not FINRA notice.
Reg FD requires the issuer to disclose; it doesn't bar trading.
m: Intentional = simultaneous; accidental = prompt.

q: While its investment bankers advise on a pending acquisition, a broker-dealer bars employees from trading or soliciting the target's stock and announces the ban internally. The company has been placed on the firm's:
e: A restricted list limits trading, solicitation and research in an issuer while the firm has MNPI. A watch list is kept confidential and used only for monitoring.
k: Restricted list limits employee trading/solicitation; watch list is confidential monitoring by compliance.
w: A watch list is confidential and used for monitoring, not announced trading bans.
Do-not-call lists govern telemarketing.
OFAC lists name sanctioned persons and countries.
m: Watch = quiet monitoring; restricted = limits on activity.

q: A 79-year-old customer names her nephew as her trusted contact person. Which action may the firm take with the nephew?
o: Let him request withdrawals from the account
Ask him about the customer's health status or possible exploitation
Send him copies of all account statements automatically
e: A trusted contact may be contacted about possible exploitation, the customer's contact information or health, or a guardian or POA. The trusted contact has no authority over the account.
k: Trusted contact (18+): firm may consult them, but they have no authority over the account.
w: A trusted contact cannot place trades.
A trusted contact cannot move money.
Naming a trusted contact doesn't give them routine access to statements.
m: Trusted contact = someone to call, not someone in control.

q: Which customer is a specified adult under FINRA Rule 2165?
o: A 45-year-old whose cognitive impairment keeps him from protecting his own interests
A 16-year-old beneficiary of an UTMA account
A healthy 58-year-old widow who just inherited money
e: A specified adult is anyone age 65 or older, or anyone 18 or older with a mental or physical impairment that keeps them from protecting their own interests.
k: Specified adult: age 65+, or 18+ with an impairment preventing self-protection.
w: The age test is 65, and no impairment is mentioned.
Specified adults must be at least 18.
She is under 65 and has no impairment; inheriting money doesn't qualify her.
m: 65+, or 18+ and impaired.

q: A firm places a temporary hold on a specified adult's disbursement and extends it once based on its own internal review. No regulator or agency has asked for more time. What is the maximum total length of the hold?
e: The initial hold is up to 15 business days, and the firm may extend it by 10 more. A further 30 days is available only if a regulator or agency requests it.
k: Temporary hold: 15 business days + 10-day firm extension (+30 more only on regulator/agency request).
w: 10 days is only the extension.
15 days is only the initial hold.
55 days requires an additional extension requested by a regulator or agency.
m: 15 + 10 = 25 business days.

q: After placing a temporary hold because it suspects financial exploitation of a specified adult, the firm must notify the trusted contact and all authorized parties (other than suspected exploiters) within:
e: Notice to the trusted contact and all authorized parties must go out within 2 business days of the hold. Anyone suspected of the exploitation is not notified.
k: Temporary hold notice to trusted contact and authorized parties: within 2 business days.
w: Notice is required within 2 business days, not 5.
10 business days is the length of the firm's extension.
30 days relates to the regulator-requested extension, not the notice.
m: Hold placed, notify within 2 business days.

q: Under Regulation S-P, a broker-dealer's customers have the right to opt out of having their nonpublic personal information shared with:
o: Law enforcement acting under a subpoena
e: Reg S-P gives customers the right to opt out of information sharing with nonaffiliated third parties. Customers also get a privacy notice at account opening and every year after.
k: Reg S-P: privacy notice at opening and annually; customers may opt out of sharing with nonaffiliated third parties.
w: Customers cannot block legally required disclosures to regulators.
Reps need customer data to service the account.
Lawful subpoenas override opt-out choices.
m: Opt-out applies to nonaffiliated third parties.

q: A rep's firm files a Suspicious Activity Report on a customer's repeated cash deposits just under $10,000. The customer later asks the rep why compliance has been asking questions. The rep should:
o: Explain that a SAR was filed so the customer can respond
Tell the customer that a CTR was filed instead
Suggest combining future deposits into one deposit over $10,000
Not reveal that a SAR was filed
e: A customer may never be told that a SAR was filed. Deposits kept just under $10,000 to avoid a CTR are structuring, which is itself a crime.
k: Never tip off a customer that a SAR was filed; structuring to avoid CTRs is illegal.
w: Disclosing a SAR to the customer is prohibited.
Making up an explanation is misleading and still tips off the customer.
Coaching around reporting rules would help the customer launder money.
m: SARs are secret from the customer.

q: A prospect describes a private fund that has paid a steady 2% every month for six years, even during market crashes. The manager won't provide audited statements, and withdrawals are often delayed. These facts most strongly suggest:
e: Consistent high returns regardless of the market, no audited statements and trouble getting paid out are classic Ponzi red flags. Early investors are usually paid with new investors' money.
k: Ponzi red flags: steady high returns in any market, secrecy, unaudited statements, payout delays.
w: A pump-and-dump hypes a thinly traded stock, then sells.
An advance-fee scheme demands upfront fees for a promised payoff.
Real investments don't produce steady returns through crashes without audits.
m: Too smooth, too high, too secret = Ponzi.

q: A whistleblower gives the SEC original information that leads to $4 million in sanctions. Under the Dodd-Frank program, the whistleblower's award would range from:
e: Awards are 10% to 30% of sanctions when sanctions exceed $1 million. Of $4 million, that is $400,000 to $1,200,000.
k: Dodd-Frank whistleblower award = 10%-30% of sanctions over $1 million.
w: This uses 1%-10%; the range is 10%-30%.
The top of the range is 30%, which is $1.2 million, not 25%.
The bottom of the range is 10%, which is $400,000.
m: Whistleblower = 10% to 30%.

q:
Which of the following are anti-money laundering red flags?
I. A new customer is reluctant to provide identification
II. Funds are wired in from a high-risk country and withdrawn days later without being invested
III. A customer invests the same amount each month through payroll deduction
IV. Deposits arrive from unrelated third parties with no explanation
e: Reluctance to provide ID, quick in-and-out wires with high-risk countries and unexplained third-party payments are all red flags. Regular payroll investing is normal behavior.
k: AML red flags: secrecy, reluctance to provide ID, high-risk wires, in-and-out funds, unexplained third-party payments.
w: Unexplained third-party deposits (IV) are also a red flag.
Regular payroll investing (III) is ordinary, and I and II are red flags.
Regular payroll deductions (III) show no suspicious pattern.

q: Which law amended the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 to allow a national securities association to regulate the over-the-counter market?
e: The Maloney Act of 1938 allowed a national securities association (the NASD, now FINRA) to regulate the OTC market.
k: Maloney Act (1938): created the framework for NASD/FINRA to self-regulate the OTC market.
w: The Trust Indenture Act requires indentures for corporate bond issues.
The 1975 amendments created the MSRB.
The Advisers Act regulates investment advisers.
m: Maloney = the law that led to FINRA.

q: Regulation S-P, which requires broker-dealers to protect customers' financial privacy, was adopted under which law?
e: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 addressed the privacy of consumer financial information. The SEC carried this out through Regulation S-P.
k: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (1999) leads to Regulation S-P (privacy).
w: Sarbanes-Oxley covers corporate accountability and auditor independence.
The PATRIOT Act covers anti-money laundering programs.
Dodd-Frank covers post-crisis reform and the whistleblower program.
m: Privacy = GLBA = Reg S-P.

q: Which SEC regulation governs short sales, including the locate requirement before a short sale?
e: Regulation SHO governs short selling, including locating shares before the sale. Naked shorting without a locate is a short-sale abuse.
k: Reg SHO = short sales; Reg M = distributions; Reg NMS = national market system; Reg T = margin.
w: Reg M addresses manipulation during distributions.
Reg NMS deals with order protection and the national market system.
Reg T is the Fed's margin rule for broker-dealer credit.
m: SHO = SHOrt sales.

q: Which law eased capital raising by creating equity crowdfunding and permitting general solicitation in Rule 506(c) offerings?
e: The JOBS Act of 2012 created emerging growth company status, crowdfunding and Reg A+, and allowed general solicitation in 506(c) offerings.
k: JOBS Act (2012): EGCs, crowdfunding, Reg A+, general solicitation under 506(c).
w: Dodd-Frank was post-crisis reform: CFPB, Volcker rule, whistleblowers.
Sarbanes-Oxley addressed corporate accountability after Enron.
The 1933 Act set up registration; 506(c) came much later.
m: Easier capital raising = JOBS Act.

q: A rep in New York (Eastern time) wants to cold-call a prospect in California (Pacific time, 3 hours behind). What is the earliest Eastern time the rep may place the call?
e: Cold calls are allowed only from 8 am to 9 pm in the called party's time zone. 8 am Pacific is 11 am Eastern.
k: TCPA calling window: 8 am-9 pm in the called party's local time.
w: 8 am Eastern is 5 am in California.
9 am Eastern is 6 am in California.
Subtracting the 3 hours goes the wrong direction.
m: Always use the called party's clock.

q: Which call is exempt from the TCPA cold-calling restrictions, even if the number is on the National Do-Not-Call Registry?
o: A call to a customer who last traded with the firm 12 months ago
A call to a former customer whose last trade was 3 years ago
A call to a number taken from a purchased list of local doctors
A prerecorded sales message sent to a prospect's cell phone
e: An established business relationship within the past 18 months exempts the call. Older relationships, purchased lists and robocalls to cell phones without consent are not exempt.
k: TCPA established-relationship exemption: transaction or account within the past 18 months.
w: Three years exceeds the 18-month established relationship window.
A purchased list gives no consent or relationship.
Prerecorded calls to cell phones need prior express consent.
m: Established relationship = within 18 months.

q: A cold caller must do all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Give the caller's name and the firm's name
Provide the firm's telephone number or address
State that the call's purpose is to solicit securities business
Disclose the rep's CRD number and exam history
e: Callers must identify themselves, their firm, and the firm's phone number or address, and state that the call is to sell securities. CRD details are not required.
k: Cold-call disclosures: caller name, firm name, firm phone or address, and the securities sales purpose.
w: The caller's name and the firm's name are required.
The firm's phone number or address is required.
Stating the sales purpose is required.
m: Who, which firm, how to reach, why calling.

q: Within a 30-day period, a rep emails the same market commentary to 22 retail investors and 10 institutional investors. Under FINRA Rule 2210 this is:
o: A retail communication, because it reached 32 people
e: Only retail investors count toward the more-than-25 threshold for retail communications. Sending to 22 retail investors within 30 days is correspondence.
k: Correspondence: 25 or fewer retail investors in 30 days; institutional recipients don't count toward the threshold.
w: Institutional recipients don't count toward the 25-retail-investor threshold.
Institutional communications must go only to institutional investors.
Public appearances are live, unscripted events such as seminars.
m: Count only retail recipients.

q: A broker-dealer that has been a FINRA member for five years creates a new mutual fund sales brochure. When must it be filed with FINRA?
o: At least 10 business days before first use
Within 10 business days of first use
It never needs to be filed
e: Retail communications about investment companies, such as mutual funds and variable annuities, are filed within 10 business days of first use. Filing 10 days before first use applies to a new firm's first year.
k: Investment company retail communications: file within 10 business days of first use (new firms: 10 days before).
w: Filing beforehand is required for new firms in their first year.
The deadline is 10 business days after first use, not 30 days.
Mutual fund retail communications are among the types that must be filed.
m: Fund literature: file within 10 days after use.

q: Which social media content requires prior approval by a registered principal?
o: A reply posted in a real-time chat
A direct message to one existing customer
An interactive comment on a firm blog post
A static profile page describing the rep's services
e: Static content, such as a profile or background page, is a retail communication and needs principal pre-approval. Interactive posts are supervised like correspondence.
k: Social media: static content = retail communication (pre-approval); interactive content = supervised like correspondence.
w: Real-time interactive posts are supervised, not pre-approved.
A message to one customer is correspondence; it's reviewed, not pre-approved.
Interactive comments are treated like correspondence.
m: Static = pre-approve; interactive = supervise.

q: A hypothetical variable annuity illustration used with retail investors may show a 0% gross rate of return and a maximum gross rate of:
e: VA hypothetical illustrations may show a 0% rate and other rates up to 12% gross. Otherwise, performance predictions and projections are prohibited.
k: VA illustrations: may show 0% and rates up to a maximum 12% gross.
w: The cap is 12%; 6% is just one rate that could be shown.
The cap is 12%, not 8%.
The cap is 12%, not 10%.

q: A retail communication shows a mutual fund's performance. It must include all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Standardized 1-, 5- and 10-year average annual total returns
Returns that reflect the maximum sales charge
A statement that past performance doesn't guarantee future results
A projection of next year's expected return
e: Fund performance must show standardized 1-, 5- and 10-year returns reflecting the maximum sales charge, with a past-performance disclaimer. Projections of future performance are prohibited.
k: Fund performance: 1/5/10-year standardized returns at maximum load plus a past-performance disclaimer; no projections.
w: Standardized 1-, 5- and 10-year returns are required.
Performance must reflect the maximum sales charge.
The past-performance disclaimer is required.
m: Projections are never allowed in fund ads.

q:
Which of the following are institutional investors for purposes of FINRA's communications rules?
I. An insurance company
II. An individual with a $5 million portfolio
III. An employee benefit plan with 150 participants
IV. A registered investment adviser
e: Insurers, investment advisers and benefit plans with at least 100 participants are institutional investors. An individual with $5 million falls well short of the $50 million total-assets test.
k: Institutional: banks, insurers, investment companies, RIAs, $50M+ entities, plans with 100+ participants, FINRA members.
w: II is retail: $5 million is below the $50 million test.
II is retail at $5 million; I and IV are also institutional.
II is wrong; $5 million is below the $50 million threshold.
m: Persons need $50 million in total assets to be institutional.

q: A customer whose shares are held in street name does not return voting instructions by the deadline. On which matter may the broker-dealer vote the shares?
o: Ratification of the company's independent auditor
An advisory say-on-pay vote on executive compensation
e: Without instructions, a broker-dealer may vote street-name shares only on routine matters such as auditor ratification. Director elections, mergers and compensation are non-routine.
k: Uninstructed street-name shares: broker may vote only routine items, such as auditor ratification.
w: Uncontested director elections are no longer routine.
Mergers are non-routine, so the broker cannot vote.
Executive compensation votes are non-routine.
m: Routine = auditor ratification.

q: A broker-dealer holds shares in street name for its customers. Who pays the cost of forwarding proxy materials and annual reports to the beneficial owners?
e: The broker-dealer must forward proxy materials and annual reports to beneficial owners, and the issuer pays for it.
k: Broker-dealer forwards proxy materials to street-name owners; the issuer pays the costs.
w: The broker-dealer forwards the materials but is reimbursed.
Customers are not charged for proxy delivery.
The transfer agent keeps ownership records; it doesn't pay forwarding costs.
m: Firm forwards, issuer pays.

q: Ana passed the SIE in March 2025 but has never been associated with a member firm. To use her SIE result, she must pass a representative exam and become registered no later than:
e: SIE results stay valid for 4 years. Ana must pass a top-off exam and register by March 2029 or retake the SIE.
k: SIE result valid 4 years from the pass date.
w: One year is too short; the SIE is valid 4 years.
Two years is the registration lapse period, not the SIE validity period.
Five years is the MQP maximum, not the SIE validity period.
m: SIE is good for 4 years.

q: A candidate fails the Series 7 for the second time on June 1. Under FINRA's waiting-period rules, the earliest date she may retest is about:
e: After a first or second failure the wait is 30 days. The 180-day wait applies only after a third or later failure.
k: Exam retest waits: 30 days after 1st and 2nd failures; 180 days after 3rd and later.
w: There's a 30-day waiting period after a failure.
90 days is not a FINRA retest period.
180 days applies only after a third failure.

q: A broker-dealer's Firm Element continuing education program must be based on:
o: The Regulatory Element content FINRA assigns
An annual needs analysis and a written training plan
Each rep's score on the SIE exam
A three-year cycle tied to each rep's registration anniversary
e: The Firm Element is the firm's own annual training. It is built from an annual needs analysis and a written training plan, and covers products, sales practices, regulation and ethics.
k: Firm Element CE: annual, firm-run, based on a needs analysis and a written training plan.
w: The Regulatory Element is FINRA's own separate training.
SIE scores don't determine Firm Element training.
CE is now annual; older cycles were tied to registration anniversaries.
m: Firm Element starts with a needs analysis.

q: A registered rep leaves the industry and does not enroll in the Maintaining Qualifications Program. Her qualification exams will lapse if she does not re-register within:
e: Without MQP, exam qualifications lapse after 2 years out of the industry. With MQP and annual CE, they can be kept for up to 5 years.
k: Out of industry: qualifications lapse after 2 years; MQP extends this to up to 5 years with annual CE.
w: The lapse period is 2 years, not 1.
4 years is the SIE validity period.
5 years requires MQP participation and annual CE.
m: 2 years out, or 5 years with MQP.

q: Under Regulation Best Interest, a broker-dealer must deliver Form CRS to a new retail customer:
o: Within 30 days after the account is opened
Only if the customer asks for it
At or before the earliest of a recommendation, an order or account opening
With the first quarterly account statement
e: Form CRS, the customer relationship summary, must be delivered at or before the earliest of a recommendation, an order or the opening of an account.
k: Form CRS: delivered at or before the earliest of a recommendation, order or account opening.
w: Delivery must happen up front, not after the account is opened.
Delivery is required, not on request.
The first statement is too late.
m: CRS comes first, before any business.

q: Under Reg BI's conflict-of-interest obligation, which of the following must a broker-dealer eliminate?
o: A firm limited to selling proprietary funds
A sales contest rewarding reps for selling a specific fund within one quarter
Differences in fees between share classes
e: Reg BI requires firms to eliminate sales contests, quotas, bonuses and non-cash compensation tied to specific securities within a limited time. Other conflicts may be disclosed and mitigated.
k: Reg BI: eliminate time-limited sales contests and quotas tied to specific securities; disclose and mitigate other conflicts.
w: Commissions are allowed if disclosed; Reg BI doesn't ban them.
Proprietary-only menus must be disclosed and mitigated, not eliminated.
Fee differences must be disclosed and considered, not eliminated.
m: Specific-product sales contests must go.

q: A registered rep's spouse wants to open an account at a different broker-dealer to trade individual stocks. Under FINRA Rule 3210, which is required?
o: Nothing, because the account is in the spouse's name
Prior written consent from the executing firm's CEO
Approval from FINRA's Department of Enforcement
Prior written consent from the rep's employing firm
e: Rule 3210 covers accounts in which the rep has a beneficial interest, including a spouse's account. The employer must give prior written consent and may ask for duplicate confirmations and statements.
k: Outside accounts (Rule 3210): employer's prior written consent; covers spouse and dependent accounts; funds-only accounts exempt.
w: A spouse's account counts as a beneficial interest of the rep.
Consent comes from the employer; the executing firm is only notified.
FINRA doesn't approve individual outside accounts.
m: Spouse's account counts as yours.

q: In February, a rep gives a $180 gift to a customer's purchasing manager. In June, the rep takes the manager to a $400 dinner and attends. Under FINRA Rule 3220, what is the most the rep can spend on another business gift to that person this year?
e: The limit is $300 per person per year. Business entertainment the giver attends doesn't count, so only the $180 gift counts against the limit, leaving $120.
k: Gift limit = $300 per person per year; entertainment the giver attends doesn't count.
w: The attended dinner is entertainment and doesn't use up the limit.
Subtract only the $180 gift from the $300 limit, which leaves $120.
The $180 gift already counts toward the $300 limit.
m: Remaining gift = $300 - gifts already given.
steps: Dinner attended by rep = entertainment, excluded

q:
If the firm's written procedures permit it, a registered rep may borrow money from which of these customers?
I. Her mother
II. A bank in the business of lending
III. A customer she knows only through his brokerage account
IV. A registered person at her own firm
e: Allowed lenders include immediate family, lending institutions, registered persons at the same firm, and people with a personal or business relationship outside the brokerage account. A purely brokerage relationship is not enough.
k: Rule 3240 lenders: immediate family, lending institutions, same-firm registered persons, outside personal/business relationships.
w: IV, a registered person at the same firm, is also allowed.
III is not allowed because the relationship is only through the brokerage account.
III has no relationship outside the brokerage account.
m: No outside relationship, no loan.

q: Which record must a broker-dealer keep for the life of the firm?
e: Organizational documents such as articles of incorporation, minute books and stock certificate books are kept for the life of the firm.
k: Permanent records: articles of incorporation/partnership, minute books, stock certificate books.
w: Blotters are kept for 6 years.
Order tickets are kept for 3 years.
Complaints are kept for 4 years.
m: Organizational records = forever.

q: A customer closes her account in June 2026. Under the record retention rules, the firm must keep her new account form until at least:
e: Customer account records must be kept for 6 years after the account is closed. June 2026 plus 6 years is June 2032.
k: Customer account records: 6 years after the account closes.
w: 3 years is the period for confirmations and order tickets.
4 years is the period for complaints.
5 years is the period for AML/CIP and do-not-call records.
m: Account records: 6 years after closing.
steps: Retention = 6 years after the account closes

q:
Which of the following records must be preserved for three years?
I. Order tickets
II. Blotters
III. Trade confirmations
IV. Customer complaints
e: Order tickets and trade confirmations are kept for 3 years. Blotters are kept for 6 years and complaints for 4.
k: 3 years: order tickets, confirms, communications; 4 years: complaints; 6 years: blotters and ledgers.
w: Blotters are 6-year records and complaints are 4-year records.
Blotters (II) are kept for 6 years.
Blotters are 6 years and complaints 4 years.
m: Most day-to-day records = 3 years.

q: XYZ announces a rights offering in which 5 rights plus $28 buy one new share. A customer owns 2,000 shares and exercises all of her rights. How many new shares does she get, and what does she pay?
e: She receives one right per share (2,000 rights). At 5 rights per new share she can buy 400 shares, paying the $28 subscription price on each: $11,200.
k: Rights = shares owned; new shares = rights ÷ rights needed per share; cost = new shares × subscription price
w: Treats each right as buying a full share; 5 rights are needed per share
Multiplies by 5 instead of dividing by 5
Right share count, but cost uses 2,000 shares instead of 400
m: One right per old share; divide by rights needed.

q: A customer sells 300 shares of a stock in a regular-way trade on the stock's ex-dividend date. Who is entitled to the dividend that was previously declared?
o: The seller, because the buyer purchased on the ex-dividend date
The buyer, because the buyer will own the shares on the payable date
The buyer and seller split it based on days held
Neither; the dividend goes back to the issuer
e: With T+1 settlement the ex-date equals the record date, so a trade on the ex-date settles after the record date. The seller is still the holder of record and keeps the dividend.
k: Buy before the ex-date to get the dividend; sell on or after the ex-date and you keep it
w: Ownership on the payable date doesn't matter; the record date controls
Dividends are not prorated between buyer and seller
The dividend is paid to the holder of record, the seller
m: On or after ex-date: the seller gets the dividend.

q: A company's balance sheet shows current assets of $6 million (including $1.5 million of inventory), current liabilities of $2.5 million and long-term debt of $4 million. What are its working capital and current ratio?
e: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities = $6M − $2.5M = $3.5M. Current ratio = $6M ÷ $2.5M = 2.4. Inventory is subtracted only for the quick ratio, and long-term debt is not a current liability.
k: Working capital = CA − CL; current ratio = CA ÷ CL
w: 1.8 is the quick ratio, which excludes inventory
Subtracts inventory from working capital; inventory is a current asset
Applies the quick-ratio inventory exclusion to both measures
m: Only the quick ratio removes inventory.

q: A customer is short 500 shares of ABC in her margin account when ABC pays a cash dividend of $0.40 per share. Which statement is TRUE?
o: She receives $200 because she sold the shares
No one is owed the dividend because the shares were borrowed
The broker-dealer pays the $200 to the lender on her behalf at its own cost
She must pay $200 to the lender of the borrowed shares
e: A short seller borrowed the shares, so she must pay the lender any dividends declared while the position is open: 500 × $0.40 = $200 is charged to her account.
k: Short sellers owe dividends to the lender of the borrowed shares
w: The buyer of her shares gets the issuer's dividend; she owes, not receives
The lender is still entitled to the dividend and the short seller must pay it
The cost falls on the short seller, not the firm
m: Short = you pay the dividend.

q: A corporation uses excess cash to buy back 10% of its outstanding shares in the open market. Assuming net income is unchanged, which result is MOST likely?
o: Earnings per share falls because the company has less cash
Earnings per share rises because fewer shares are outstanding
The repurchased shares continue to vote and receive dividends
The number of issued shares falls by 10%
e: Repurchased shares become treasury stock, which reduces shares outstanding. The same net income spread over fewer shares produces higher EPS.
k: Buyback → treasury stock → fewer outstanding shares → higher EPS
w: With net income unchanged, fewer shares means higher, not lower, EPS
Treasury stock has no vote and receives no dividends
Treasury shares are still issued; only outstanding shares fall
m: Outstanding = issued − treasury.

q: A corporation has several preferred issues outstanding. Which one would MOST likely carry the highest stated dividend rate?
e: Features that favor the investor (cumulative, convertible, participating, non-callable) let the issuer pay less. A non-cumulative, callable issue gives the investor the least, so it must pay the most.
k: Investor-friendly features lower the dividend; issuer-friendly features (callable, non-cumulative) raise it
w: Two investor-friendly features; this pays a lower dividend
Two investor-friendly features; this pays a lower dividend
Cumulative and call-protected; investors accept a lower rate
m: Who benefits? If issuer, the dividend is higher.

q: A $50-par, 6% preferred stock was issued when comparable yields were 6%. If comparable yields fall to 5%, the preferred's market price will move toward approximately:
e: The annual dividend is 6% × $50 = $3. To yield 5%, the price must rise to $3 ÷ 0.05 = $60. Preferred prices move inversely to interest rates.
k: Approximate price = annual dividend ÷ market yield
w: Price does not stay at par when market yields change
Uses $100 par instead of the stated $50 par
Price falls only if yields rise; here they fell
m: Rates down, preferred price up.

q: A 6% corporate bond with 10 years to maturity is trading at 90. Using the approximate yield-to-maturity formula, its YTM is closest to:
e: Annual interest is $60 and the $100 discount accretes about $10 per year. Divide $70 by the average of par and price ($950): about 7.37%. As a discount bond, YTM exceeds both the coupon and the 6.67% current yield.
k: YTM ≈ [interest + (par − price) ÷ years] ÷ [(par + price) ÷ 2]
w: That is the nominal (coupon) yield, which ignores price
That is the current yield ($60 ÷ $900), ignoring the discount gain
Divides by the price ($900) instead of the average of par and price
m: Discount bond: nominal < CY < YTM.

q: A school district's $40 million bond issue has roughly equal portions maturing each year for 20 years, and dealers quote each maturity on a yield basis. This issue is a:
e: A serial issue has portions maturing in successive years, which is common for municipals, and serial bonds are quoted on yield (basis).
k: Serial = maturities each year, quoted on yield; term = one maturity date, quoted on price
w: A term issue matures all at once and is quoted on price
A balloon issue has a large final maturity, not equal portions
A bullet is a portfolio maturing around one date
m: Serial = series of maturities.

q: A customer puts half of her bond money in 1- and 2-year notes and the other half in 25- and 30-year bonds, with nothing in between. This approach is a:
e: A barbell concentrates holdings at the short and long ends of the maturity range, with little or nothing in the middle.
k: Barbell = short + long ends; ladder = staggered maturities; bullet = one maturity date
w: A bullet clusters maturities around a single date
A ladder spreads money evenly across staggered maturities
A sinking fund is an issuer's provision to retire its debt
m: Picture the weights on both ends.

q: Interest rates have been falling. Which bondholder faces the GREATEST reinvestment risk?
o: Holder of a high-coupon callable corporate bond trading at a premium
Holder of a low-coupon non-callable bond trading at a discount
Holder of a 5-year puttable bond with a low coupon
e: Large coupons must be reinvested at the new lower rates, and a callable bond is likely to be called when rates fall, returning principal that must also be reinvested at lower rates.
k: Reinvestment risk is highest for high-coupon callable bonds; zero-coupon bonds have none
w: STRIPS are zero-coupon and have no coupons to reinvest
Small coupons and no call feature mean little reinvestment exposure
Low coupons; the put is used when rates rise, not fall
m: Zeros have no reinvestment risk.

q: Which money-market instrument typically pays interest at maturity rather than being sold at a discount from face value?
e: Negotiable CDs are bank time deposits of $100,000 or more that pay stated interest at maturity. Commercial paper, banker's acceptances and T-bills are sold at a discount and mature at face value.
k: Negotiable CDs pay interest at maturity; CP, BAs and T-bills are discount instruments
w: Sold at a discount; the discount is the investor's return
Traded at a discount to face value
Sold at a discount and quoted on a discount yield

q: A US investor who spends and saves only in dollars buys each of the following. Which one exposes her to currency risk?
o: A Yankee bond issued in the US by a Japanese company
A Eurodollar bond issued in London by a US company
A yen-denominated Eurobond sold in London
e: A bond denominated in a foreign currency pays interest and principal in that currency, so a dollar-based investor bears exchange-rate risk. Yankee and Eurodollar bonds are both denominated in US dollars.
k: Currency risk depends on the bond's currency, not where it is issued
w: Yankee bonds are dollar-denominated, so no currency risk
Eurodollar bonds pay in US dollars despite being issued abroad
Treasuries pay in dollars and carry no currency risk
m: Ask what currency pays you.

q: A customer holds a $200,000 CD in her individual name and a $200,000 CD in her IRA at the same FDIC-insured bank. She has no other deposits there. How much of her money is NOT FDIC-insured?
e: FDIC coverage is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Individual accounts and IRAs are separate categories, so each $200,000 CD is fully covered.
k: FDIC: $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category
w: Wrongly combines both categories ($400,000 − $250,000)
Assumes the IRA CD has no FDIC coverage
No single category exceeds $250,000, so nothing is uninsured
m: Separate ownership categories get separate $250,000 limits.

q: A municipal bond yields 3.5% and a corporate bond of similar quality and maturity yields 5.0%. For which investor would the municipal bond provide the higher after-tax yield?
e: The muni beats the corporate only when its tax-equivalent yield exceeds 5.0%. At 32%, 3.5% ÷ 0.68 ≈ 5.15%. At 24%, 3.5% ÷ 0.76 ≈ 4.61%, which is too low.
k: TEY = muni yield ÷ (1 − tax bracket)
w: TEY ≈ 3.98%, well below the 5.0% corporate
TEY ≈ 4.49%, below the 5.0% corporate
TEY ≈ 4.61%, still below the 5.0% corporate
m: Higher bracket, more valuable muni.

q: A town installs new sidewalks and sewer lines in one neighborhood and issues bonds repaid only by charges levied on the properties that benefit from the improvements. These are:
e: Special assessment bonds are repaid from assessments on the specific properties that benefit from the improvement, not from general taxes.
k: Special assessment bonds = paid by assessments on benefiting properties
w: Special tax bonds are backed by a specific tax, such as a gas or hotel tax
G.O. bonds pledge the town's full taxing power
Lease-rental bonds are paid from a government user's lease payments
m: Assessment = only the benefiting properties pay.

q: A state housing agency borrows short-term to fund construction of an apartment project. The notes will be repaid from permanent mortgage financing once the project is completed. These notes are:
e: Construction loan notes provide interim financing for housing projects and are repaid when permanent financing is put in place after construction.
k: CLNs = interim housing construction financing repaid from permanent financing
w: BANs are repaid from a planned long-term bond issue
RANs are repaid from future non-tax revenue such as state aid
GANs are repaid from expected federal or state grants

q: A small city with an A rating buys bond insurance on its new revenue issue from an insurer rated AA. The insured bonds will generally carry:
o: The city's own A rating, since insurance does not affect ratings
No rating, since insured munis need not be rated
e: Municipal bond insurance guarantees principal and interest, so insured bonds carry the insurer's credit rating.
k: Insured munis carry the insurer's rating
w: Insurance replaces the issuer's credit with the insurer's
The rating matches the insurer's rating, not an automatic AAA
Insured bonds are rated, at the insurer's rating

q: A customer wants a direct obligation of the US Treasury that pays semiannual interest and matures in about 7 years. She should buy a:
e: Treasury notes mature in 2 to 10 years (including a 7-year note) and pay interest semiannually.
k: T-bills ≤ 1 yr (discount); T-notes 2–10 yrs; T-bonds 20–30 yrs
w: T-bills mature within one year and pay no coupon
T-bonds are issued with 20- to 30-year maturities
STRIPS are zero-coupon and pay no semiannual interest
m: Notes are the 2–10 year range.

q: Which CMO tranche receives no current interest or principal while earlier tranches are being paid, with its interest instead added to its balance like a zero-coupon bond?
e: A Z-tranche (accrual tranche) accrues interest instead of paying it until earlier tranches are retired, so it behaves like a zero-coupon bond.
k: Z-tranche accrues like a zero; PAC has the most predictable cash flow
w: PACs receive scheduled payments and have the most predictable cash flow
Companion tranches receive payments and absorb prepayment variability
The first sequential tranche receives principal first, not last
m: Z = zero-coupon-like.

q: The Federal Reserve raises the rate it pays banks on reserve balances held at the Fed. This action is most likely intended to:
o: Push the federal funds rate higher as part of a tighter policy
Encourage banks to lend reserves to each other at lower rates
Add reserves to the banking system to stimulate lending
Lower the discount rate charged at the discount window
e: Banks won't lend reserves overnight for less than the Fed pays them to hold reserves. Raising interest on reserve balances lifts the fed funds rate, which tightens policy.
k: Raise interest on reserves = tighten (fed funds up); lower it = ease
w: Higher pay for holding reserves makes banks demand higher, not lower, rates
Raising the rate does not add reserves; Fed purchases do that
The discount rate is a separate tool and was not lowered
m: Modern main tool for steering fed funds.

q: Which index measures prices at the wholesale level and is often watched as an early signal of consumer inflation?
e: The PPI measures wholesale (producer) prices. Increases in producer costs tend to pass through to consumers, so the PPI tends to lead the CPI.
k: PPI = wholesale prices, tends to lead CPI; CPI = consumer prices, main inflation measure
w: CPI measures retail consumer prices and is a lagging indicator
GDP measures total output, not price levels
M2 measures money supply, not prices
m: Producer prices come before consumer prices.

q: Which of the following lists these interest rates in their typical order from LOWEST to HIGHEST?
o: Federal funds rate, broker call rate, prime rate
Prime rate, broker call rate, federal funds rate
Broker call rate, federal funds rate, prime rate
Federal funds rate, prime rate, broker call rate
e: Fed funds is the overnight bank-to-bank rate. Broker call is usually slightly above fed funds, and prime (about fed funds + 3%) is the highest of the three.
k: Lowest to highest: fed funds ≈ discount rate < broker call < prime
w: Reverses the order; prime is the highest
Broker call is set slightly above fed funds, not below
Prime is above the broker call rate
m: Prime is the highest of the group.

q: A presidential candidate argues that cutting tax rates and easing business regulation will spur production and investment, leading to stronger economic growth. This view reflects which economic theory?
e: Supply-side economics holds that lower taxes and lighter regulation encourage production, and growth follows.
k: Supply-side = cut taxes and regulation; Keynesian = government spending; Monetarist = money supply
w: Keynesians stress government spending to boost demand
Monetarists focus on steady growth of the money supply
Contractionary fiscal policy raises taxes or cuts spending

q: A management company has 20% of its assets in one issuer's stock, a position equal to 4% of that issuer's voting shares. Every other holding is under 5% of the fund's assets and under 10% of each issuer's voting stock. Which statement is TRUE?
o: It must be classified as non-diversified because one position exceeds 5% of assets
It can be classified as diversified because the 20% position fits within the unrestricted 25%
It must be classified as non-diversified because any position over 10% of assets is prohibited
It can be classified as diversified only if shareholders vote to approve the 20% position
e: The 75-5-10 test applies only to 75% of assets; the remaining 25% is unrestricted. Since the other 80% meets the 5% and 10% limits, the fund still qualifies as diversified.
k: Diversified (75-5-10): on 75% of assets, ≤5% per issuer and ≤10% of any issuer's voting stock.
w: The 5% limit applies only within the 75% bucket, not to every holding.
There is no 10%-of-assets cap; the 10% limit is on an issuer's voting shares.
Diversification status is a test result, not something shareholders vote to grant position by position.
m: Remember the 25% 'free' bucket in 75-5-10.

q: A customer wants a single fund that invests in both US and foreign companies, leaving the country mix to the portfolio manager. Which type of fund BEST fits?
e: A global fund holds both US and non-US companies. An international fund invests only outside the US.
k: Global = US + foreign; international = non-US only.
w: International funds exclude US companies.
A sector fund concentrates on one industry, not a geographic mix.
Emerging markets funds hold only developing-country issuers, excluding the US.
m: Global includes home; international leaves home.

q: A customer invests $10,000 in a mutual fund with an NAV of $14.10 and a 6% front-end sales charge. How many shares does she receive?
e: POP = $14.10 ÷ 0.94 = $15.00, and $10,000 ÷ $15.00 = 666.667 shares. Mutual funds issue fractional shares.
k: POP = NAV ÷ (1 − sales charge %); shares = dollars invested ÷ POP.
w: Double-counts the load: deducts 6% from the $10,000 and then also buys at POP.
Mutual funds issue fractional shares, so the amount is not rounded down.
Buys at NAV, ignoring the 6% sales charge entirely.
m: Buyers of load funds pay POP; fractional shares are allowed.

q: A customer's account in a fund family is worth $32,000, and her husband's separate account in the same family is worth $14,000. She plans to invest another $6,000. The family's next breakpoint is $50,000. Which is TRUE?
o: Her $6,000 purchase qualifies for the $50,000 breakpoint by combining both spouses' holdings
She does not qualify, because only holdings in her own name count toward breakpoints
She qualifies only if she signed a letter of intent before her earlier purchases
She qualifies, and the lower charge is refunded on all of her earlier purchases
e: Married couples may combine holdings, and rights of accumulation use the current value of family holdings plus the new purchase: $32,000 + $14,000 + $6,000 = $52,000. The reduced charge applies to the new purchase only.
k: ROA: current value of family holdings (spouse included) + new purchase crosses breakpoint → lower charge on new purchase.
w: Spouses' accounts may be combined for breakpoint purposes.
ROA needs no letter of intent; it is based on current account values.
ROA applies to future purchases only; it is not retroactive.
m: ROA is forward-looking; LOI can be backdated 90 days.

q: Which statement BEST describes how a closed-end fund raises its capital?
o: It continuously issues new shares at NAV plus any sales charge
It sells shares privately to accredited investors under Regulation D
It issues units under a trust indenture and redeems them at NAV
It sells a fixed number of shares once in an IPO, after which they trade between investors
e: A closed-end fund raises money once through a prospectus-based IPO. After that, shares trade on exchanges at market prices, and the fund does not redeem them.
k: Closed-end fund: one-time IPO, fixed shares, then secondary-market trading at a premium or discount.
w: That describes an open-end mutual fund's continuous offering.
That describes a hedge fund private placement, not a registered closed-end fund.
That describes a unit investment trust.
m: Prospectus for a closed-end fund: only at the IPO.

q: An index rises 10% on Monday and falls 10% on Tuesday. Ignoring fees, what is the approximate two-day return of an ETF that seeks 2× the index's daily return?
e: The ETF gains 20% Monday and loses 20% Tuesday: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, a 4% loss. Daily leverage resets make multi-day results diverge from 2× the index's −1% return.
k: Leveraged ETFs reset daily; compound each day's leveraged return: (1 + 2r₁)(1 + 2r₂) − 1.
w: Doubles the index's two-day −1%; the daily reset makes the actual loss larger.
Assumes the up and down days cancel; percentage losses on a larger base don't.
That is the index's own two-day return, not the 2× fund's.
m: Leveraged/inverse ETFs: daily objective only, not buy-and-hold.

q: Which of the following statements about portfolio risk measures is NOT correct?
o: Standard deviation measures a fund's total volatility
An R-squared of 100 means the benchmark explains all of a fund's movements
Beta measures the risk that can be eliminated through diversification
A higher Sharpe ratio indicates more return per unit of risk
e: Beta measures systematic (market) risk, which diversification cannot eliminate. The other three statements are accurate.
k: Beta = systematic, non-diversifiable risk; standard deviation = total risk.
w: True: standard deviation captures systematic plus unsystematic volatility.
True: R-squared of 100 means a perfect benchmark tracker.
True: Sharpe = (return − risk-free rate) ÷ standard deviation.
m: NOT question: find the single false statement.

q: A hedge fund wants to accept more than 100 investors without registering as an investment company under the Investment Company Act of 1940. Relying on Section 3(c)(7), it must limit its investors to:
e: Section 3(c)(7) exempts funds whose investors are all qualified purchasers (generally $5 million+ in investments). The 3(c)(1) exemption instead caps a fund at 100 investors.
k: 3(c)(1): ≤ 100 investors; 3(c)(7): qualified purchasers only ($5M+ in investments).
w: Accredited status alone suits a 3(c)(1) fund, which is capped at 100 investors.
QIBs relate to Rule 144A resales, not the 1940 Act fund exemptions.
The 35 non-accredited limit belongs to Reg D Rule 506(b) offerings.

q:
A limited partner in a real estate program may do which of the following without jeopardizing limited liability?
I. Vote on a proposed sale of the partnership's properties
II. Inspect the partnership's books and records
III. Sign leases with new tenants on the partnership's behalf
IV. Sue the general partner for breach of fiduciary duty
e: Limited partners may vote on major matters, inspect the books, and sue the GP. Signing leases is management activity reserved to the general partner and can cost an LP limited liability.
k: LPs: vote on major matters, inspect books, sue GP; managing the business risks limited liability.
w: Leaves out the LP's right to sue the general partner.
Signing leases is management; it also omits the right to vote on asset sales.
Signing leases on the partnership's behalf is management activity reserved for the GP.
m: LPs are passive: voting and oversight yes, day-to-day management no.

q: XYZ is trading at $63. Which of the following options has the GREATEST intrinsic value?
e: The 55 call is 8 points in the money (63 − 55). The 70 put is only 7 in the money; its higher premium includes 2 points of time value.
k: Call intrinsic = stock − strike; put intrinsic = strike − stock; premium = intrinsic + time value.
w: Intrinsic value is only 3 (63 − 60); the rest is time value.
Highest premium, but intrinsic value is 7 (70 − 63); 2 points are time value.
Intrinsic value is only 2 (65 − 63).
m: Don't pick the highest premium; compute stock vs. strike.

q: An investor holds 1 XYZ 15 call. XYZ completes a 1-for-4 reverse stock split. After the OCC adjustment, the investor most likely holds:
e: In a reverse split, shares per contract decrease and the strike increases proportionally. 100 ÷ 4 = 25 shares and $15 × 4 = $60, keeping the aggregate exercise value at $1,500.
k: Reverse split: fewer shares per contract, higher strike; total value (shares × strike) unchanged.
w: Adjusts shares but not the strike, cutting the contract's value to $375.
Raises the strike without cutting shares, quadrupling the value to $6,000.
Applies the split backward, as if it were a 4-for-1 forward split.
m: Check: shares × strike before = shares × strike after.

q: An investor owns 100 shares of LMN bought at $55 and writes 1 LMN 60 call at 2.50. What is the investor's maximum potential loss?
e: If LMN goes to zero, the investor loses the $55 cost but keeps the $2.50 premium: ($55 − $2.50) × 100 = $5,250.
k: Covered call max loss = (stock cost − premium) × 100.
w: That is the maximum gain: (60 − 55) + 2.50 = 7.50 × 100.
Ignores the premium received, which cushions the loss.
Unlimited loss applies to a naked call; owning the stock covers the call.
m: Covered call breakeven and max loss both use cost − premium.
steps: Stock falls to $0: loss on stock = $55

q: Two weeks before expiration, a customer holds a European-style S&P 500 index call that is well in the money. She wants to capture its value now. She can:
o: Sell the call in a closing sale, since she cannot exercise before expiration
Exercise the call today and receive the cash settlement the next business day
Exercise the call today and receive the stocks in the index
Ask the OCC to settle the contract early at its intrinsic value
e: European-style options can be exercised only at expiration, but they can be sold in the market at any time. A closing sale captures both intrinsic and remaining time value.
k: European style = exercise only at expiration; holder can still close the position anytime by selling.
w: Early exercise is American style; most broad-based index options are European.
Index options are cash settled; no stocks are delivered.
The OCC doesn't settle contracts early on request; only exercise at expiration or a closing trade.
m: Closing sale is how most option buyers take profits.

q: An investor buys shares of a US corporation 20 days before the ex-dividend date, collects the quarterly dividend, and sells the shares 15 days after the ex-date. How is the dividend taxed?
o: At long-term capital gains rates, because it was paid by a US corporation
As a short-term capital gain, because the stock was held for one year or less
As ordinary income, because the holding period requirement was not met
It is not taxed, because the stock was sold before the payable date
e: Qualified dividend treatment requires holding the stock more than 60 days around the ex-dividend date. A 35-day holding period fails, so the dividend is non-qualified and taxed as ordinary income.
k: Qualified dividends: US corporation + held more than 60 days around the ex-date → 0/15/20% rates.
w: Being a US corporation is not enough; the 60-day holding test also applies.
Dividends are dividend income, not capital gains; the one-year test is for sales.
The owner on the record date receives and is taxed on the dividend.
m: Short holding around ex-date → ordinary dividend rates.

q:
A New York resident wants interest that is exempt from both federal and New York State income tax. Which of the following bonds would provide it?
I. A New York City general obligation bond
II. A Puerto Rico general obligation bond
III. A US Treasury note
IV. An Ohio general obligation bond
e: In-state munis and US territory bonds are exempt from both federal and state tax. Treasury interest is federally taxable, and Ohio bond interest is taxable by New York.
k: Double tax-free: in-state munis and territory bonds (Puerto Rico, Guam, USVI) for any state's residents.
w: Treasury interest is state-exempt but fully taxable federally.
Treasury interest is federally taxable; this also omits the in-state NYC bond.
Includes the Treasury note, which is taxable at the federal level.
m: Treasuries: federal yes, state no. Territories: tax-free everywhere.

q: An investor bought 100 shares of a REIT at $25. Over several years she received $3 per share of return-of-capital distributions. She now sells the shares at $30. What is her capital gain?
e: Return of capital isn't taxed when received; it reduces cost basis to $22. Selling at $30 produces an $8 gain per share, or $800.
k: Return of capital reduces cost basis; gain = sale price − (cost − ROC).
w: Subtracts the ROC from proceeds instead of from basis.
Treats only the ROC amount as the gain.
Ignores the basis reduction from return-of-capital distributions.
m: ROC: no tax now, bigger gain later.
